PLIGHTED. ' Before great God the rather of us both That makes the love that rises in us two, I swear that henceforth I am true to you By that which binds men more than any oath 3 And freely I come to you, and not loth To lose this aimlessness in what I do, This wild life—wandering without end or view, This gainless haste or most unseemly sloth. And you—Love is not Love that spends his cry With piteous plain for entrance at the heart- -Bose up with new waked wonder in your eye For all your power, ne'er brought to public mart, Stretched out your arms and took him tlnderly, And henceforth from the world we walked apart! " JOHN CAMERON GRANT.

ASTREA. REDUX. Stanzas some way after Dryden. 1 ON THE HIPPY RESTORATION TO PUBLIC LITE OF HER MOST GRACIOUS MAJESTY QUEEN VICTORIA. lIVERPOOL, MAY 11TH, 1886. low, whilst with general strife the world is vexed, And England with divisions sore perplexed, 1, A welcome lull here intermits the war, And parting clouds show the returning Star. Astrwa, r. Saturnian times no more Make gay our wealthy or make glad our poor ; Praise -ot our Golden Age no more resounds, Nor jubilation at Trade's leaps and bounds. ' The leaden incubus, Depression, still Our power oppresties, and obscures our skill. Rise, Star of Hope! Our freer days refuse The flatteries of the Dedicatory Muse, Which marred the manhood e'en of Glorious John. Yet, welcome! Now Astryea shines upon Her people once again, may hope not deem There Is some quickening influence in:the beam? London in yon vast hall'has seen that ray, It is the turn of Liverpool to-day. The Star of India and the lesset lights Of southern skies or western, jewel-flights Of unreluctant satellites, attend Your rising, and with loyal homage bend ' As in young Joseph's dream, bend unconstrained. So round some central orb swift planets, reined! But by attraction, circle happily. England, and all her sons from every sea! A glorious constellation! On this day Glad with the verdant pomp of pleasant May ' (A month which owns an interest in your name, You and its flowers combine to give it fame), It shines anew. For ever be it bright. May Fate's black shadow ne'er eclipse its light. May sullen clouds that now o'ercast our sky, Chased by the rising dawn of fortune fly; Our Empire, with united interest blest, In newer and mutual love find prosperous rest'; At home the hateful feuds of Party cease. The Star of Honour is the Star of Peace,, The true Astrtea for whose late return All wise souls watch, all patriot spirits burn. —Punch.

"I think," said a farmer, "I should make a good legis- lator, for I use their language. I received two bills the other day, with requests for immediate payment; the one I ordered to be laid on the table—the other to be read that day six months." "Hiyiydo you contrive to amuse yourself ?" Amuse !" said the other starting. "Do you know I have my house- hold work to do?" "Yes," was the answer, "I see you have it to do; but as it is never done, I concluded you must have some other way of passing your time!, An American tourist was visiting Naples, and saw Vesuvius during an eruption. "Have you anything like that in the New World ?" was the question of an Italian spectator. "No," replied Jonathan; "but I guess we have a mill dam that would put it out in five minutes." "I hope, my dear," said Mrs. Wise, who very properly dislikes owing money, "that you paid Mr. Friend the sovereign he lent you last week." "Of course I did," replied her husband; "I always pay my debts promptly. I borrowed five pounds of him yesterday, and gave him back one." Loma Baotremet Ocewerren.—The anecdotes of "hair- breadth escapes" of some of the gallant sportsmen, and of other incidents connected with the Epping Hunt, as laay be supposed,are "plentiful as blackberries" among the older inhabitants of these parts. Among anecdotes of another kind, the following is perhaps worth record- ing :—Lord Brougham, when staying in the neighbour- hood. went on one occasion to witness the hunt, about wk:ch he was "very facetious," and asked many ques- tions. He said to a man, "I suppose you are waiting for The Lord Mayor and:Aldermen ? If you will show me them when they arrive, I will give you a crown." The man said, "I do not think I should know them for cer- tain; but if you will give me half-a-crown, I will show you Lord Brougham alive." This so disconcerted his lordship, that he went home immediately.—Cassell's Greater London. Lrrsaartree TO PLEASE.—Cooki, warriors, and authors must be judged by the effects they produce; toothsome dishes. glorious victories, pleasant books—these are our demands. We have nothing to do with ingredients, tactics, or methods. We have no desire to be admitted into the kitchen, the council, or the study. The cook may clean her saucepans how she pleases, the warrior place his men as he likes, the author handle his material or weave his plot as best he can—when the dish is served we only ask, is it good? When the battle has been fought, who won? When the book comes out, does it read? Authors ought not to be above being reminded that it is their first duty to write agreeably—some very. 4lisagreeable men have succeeded in doing it, so there is no need for any one to despair. Every author, be he grave or gay, shouki try to make his book as ingratiating as possible. Rasiling is not a duty, and has therefore no business to b. -made disagreeable. Nobody is under any ligation tr read any other man's book. Literature exists to please; to lighten the burden of men's lives; to make them for a short while forget their sorrows and their sins, their silenced hearths, their disappointed hopes, their grim futures—and those men of letters are the best loved who have best performed literature's truest office.—Manaillan's Magazine. NEURALOTA.—One of the best remedies for neuralgia is Offline. In all cases in which there is any suspicion of ague, or when the patient is residing in a district where ague is prevalent, this is the remedy to give. It is in- dicated, too, when the attacks come on at regular inter- vals. It has long been recognised that quinine readily controls that form of neuralgia in which:the pain is ex- perienced at a spot just above one or other of the eye- brows. Qt mine, to do any good in neuralgia, must be taken in fairly large doses—thus two tablespoonfuls of strong quinine mixture should be taken every four hours. &lone chemists now keep five-grain quinine pills, made ap with a drop or two of syrup; and, by many, these will be preferred to the mixture; one should be taken every four hours. Quinine is said to control neuralgia and ordinary faceache more effectively when the powder is taken in small quantities every few minutes—as much, far instance, as will adhere to the tip of the finger slipped into the powder. We need hardly point out the importance of getting your quinine pure. The three great indications for the use of quinine are—(l) suspicion of agile; (2) paroxysms being periodical; (3) pain being experienced chiefly over eyebrow. In very obstinate cases of neuralgia, which have resisted all other treat- ment, the Germans often give what we should consider enormous doses of quinine—from forty grains to two drachms a day.—The Family Physician. GERMAN POETRY.—Dr. Strauss commencedghis new course of lectures on German literature on Wednesday, in the Yorkshire College. The subject for this term is Leman, one of the foremost lyrical poets of the century. Introductorily, the Lecturer observed that every litera- ture, especially the lyrical, bore the stamp of its time. In the Middle Ages poetry was chivalrous, its " minne" er "love sang" played a great part. The two centuries of Reformation (1517-1750) produced religious lyrics. Whilst the end of the last century, being influenced by the tendencies of the great French Revolution, gave birth to the poets of toleration, of freedom in religion and State, and of the dignity of man. Lessing, Schiller, atori partly Goethe, were the representatives of these ideas. In the beginning of our century, with the poli- tical reaction against constitutional government, the so- Jealled Romanticists arose—men who introduced the IsediTyal spirit into poetry and art. Against reason 4hey set imagination, as did Schlegel, Tieck, Fouqus, and ethers. To no particular school, however, belonged men such as Heine and Lenau. They occupied separate posi- tions in the history of German literature. Both con- tinued to write on behalf of the free development of political life. But they were both great lyrical poets, • and quite unique as the representatives of the so-called ▪ Weltschmerz," a word difficult to render in English. Byron suffered of this " Weltsehmerz," which was a kind .of melancholy dissatisfaction with the state of the world in generaL In all three—in Byron, Heine, and Lenau—besides their peculiar natural predispositions we found unhappy love the outward promoter of their melancholy. Referring to Lenau, the Lecturer said that his father (a Hungarian officer) was a most careless hus- band and parent, and died in consequence of his dissipa- tion. The mother, who was of humble birth, was too fond of her son Nikolaus, and spoiled him. Lenau never succeeded in learning a proper profession; he was a student for the greater part of his life, but lie gave us a -good many beautiful poems, which had become universal Property. The power of his imagination made him a lyrical poet of the first rank. He sung because he felt. song within him, whilst the acuteness of his intellect in- dined towards criticism and scepticism. The latter was nurtured by a sceptic uncle. So far he had another great - similarity with Heine, but he somewhat lacked the cynicism of the latter. Lenau, whose proper name was NAkolaus Franz Nimbsch Edler von Strehlenau, was born in 1802, and died in 1850. His mind was so over Whelmed by melancholy that he lost his reason six :years before as encl. The lectures will be continued during the pre- sent term.

"LITTLE VENICE " IN SocraTt AMERlCA.—Venezuela is entirely tropical, and is misnamed. It has nothing at all of Venice about it, and even if it had, is not "Little Venice," as its name signifies, for a region full of piled-up mountains as great as the Alps, containing forests larger than France, steppes as great as those of Gobi, and an area altogether four times that of Prussia, can have little in common with the picturesque city on the Adriatic. But, like many other designations, that of Venezuela originated in a mistake. The conquistadores, when they first visited it, found the Indians of the shallow " Lake " of Maracaibo living in "lake dwellings "—huts built on poles in the water. This suggested a likeness to Venice, and hence the name and the misnomer.—Countries of the

_ THE KING'S COIN; OR GOD'S FRAcrroN.—This is the title 'selected by Mr. Bass for his little work (published by James Nisbet and Co.) on the duty of giving to chari- table and religious purposes a fixed proportion of our income. Most give less than they suppose, like the man who, with an income of £2OO per annum, thought he ' contributed a tenth yet, on reckoning, found all his giv- ing amounting to but £4- 9s. 7id. The Jews not only gave one-tenth, which was devoted to the support of the Levites, but also another which was held in trust by the priests for the good of the people and the service of the sanctuary. They had also to furnish trespass offerings, and leave for the poor-and needy the gleanings of their fields and vineyards. In addition, there were free-will offerings which were given upon exhortation. The three principal occasions of these were the construction of the tabernacle building of the temple, and its restoration after the Babylonian bondage. They were, besides, often subject to an oppressive taxation. In the days of Nehemiah this was so burdensome that many were com- pelled to sell their property to pay the tribute to the King; of Persia. Dr. R. Payne Smith, who writes an introduc- tion to Mr. Bass's work, says that " if the Church of Eng- land is disendowed it will be a Nemesis upon it for liv- ing upon the piety of the past, and neglecting the prac- tice of this piety in the present." The principal chapters are—" What fraction?" "Its variableness," "When to offer it," "Its advantages," and "Objections met." A list is given of Old and New Testament passages referring to such duties. A sufficiently minute and helpful table of contents, or rather conspectus, is added. The author having reviewed the Patriarchal, Jewish, and Christian dispensation, finds no instance teaching us to contribute less than a tenth. In every New Testament instance more than a tenth was given. A proper motive is neces- sary. A laird in Fife became rich, but continued to give only his usual weekly penny. One day he dropped by mistake a five-shilling piece into the plate. On discover- ing what he had done, he hurried back to replace it by his penny. But the elder in attendance cried out, " Stop, laird; ye may put in what ye like, but ye maun tak naething out !" The laird finding it useless to explain, at last said, " Aweel, I suppose I'll get credit for it in heaven." "Na, na, Laird," said the elder, " ye'll only get credit for the penny." _ .

, THE SCOTCH FlR.—Accustomed as we are to the short, much-branched stems of our deciduous, or hardwood trees, the Pine is to us the very type Of lofty upright- ness. Its straight stem, seldom exceeding twelve feet in girth, attains a height of from fifty to a hundred feet or more; but most of us who remember such from our earliest years will echo Hood's reminiscence of their im- pressive grandeur : I remember, I rememberl ; The fir-trees dark and high; • • I used to think their slender tope • rfunlsi Were close against the sky. , , llt was a childish ignorance; .• But now 'tis little joy , To know I'm farther oft from heaven; Than when I was 4 boy. One of the great beauties of the tree is its rough, reddish bark, made up of flaky scales, and deeply ridged down the stem, givinc, it a curiously mottled effect. The branches are not usually large in proportion to the trunk, but they are given off numerously in whorls, so that, when the trees are grown close together, the lower boughs die off, and, as Shakspere says : Knots, by the conflux of meeting sap, Infect the sound Pine, and divert his grain, 7 Tortive and errant from his course of growth. The leaves, or "needles," are given off in pairs from the axil of a fringed membranous sheath. The number of needles thus grouped together on what is termed a "dwarf shoot," is one of the distinctive characters of the sub-divisions of the genus Pima. The needles of the Scotch Fir do not exceed two or three inches in length, although in allied species they are sometimes as much as a foot long; they are grooved along their upper surface, curved and often twisted, and finely toothed throughout their length; and they remain on the trees for two or three years. The arrangement ofahe resin-passages and other constant features in the microscopic character of the interior of the leaf, seen in a cross-section, have been used as a means of discriminating the species of the genus. It is the remarkable dark indigo-tinted colour of the needles that lends to the tree the air of gloom with which it is generally associated, an effect which is heightened by the brown needle-carpeted ground beneath, silent and bare, since, owing to the absence of light, scarcely anything will grow. At a slight distance the young leaves produce quite the impression of a bluish haze, which no doubt led the laureate to associate the " thick mysterious boughs" of the Pine with "many a cloudy hollow."—Cassell's Familiar Irees. THE MIGRATION OF TUE GEESE.—The wild geese, whose large V-shaped flocks continue to pass over Connecticut daily and nightly, heading for the frozen shores of Labrador and Baffin's Bay, are adding their lofty testi- mony to the multiplying proofs of the great fact that at Northernisweoinntteinreinstagohneit TswheeeTsghfrtoomf the e Claasntatdhie long nnlowildgoose bayous and sounds of the far South to the desolate shores of the icy Arctic seas. These large birds of the black head, neck, and feet, whose wild gurgling cries, corning down confusedly from the upper air, seem to mix and blend with the wind and the cloud in which they move, are on their way perhaps from the Everglades of Southern Florida; nor will they make much delay till they reach the far northern wastes where they breed. It would seem that their winters are passed in brighter and pleasanter weather than their. summers. but the north is their true habitat. There they rear their broods, and there they probably best enjoy life, for there they spend at least seven of the year's twelve months on shores too chill and grim for human kind, albeit there the ice will melt and there the sun shine for awhile all flight. Just at present they must find it an inhospitable region. From the northern shores of the Gulf of St. Lawrence on northward indefinitely the rocks are still deep in snow and ice, and the weather is cold. But in the north great changes are effected rapidly as the sun mounts higher. Even in Lake Champlain the ice is said to be isntilslotmewo ootrhtherreneorfrhet northern vyhicka,tbersut inthtehaicte7wrihoeuns it goes, eass, disappears suddenly. It may show at sunset a lake sur- face e of mniolest a it f iceohnmoileso is f solid-looking be n oksieneg e—Bnandietehoor nnexot mornice, it is all one to the wild geese. They are sure of their own pastures and still waters—albeit the former may not be green nor the latter very still; but the grim rocks in the chill seas along Upper Labrador, Baffin's Bay, and Smith's Sound are the places that they are after. May it also be that they go still further and find a milder clime surrounding the earth's northern pole ? The Hartford Times, April 13th.

NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, ETORTIO 4 fiI7LTURE. •Scctr, t A A consignment of fifty-seven black-polled cattle from the farm of Corksie (Mr. Hannay) has left for Glasgow sa route for America. Mr. Duthie, Collynie, Aberdeenshire, has sold a hand- some red yearling Shorthorn bull, at a high price, to Mr. Goodbrand, Culnaha, Ross-shire. A large landowner in Cheshire has discharged all his gamekeepers, and has given permission to his tenants to kill any game that may be seen on their farms. The tenants, who are much pleased, have assured their land- lord that they will take care that he is never without sport NORTH LANCASHIRE NarEs.—Oat and barley sowing are completed, and the plants are mostly showing above ground, in some cases ten days after the seeding. Man- golds and potatoes are mostly in, and swede seeding is progressing, in a nice bed. The cuckoo and corncrake are with us, but although grass is growing, there is not yet sufficient in the meadows to hide the latter bird. To SALT &Term—Rather more than one ounce of salt to the pound avoirdupois is required when the butter is intended to be kept for some months. The whole of the buttermilk should be extracted from the butter, and the salt thoroughly incorporated with the latter. There is no necessity to use saltpetre. The butter may be stored away in crocks or pans, and if there is not enough to fill the vessel, that ;made in the succeed- ing week can be placed on the top, and so on, until the pan is full. Care must be taken to keep all dust and insects from getting into the butter, and it should be stored in a cool place. HOME-MADE CHEESE.—I strain the milk as soon as it is brought in, and put one teacupful of good, strong rennet to one hundred pounds of milk, stirring while putting the rennet in. After letting it stand half an hour, or until the curd is well set, cut it several times each way, which starts the whey. Then let it stand ten minutes, after which dip it out carefully with a dipper into a thin cloth strainer. For convenience, I make the strainer in the form of a bag, having it just large enough to go over the four corners of a rack, which fits over a large tub. The tub that I use is a half-barrel, which I keep especially for the purpose. Let the whey all drain off, and help it to do this by tying up the strainer occasionally, and also by putting on a weight. When the whey is all drained off, cut the curd into small pieces, and pour hot, not boiling, water over it, stirring gently all the time to prevent scalding some pieces too much. Let it stand twenty minutes, drain off the water, salt it, and it is ready for the press. I use a half teacupful of salt for the curd from one hundred pounds of milk; a little more or less salt could be used to suit the maker's taste. If the cheese is put in the press in the morning, leave it until night; then take it out, rinse the strainer in cold water, turn the cheese, return to press, and leave until morning, when it is ready for the curing- room.—W. H. S. HAYMAKING IN THE NORTlL—Although we hear a great deal of hay being spoilt in the making owing to bad weather, and consequent necessity for ensilage as a substitute for hay, yet strangely enough, in all discussions as to how to make hay, we find that the one vital point to which all speakers ultimately tend is, how to make hay with the minimum of trouble. Certainly this is a very desir- able end to be kept in view; but, on the other hand, how often is it in the ordinary affairs of life that we find the limit of cheapness combined with the highest efficiency? When the ensilage movement set in it was argued that it would be found most useful in those Northern Coun- ties of England where the rainfall was the greatest, and where it would have been thought, the greatest i diffi- culty would be found to exist n making good lay. What has been the result? Why, that the tenant far- mers who have adopted silos in those counties may be counted on the fingers of the hand. The reason for this non-adoption of silos is that in these counties the sys- tem of haymaking is such that spoilt hay is of very un- usual occurrence, despite the excessive rainfall. In these counties labour is of secondary consideration, simply because the men employed are engaged by the half-year, and extra work in the hay harvest does not entail so much extra expense as in case of day labourers. The same applies to the harvesting of grain, although in both cases some extra expense is incurred during dilatory harvests inasmuch as additional day men are ployed during the harvests; but the Northern farmers, ' looking to the coldness of their winters, argue that good hay is a sine qua non for their live stock, that it imparts warmth to their stomachs, and keeps them in better con- dition than does ensilage, at the same time enabling them the better to withstand the changes and vicissi- tudes of Northern winters. After cutting the grass, and so soon as it is comparatively dry on the top, it is scaled evenly over the field, either by hand or machine. Should the weather remain fine, the following dty it is put up into small cocks, and allowed so to stand overnight; if fine on the third day, it is broken out into broad cast and housed. Should rain intervene, it is put as quickly as possible into big cocks. In this latter state it will withstand a long continuance of bad weather, if only the cocks are occasionally turned on to a fresh place on the field, 3therwise the standing cocks will mark the mea- dow, leadinc, up to loss of bottom hay and loss of after- grass. Whether the cocks are broken out again, or the hay is carted from the cocks, depends upon the weather. —Samson. A SANGUINE VIEW or ENSILXGE.—Mr. Edwd. T. Blunt, of Blaby Hill, Leicester, writing to a contemporary, says:—" On the whole, I think sweet silage is of more value than sour, although the latter may be the best for dairy cows where the sale of milk or butter is the chief consideration; but for dairy cows where cheese is the chief production, and for all feeding purposes for young stock, sheep, and horses, there can be but little doubt that the sweet silage will be found to be the more valu- able. Practical experiments have taught us that it is easier tgi make silage, whether sweet or sour, in stacks than in silos. To obtain sweet silage the green crop should be stacked slowly, and it should not be weighted for a few days until the temperature has reached at least 130 degrees; but to make sour silage the crop must be stacked as quickly and weighted as soon as possible. But it is very difficult, if not impossible, to obtain sweet silage in a silo from a crop cut and carted in a wet con- dition, but not so if it is placed in a stack. It has now been fully proved that stacks may be built with a loss at the sides of not more than six inches in depth (not much more than where silos are used), and at a cost, including that incurred in weighting, so small as to compare fa- vourably with the making and getting of hay in fine weather. The stacks I intend to build this year will be each 36ft. long, 15ft. wide, and from 12ft. to 15ft. high, containing from 130 to 165 tons of silage, and the weighting will cost, allowing 15 per cent. for interest and depreciation on the cost of the pressing apparatus, less than'6d. per ton of silage. If we look at the evidence given before the Ensilage Co_mmission both this year and last, and also at all that has 'been written and published on the subject, it will be found that 95 per cent. of those who have tried the system agree that there is a saving of at least 25 per cent. (some even go so far as to place it at 50 per cent.) in the rearing and feeding of stock. I believe 25 per cent, is nearer the mark for cattle and sheep, and not quite so much for horses. This saving of 25 per cent. means that we can produce beef and mutton at 6id. per pound, as against 9d. under the old system. And not only this, but land now growing corn at a loss can be made capable of :producing, meat at a profit, and at such a price that, certainly for some years to come, we need not fear foreign competition. On dairy farms with ensilage milk can be produced at 71d. per gallon, against 10d. without it; and when this is done, and that vast imposture thutterine' is got rid of or put in its proper pla3e we may, as dairy farmers, look forward to our farms before long becoming remunerative." PEDIGRER—The best profit efarmer can have, we are told, is dairy, in these depressed times; also we are con- stantly reminded of keeping good cattle, as a good bul- lock costs no more to keep than a bad one. But I find many of the best animals are useless for milk, so much so that the offspring is a dwarf, if no other assistance be given it. Many cows of this description, particularly pedigree cows, are minus a quarter or so. An instance of this is a herd of ten cows I viewed recently, that had been reported a column long in the newspapers of their grand points, character, symmetry, and family prizes of its distinguished ancestors. Three of the number had lost five quarters of their udders. A few years previous the owner remarked from various causes cows to the above number had only produced three calves in the year. Whether the heifers required working, or from other causes, I cannot say, but easy to imagine. I fancy any class of animals that cannot produce milk sufficient for their offspring must be a decided loss to the owners, on the whole, to breed. The small black breed of pigs, of which Mr. Fisher Hobbs obtained such notoriety in his day, never went out of his herd for a boar for forty years, hence all kinds of weakness followed. Small lit- ters, seldom averaging six, many weak, most of them losing their tails, except topped-in time; such animals I do not now find in my rambles, except in wealthy hands —wealthy hands proving the fact they were unprofitable —more so as I never saw them in the renting dairyman's possession. I also heard that several lots of fine Hereford bullocks are being located on some of the best grazing ground on the river Swale, where they are now grazing Irish cattle and Shorthorns; this will again be a highly interesting ex- periment. When such men as Sir Frederick Milbank, M.P., Messrs. Mason (agent for the Marquis of Ripon), Snowdon, of Hutton Moor, Nicholson, Trotter, Pease, and the four Messrs. Gothorp, have entered into these trials; we may be sure that full justice will be done to both breeds. It is a curious coincidence that Mr. Mason, who is one of those most eager in the undertaking, should be of the same family as the Mason of Shorthorn fame, and one of the earliest breeders of these cattle. It matters little to the beef producer what'his animals are called, and whether they are red, white and roan, or red with white faces; what he wants is early maturity, quick re- turns, and the smallest consumer."

THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. THE SPANISH FAMILY. With the exception of the Dorking and the Game, the oldest of our English breeds is the Black Spanish, which has been bred very largely in England for many years. At one time it was perhaps the most popular of all breeds, its prolific laying and large eggs winning for it hosts of friends. Long before the advent of poultry shows as at present conducted, there were small gather- ings of breeders in public-houses, who brought the birds they had produced and compared them with the others brought for the same purpose. These gatherings took place principally in the neighbourhood of the metropolis, and, as might be imagined, did much to popularise the variety. Eveh yet, though the economic glory of the breed has waned and its place has been taken by others, there are many who regard the Black Spanish as the best layer we have, and who are more than satisfied if they can obtain anything bearing its name. Early in the century the Black Spanish was evidently not merely a good laying fowl, but also had other quali- ties. Moubray says but little about it, but that which he does says is very suggestive. He states that the Spaniard is "A large fowl, the plumage black, flesh white and delicate, but inferior in size to the old Duke of Leeds breed. They are well adaPted for capons, and produce eggs nearly equal in size to those of the Malay hens. This breed is now common, particularly in Lon- don; all black, black legs, large red combs and gills, far too high on the leg, and in want of improvement in that particular." Here is no mention whatever of the white face, which was a later introduction. In a work in our possession, published by Charles Knight, we believe, somewhere about 1850 (for there is no date upon it), the white ears are mentioned. This states that in the Black Spanish the "Comb is remarkably large, single, and often pendent on one side; the wattles are extremely developed, and the skin below the ear on each cheek is white, contrasting strongly with the scarlet of the comb and wattles, and the glossy black of the plumage. . . To those who breed fowl for the sake of the flesh and eggs, this fine variety cannot be too strongly recom- mended. The flesh is delicately white, tender, and juicy, and the hens are free layers. Some persons complain that the hens are far better layers than sitters. Better layers are none, but we cannot say that we subscribe to this complaint; indeed, a breeder of these fowls for his own use, in the neighbourhood of the writer, affirms that the hens make excellent sitters and nurses, and he has had many years' experience respecting them. The eggs are of very large size, and of first-rate flavour." As the name implies, the home of this breed is on the shores of the Mediterranean, from whence we have re- ceived some of the most valuable of our breeds, especially those best in laying qualities, namely, the Minorca, the Leghorn, and the Andalusian. These are known as the Spanish sub-varieties, and are all of the same type. They are not specially confined to the Spanish peninsula, where poultry breeding is at a very low ebb, and no care is taken to keep them pure, but are to be found all along the shores of the great sea. In fact, as Mr. Tegetmeier points out, all along the Mediterranean, from Gibraltar to Syria, the countries that border on that vast, inland sea, with its numerous islands, abound with fowls that bear so close a degree of resemblance to the Spanish race as may warrant our assigning them to one common stock. The employment of the names used to indicate some of the varieties of this typo of fowl are almost ex- clusively those which point to a Mediterranean origin, and some of the characteristics could only have been developed in a southern clime. Travellers tell us that enormous numbers of poultry are kept on both shores of the Mediterranean, especially the northern one, but that whilst the fowls are almost entirely of the Spanish type, I little regard seems to be paid to purity of race, and there are no birdssto be seen in any way to be compared with j those that are quite common both in England and America. So far as the Black Spanish fowl itself is concerned, it ' does not seem at all probable that at any time good specimens have been received direct from Spain into England, for these came by way of Holland and Belgium, or the Low Countries, as they were formerly called. Poultry-breeding was at one time a great pursuit in Holland especially, and we are indebted to it for the white-crested Black Polish and for the Pencilled Ham- burghs. The Low Countries, to the latter end of the sixteenth century, were subject to the Spanish Crown, and as there would be large numbers of Spaniards living there, many of them would be largely cut off from all congenial society and have comparatively little to do, it is not difficult to imagine that they would bring over [fowls from their native land and give time to their im- provement. This is being done at the present time by Britons all over the globe, and some day it may be, when the records of the present are lost, future writers upon poultry will enter into abstruse speculations as to the j causes which led to the scattering of the Game, or the I Spanish, or the Cochin all over the globe. The migra- tions of men seem always to be followed by the migra- tion of those plants, and birds, and animals to which they:have been familiar at home, and this natural desire to modify the unfamiliar conditions of their new habita- tion, has led to nearly all those changes which have so altered the distribution of domesticated animals and plants. In the absence of documentary evidence we may take it for granted that the Black Spanish was taken by Spaniards into the Low Countries during their occupation of that portion of Western Europe. The birds so imported wese developed in one direction, but it would appear that importations also took placo into England, probably about the same time, if not at an earlier period. The Minorca/ which for so long has been bred in the south-western districts of England—Devon- shire and Cornwall—for it is only of recent years that it has spread from thence, is undoubtedly allied to the Spanish, and it is more than likely that it is descended from exactly the same stock as the White-faced Spanish; in fact, it was at one time known as the Red-faced Spanish. The frequency with which ships from Spain and the Mediterranean were driven, through stress of weather, to take shelter in the harbours in the two coun- ties named, and the frequency with which marauding parties went from thence to play upon the towns on the Spanish seaboard, would give many opportunities for securing what would then be regarded as a new variety of poultry. The difference between the Black Spanish and the Minorca as we now see them would be simply sportive variations which, taken hold of and accen- tuated, have produced for us two distinct varieties of domestic poultry. A similar course of events had worked with both the Andalusian and the Ancona in England and the Leghorn in America. It is somewhat strange that the latter found their way to Britain through America, where it would appear an importation actually took place—an accidental importation, it is true —in 1835. Another is recorded as taking place in 1852, but the real commencement occurred in 1860, when the birds taken over fell into the hands of Mr. W. E. Bonny. Their merits soon won for them fame, and now this is one of the most popular of all our laying breeds. • We are now nearly half way through the month of May, and in the majority of poultry yards the breeding season will be almost, if not entirely over, and when this is so the breeding pens should be broken up. If it is intended to breed any chickens for Christmas or the early spring' the pens for that purpose must be made an exception. The old birds should be carefully examined and those not likely to be wanted as breeders next year had better be sold or fattened off as soon as possible in order to make room for the chickens, which are growing daily in size, strength, and vigour. If there is plenty of room and the hens are laying well they may all be put into a large house and kept there for a couple of months, but the gentlemen had better be got rid of at once. Every useless or non-productive bird is a direct loss, and should not be kept where profit is desired, for it takes the profit of one good bird to pay for every useless one.

Some years ago, at a public dinner, a Dutchman, just from Holland, was one of the company, and during the banquet he paid so much attention to a roasted sucking pig immediately in front of his plate that he devoured the entire animal. As he finished the lasf morsel, unc- tuous and savoury, a bustling waiter asked him what he would like to be helped to next. "Oh," replied the feeder, "I'll dank you for von more of dem leetle bolls !" BABIES HAVE A RIGHT TO BE.—lt is a common saying that we owe our parents a debt of gratitude for bringing us into the world. Too frequently children are born to such an inheritance of suffering and woe that it is a doubtful question whether they owe any gratitude for the uncertain boon of existence; but, in any case, an infant has a right ,to a kindly reception, to loving thoughts, to dainty stitches, to its own little niche in the family structure. If the portion of worldly goods for the infant's inheritance is small, yet there are three precious jewels that every father and mother should strive to give the little one—a strong frame, a good head, and an earnest, hearty welcome. div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

PEAS,—If a succession of these is desired it is a safe rule to sow as soon as the 1 ist sown is well above ground. William the First, though classed with the early ones, is a good Pea to sow yet. Market Favourite is a very heavy cropper, and fills up well. Laxton's Supreme and the same raiser's Prolific are distinguished by their large pods. Telegraph and Telephone are larger still and finer, consequently are much sought for exhibiting. We noticed last year in two or three gardens a remarkable heavy cropping Pea named Prince, of Wales, which seems to be one of the best for a cottager to grow for sale or consumption. Mcst persons sow their Peas too ',thick, and when all are in full growth there is a struggle for existence, and so many roots are formed that they can- not find food within their reach. We used to sow a quart in a row 50ft. long; now we make the same do 701 t. with better results. In sowing Peas from this time onwards it is a good plan to form shallow trenches to receive the seed in order to facilitate watering during dry weather, and some of the soil may be placed back as a mulching after a good watering has been given. ScAnim RIINNEIRS.—A sowing of these may be ven- tured now in trenches six or seven inches deep. Some make the trench so deep as to admit a few inches of manure being placed in as for Celery. Rich circular patches may be made at convenient distances in the garden, and in the centre drive in a strong pole or piece of quartering to which either wire or string may be at- tached and secured to stumps fixed in the ground for the bine to cling to. The height of the pole should be 6ft, above the soil and the diameter of the circle not less than 4ft. The seed need a covering of four inches of soil over them, and the seedlings must be watched as they emerge out of the soil or the slugs will destroy them. Mustard and Cress will come on freely if sown any- where out of doors. The seed require no more covering than will hide them, And a shallow drill made by draw- ing the finger along and then levelling the surface down after the seed are sown is all that is required. The wel- come showers we have had enabled us to plant out Cauliflowers, Lettuce, as well as some Onions we had raised in a frame in consequence of those sown last autumn being.destroyed by the frost and other agencies. TRI3 FRONT GAR.DEN.—Where Echeverias are used as edging to beds or borders it will be found quite safe to plant them out now. They show to better advantage when slightly raised above the level of the soil. Calceo- larias and verbenas, if they have been well hardened by being fully exposed, may be placed in their summer ' quarters, but before doing so it may be necessary to exercise a little forethought as to habit and colour of those plants that are likely to be their neighbours in order that they may not be hidden by one or encroached upon by another, or have their beauty and effectiveness destroyed by the introduction of unsuitable colours next to them. This harmonising of colours should not be overlooked as planting is being proceeded with. Where i the planting space is n beds, Scarlet Geraniums might occupy the centre, Calceolarias next, and a Purple Ver- bena for an outer line, as it is dwarfer than the other two. But should it take a liking to the soil it is in, and be disposed to raise above the Calceolarias, a few pegs will bring it to the desired level. They are neatest when made of thin wire similar to that used for making hair pins, and as a matter of fact we have frequently seen lady gardeners use these portions of their head furniture for pegging down any of their small favourite plants that might require it. If the mixed border is the plant- ing space it is a mistake to dot plants here and there. A far better plan is to group the plants in threes, fives, or sevens according to the size they grow and the number at disposal. Take, for instance, the Scarlet Geranium; if half a dozen plants are scattered over so many yards of ground they have very little effect, but if made into two groups equidistant from the ends, and surrounded with other suitable plants, they become particularly at- tractive. Lily of the Valley will grow almost anywhere and in any aspect. We have transplanted it at all times from November to the end of May, but found it to suc- ceed best after the plant has made two or three inches of growth, providing the crowns are carefully separated and not allowed to get dry previous to planting. TRH GREHNHOUSll.—Chrysanthemums are now quite safe outside, but a close watch must be kept on them lest they should get dry. Secure the shoots to stakes to prevent them being broken by the wind. If cuttings have not been taken, the old roots might be divided into pieces with three or four shoots on each, potted and stood in a shady place for a few days. They require kberal treatment to produce fine flowers, and at no time must they suffer for want of water. The following will be found a good mixture to grow them in :—Three parts loam, one leaf mould or decayed manure, adding a hand- ful of bone dust and the same of soot to every peck of soil. Sand should also be added if a good proportion is I not present in the soil. Pot rather firm, using a blunt pointed stick to press the soil down. Plunge the pots in ashes half their depth to prevent the wind blowing them over. - -

A few years ago the Russian Chancellor, Prince Gort- chakoff, was on a visit to Berne, where his son held the post of Minister Plenipotentiary of Russia. The fête of the Czar occurred at the time. "The ceremony takes place to-morrow," remarked the Chancellor to his Son; "and you know that at its termination every one who has taken part in it goes to the altar to kiss the cross. It is understood that Igo first." "Pardon, my father; in my quality of Minister at Berne I ought to pass before you, for I represent the Emperor here." "But I, in my quality of Grand Chancellor, represent him everywhere. However," added the Prince, after reflecting a moment, "since you are anxious to retain your prestige, I give place to you in the circumstances." On the day of the ceremony the Chancellor followed his son; but as the latter approached the cross, his father, tapping him on the shoulder, said, in a voice loud enough for every one to hear, "Proceed, my son; go first—l authorise you to do so." Tali KIND OF MAN WerrEn.—Jack Williams was a brave sergeant of a regiment which, undrilled and un- disciplined, had joined the army of the Potomac just as the terrible campaign of 1864 began. Before the army reached Petersburg, Jack commanded his company, the captain and lieutenants having been killed. His gallantry was so conspicuous that he was recommended for a cap- taincy in the regular army. Ordered before an Examina- tion Board at Washington, Jack presented himself, dressed in a soiled uniform, with bronzed face and uncut beard. The trim, dapper officers composing the Board had never been under fire or roughed it in the field, but they were posted in tactics and in the theory of war. Though shocked at JaCk's unsoldierly appearance, they asked him all sorts of questions about engineering, ma- thematics, ordnance, and campaigns. Not 6a single ques- tion could Jack answer. "What is echelon ?" asked one of the Board. "Don't know," answered Jack. "What ' is abatis ?" "Never saw one." "A redan?" " You fel- lows have got rne-gain," replied Jack. "Well, what is a hollow square, sir ?" "Never heard of one before. Guess they don't have them down at the front, do they ?" "What would you do, sir, if you were in command of a company, and cavalry should charge on you ?" asked a lisping fellow in white kids. ''Do, you fool ?" thundered Jack; "I would give them Hail Columbia, that's what I'd do !" This ended the examination, and the report of the questions and answers, with the adverse judgment of the Board, were sent to President Lincoln. His private secretary read the report to him, and when he came to the only answer Jack had given, the President said, "Stop! read it over again." " That's just the sort of men our army wants," said the President, taking the re- port and dipping his pen in the inkstand. On the back of the paper he wrote in a clear hand, " Give this man a captain's commission,—A. LINCOLN." ,
:A NEW CHAPEL FOR SUTTON 1 WEAVER.

_ ~.- Since March, 1879. a oongregation of worshippers have regularly met for Divine service and Sunday school work in a room of the corn mill at Frodsham bridge, and their increase as a religious body led to the determination to erect a suitable chapel and school, which determination resulted on Tuesday ia the laying of the foundation stones of a new banding on a site of land on the Frodsham-road, which will be called the Union Church, Sutton Weaver. The promoters of the work are Protestant dissenters from , the State Church of England, who hold the Baptist and Congregational views of church government and Christian doctrine. They meet together under the dis- tinctive name of a union church, with the chief de- sire of promoting the glory et God. When completed the new buildings will comprise a chapel and school, with class- rooms and vestries, and will have an entrance from the main road. Accommodation will be provided for 200 people, and the building will be built in the early pointed Gothic style. Local bricks, with red brick dressings are , to be used in its construction, and the whole of the wood work will be of pitchpine; a pulpit and baptistry will be Placed at one end. The aim of the promoters has been to , obtain a simple and economical, but at the same time cot:le- i modious building. The estimated cost is £l,lOO. Mr. Thomas Huxley, of Ma!pas, is the contractor for the work, and Messrs. Douglas and Fordlaam, of Chester, are the , architects. The freehold site has already been paid for by monies earned by ladies of the congregation by means of a periodical sewing meeting, and from a sale of work held last year. When the work was resolved upon £7OO was promised by members of the congregation and a few friends, and by the day fixed for the laying of the foundation stones an additional £3OO had been promised. The names of the trustees are:—Messrs. Thomas A. Rigby, Wm. Wilkinson, John Dobson, Samuel Maddock, Abraham Rothwell, Thomas Moores, Edward Boden, W. B. Gibson, Alfred Lomas; Thomas Rigby and J. 0. Jackson, (treasurers), and S. Ormrod and Ed. Jackson (secretaries). At the hour announced for witnessing the ceremony of lay- ing the stones, the rain, which had been coming down almost incesuntly for two or three hours, continued to pour heavily, and it was decided to make the proceedings as short as possible. The Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, near at hand, having been placed at the disposal of the gathering in consequence oi the inclemency of the weather, it was thought best to quickly lay the stones and then proceed to that Place of worship to conclude the service. Amongst those who stood in the drenching rain on the site of the pro- posed building were the Rev. A.. McLaren. D.D. (Manches- ter), Mr. William Crosfield (Liverpool). the Revs. Thomas Lewis (Prince's Park Baptist Chapel, Liverpool), J. D. IThomas (Runcorn), A. Potts (Crewe), G. K. Walker (Mid- dlewich), E. Mosicrop (Frodsham), Mr. and Mrs. Samuel i Rigby (Chester), Mr. Arthur Rigby, Mr. Thomas Rigby, the Misseri Rigby, Mr. J. Occleshaw Jackson, Mrs. Jacks-in, Miss Jackson, and Mr. and Mrs. Pickering. After a hymn had been sung, Mr. Thomas Rig'ey handed a handsome sil- ver trowel, bearing an inscription, to Dr. McLaren, and Mr. J. 0. Jackson presented a similar trowel to Mr. William Crosfield. The first stone was laid by Mr. Crosfield. The second, underneath which was placed a bottle containing three newspapers and a short written history of the move- ment, was laid by Dr. McLaren. An adjournment was then made to Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, where, after a brief service, a very interesting ad- dress was delivered from the pulpit by Dr. McLaren. The speaker said that he could not commence his remarks with- out expressing on his own and on their,behalf, their thank- fulness to the Wesleyan community, for the kind accommo- dation they had given that afternoon. It was a matter of great satisfaction to him, and, he was sure, to Mr. Crosfield also, that they had been laying the stones that morning of a chapel that was dis.inctively a united church of the two denominations to which he and Mr. Crosfield respectively belonged. He thought that in their country districts Bap• tists and Congregationalists had been matting each other's throats long enough. No more fooliae or suicidal policy could nave been pursued than that which the members of those congregations had on many occasions pursued, where there had been a sperse population by each standing upon 'their own distinctive principles, and so making two weak ,I places instead of one strong one. He rejoiced ° extremely r that here they had found a more excellent way. He as a Baptist would he the last man to fall into the common way on such occasions of assuming to undervalue the import- ance of the distinctions which divided the two bodies, but even the staunchest stickler of baptism by immersion, or adult baptism, must admit that that belonged to the ritual and their faith. However closely some might think it con- nected symbolically with the doctrines of Christianity, still their difference belonged to ritual, and they had not so learnt Christ as to suppose that in his Church ritual of any I sort held a predominent place of importance. Daring his 1 'ministerial career of forty years he had been pastor of two ' churches, in both of which Baptists and Independents had united on absolutely equal terms, and he had never once known any friction, or unpleasantness of any sort, to arise In those churches which could be traced to that source. He believed that in village communities especially the true solution of the difficulty which was pressing upon both denominations, as to how their village churches were to be sustained in their efficiency, would very largely be found in walking more or lc ss closely in the footsteps they at Sutton Weaver were treading that day. It was a diffi- cult question how they were to sustain their churches in the country districts. With agricultural depression and the consequent migration of young blood to the big towns, these districts became more and more stagnated, and he was afraid that the morality of rural England was nothing but an ideal morality. They thought of the country as the home of simplicity and purity, but from what he knew of the rural districts of England he should very mach question whether the average of morality was as high as it was in the great towns. However that might be it was becoming of great difficulty to keep the little churches going, and if to that were added the alarming development of Ritualism in the Anglican Church, and the fact that by far the most vital and energetic portion of the English clergy was the Secramentarian, then he thought that the problem for Dis- senters—for Baptists and Congregationalists especially— how they were to sustain these charehes became an in- creasingly and terribly grave one. They were children of the same household, had passed substantially through the same experience, worked side by side in large centres, and he believed that the members of their churches were a great deal more ready for united action than their ministers. He noticed that it was very largely a matter now of locality and of choice of a preacher whether many people were I members of a Baptist or a Congregational chapel. Amongst what. they called their laity to a large extent the impor- tance of the point which divided them bad utterly disap- peared. He sometimes thought that if it were not for the Baptist and the Congregational Union the two bodies would go together like two globes of quicksilver when brought near each other. At all events they could live in mutual harmony, like their friends at Frodsham, who had lived unitedly in the bonds of one Christian Church. (Applause.) He was sure they would not quarrel on the Baptist and on the Independent ground at all events, and be believed they would find in that as in other unions that "Union is stren- gth," and that it was a good piece of discipline in a Chris- tian church, as anywhere else, to learn to respect one ano- thers' convictions. He did not think they would ever get a good sound solid union on the basis of never talking about their disagreements. It was far more wholesome to speak about them. They must not gag their preachers, or muzzle themselves, but speak the truth in love, and they would find that that was some- times the way to come to see eye to eye. (Applause.) Mr. WM. Crodeld also made a few remarks, reciprocating the feelings to which Dr. McLaren had given expression. He thought that their presence at the stone-laying—Dr. McLaren representing one Congregational denomination and he himself another—and the fact that they were then enjoying the hospitality of another section of the free churches, showed that the work that was to be carried on in the new building was one which bad the kindly feeling and the sympathy of all who were engaged in God's work in that neighbourhood. His connection with the home mission work of the Independent body had led him to see to how large an extent the dissenting communities were occupying the same ground, in many cases to the manifest disadvan- tage of the neighbourhood in which they were planted through no fault of their own but from the accident of cir- cumstances. The migration of population from one place to another had left many of the rural districts over supplied with religious accommodation, and Baptists and Congrega- tionalists were working side by side, though not absolutely in antagonism, in an appearance of unfrieradliness in religions work. He, with Dr. McLaren, hoped that some plan might be devised by which the two bodies could com- bine in such circumstances. (Applause.)—A collection was then made, and a vote of thanks having been passed for the use of the chapel, a verse of the National Anthem was sung. Almost immediately after the service tea was partaken of by about 300 persons in a tent erected on a piece of land near the mills at Frodsham Bridge. They did not need that they should have a fine building in which to worship God; their history of years past as a congregation had proved that, but he was glad to be able to congratulate them on the sign of life, exhibited by the evidence of growth, that

FOREIGN NEWS.

THE GREEK CRISIS. 'ME BLOCKADE OF THE GREEK COAST. CONSTANTINOPLE, 6ATURDA.Y.—NegotiatiOne are proceed tug between the Great Powers for the discovery of means whereby the task of disarmament may be rendertd easier for Greece. Should the Russian Minister to Greece remain at Athens it would be to act as intermediary between the Powers and the Hellenic Government. The Porte is an. Xiously awaiting the disarmament of Greeoe in order to at once demobilise its own forces, and thus avoid being called Von to do so by the Powers, besides putting an end to the zailitary expenditure. As soon as Greece shall have decided Von disarmament Feridow Bey will return to Athens to re- Wabash good relations with the Government. ATHENS, SATURDA.4.--A telegram received to-day from St. Anne says that a small detachment of Austrian marines lan. ded on the island of Skiathos, and made requisitions for food. Telegraphic communication with Skiathos is cut, OM full details of the affair are expected on the return of the French steamer, which leaves here to-morrow to convey Prorisions to Skiathos and Volo. The Greek Steamship Company have been ieformed that they may re-commence !?heir service to the Cycladee group, which is not included an the blockade. ATHENS, SIINDAY.—A. despatch from Aghriovotano states that a small fishing smack from the island of Skiathos to- day attempted to run the blockade, and was chased by an' Austrian torpedo boat. The fishermen, however, having in their possession some dynamite cartridges for fishing pur- poses, fired several at the pursuing vesaell, which thereupon gave up the chase and returned to Ekiathos. Communica- tion with Skiathos remains interrupted, and it is believed that the Austrians have cut the telegraph cable. FIGHTING IN THE SOUDAN. CAIRO. SCNDAT.—Spies who have arrived at Wady Haifa Import that fighting has taken place between the Kabbabish " -bribe and the dervishes. According to the latest official in- telligence.bowever, the Kabbabish merely made a raid and larded off some of the crops of the dervishes in the vicinity of Debbeh, killing two dervishes. MONDAY.—Sheik Saida, of the Kabbabish tribe, tat defeated a body of rebels at Debbeh with heavy loss. 9.e has sent a message asking for reinforcements of Egyp- hall troops to enable him to retake Dongola. According to *facial information Sheikh Mahmoud E. Kheir is in the vicinity of Abu Fatmeh with 2,000 followers, making pre- parations for attacking simultaneously the other chiefs oc- °Vying positions along the Nile between Wady Haifa and Assouan. SICKNESS IN UPPER BußmAii. &MLA, SIINDA.Y.—A. large amount of illness, principally fever dysentery, is reported among the troops in Upper Rurmab. BRITISH ANNEXATION IN THE PACIFIC. MBLBOVRNE, MONDAY.—The Home Government have .ordered. Rear. Admiral Tryon, oommander-in-chief on the Australian station, to plant the British flag on the Kerma- dec Islands, situate north of New Zealand. THE RIOTS AT CHICAGO.—SEIZURE OF ANOTHER AMERICAN VESSEL. CEICAGO, SATTIRDAY.—The police have arrested Louis Linng, the person who threw the dynamite bomb among the Mlle° during the recent Socialist riots in this city. On the police officer presenting himself Linog drew his revol- ver. The officer, however, immediately closed with his assailant., and after a severe struggle succeeded in capturing him GurcaGo. MONDAY.—Several prominent members of the Ltimbermen's Union yesterday addressed a large meeting of germane and Bohemians urging them to continue the 'Wks and to support the employees in the stockyards and the men employed by the builders. The speakers assured the meeting that the fate of the eight hours' movement de- pended upon the action of the lumbermen. A resolution Was adopted that a fresh strike should commence to-day. Further rioting is apprehended, and a large force of police has been detailed to prevent any disturbance. Twenty thousand tailors' employee who were on strike here have resumed work. Another police officer has succumbed to the injuries received through the explosion of the bombs during the recent Socialist riots, this making the sixth death.

THE RUSSIAN NIHILISTS. .BaasiN, MOND&Y.—lntelligence received here from St. retersburg states that during the last few days numerous arrests have been made, principally among students. includ- ing 20 members of the faculty of law, who are alleged to be I connected with the recent conspiracies against the Emperor at Charkoff and Novo Tcherhash. STOBX ON THE CONTINENT.—MANY LIVES LOST. BEstuN, Sarzmpai.—A terrible hurricane, causing great devastation, swept over Krossen, in the province of Bran- denburg, yesterday. Several buildings were blown down, and nearly all the houses had their roofs and windows damaged. A church tower was thrown down, and in fall- ktg destroyed a neighbourieg house. From the debris seveial bodies have been extricated. A number of persons have been injured, some seriously. Two ships on the Oder have founded, five of their crew being drowned.
