The birtk was announced to the public o'clock. by hoisting a flag on the place and firing a salute of 21 guns. The Queen and infant are reported to be going on satisfactorily. NAMING THE INFANT KING OF SPAIN. The Madrid correspondent of the "Times" writes The infant King of Spain will be baptised on Saturday as " Alfons* Leon," and will reign as Alfonso the Thirteenth. The Queen, desirous to mark her affection for her late hus- band, prefers the adoption of "Alfonso "in his memory, re- membering also that all the Alfonsos ruling in Spain have been either good or wise. She adopts" Leon" in testimony of gratitude to Pope Leo, who has shown that the nurnher thirteen does not prevent his being the wisest and most liberal of Popes, while the Lion and the Castillo form the arms of Spain. EARTHQUAKE IN SICILY. CATANIA, WHDNBSDAY.—A fresh shook of earthquake was felt here last night, as well as at Palermo, Blancavilla, and ether places in the vicinity. There has been a fresh volcanic eruption at Mount Grosio,on the north-eastern side of Nloolosi. CONSPIRACY AGAINST PRINCE ALEXANDER. Paws, WIIDNBSDAY.—A telegram received here from Sophia, of to-day's date, reports that a conspiracy has been discovered against Prince Alexander and M. Karaveloff, the Bulgarian Premier. OPENING OF THE GREEK CHAMBER. ATITHNs, WRDNESDAY Noon.—The Greek Chamber was opened at eleven o'clock this morning by Royal decree, with the usual ceremonial. Two hundred members atten- ded out of 245 forming the House, and the remainder of the Deputies are expected to arrive to-day. The vote for the election of president will be taken at ten o'clock to-morrow, M. Delyannis himself being probably the candidate who will be put forward by his party. It is not vet known who will be the candidate of the Tricoupis party. In parlia- mentary circles the opinion prevails that M..Delyannis will have a majority. ERUPTION OF MOUNT ETNA. CATANIA, WHuNBSDAY ETAINING.—The eruption oi Mount Etna is increasing in violence. Immense columns of flame are projected from the crater, and form a most imposing spectacle. Monterosso is seriously threatened by a stream of lava which is descending the mountain side in its direc- tion. Measures have been taken to rescue the inhabitants should it be necessary. PRESIDENCY OF THE GREEK CHAMBER. ATHENS, TNIMSDAY.—M. Stephanopoulos, the candidate ofthe Triceupis party, has this morning been elected presi- dent of the Greek chamber by 139 votes.

HOITSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 4-0. IRE HOME RULE DEBATE. In reply to a qaeetion from Sir M. R. Beach, the PRIME liituarrratt stated that ha could not think it possible that the debate on the Irish Goverarnent Bill could be otherwise than extended over a considerable number of days beyond the present week —The adjourned debate on the motion for the recent reading of the Irish Government Bill was re-

Burned by Mr. SHAW LBFBTER, who noticed that the opposition the measure had encountered on his side of the House had pro- oeeded from sections of the Liberal party very different and, it might be, very divergent one from the other. The noble Lord the member for Emendate had never shown any in- dication in the direction of autonomy, had never recognised that Ireland had any grievance in that direction, and his ideas of local self-government for Ireland were of a very rudimentary character. The leader of the other section, the right hoe, gentleman the member for West Birmingham, had for a long time past consistently recommended a wide measure of local self-government for Ireland. On Friday these two parties met at Devonshire House and came to a conclusion as to the policy they were to pursue, and he thought they had a right to know the conclusion at which they had arrived, the more so as the leader of the Tory party had been very open in his views. They meant a policy of twenty years' caercion, at the end ef that time some small modicum of local govern- ment, and during that period the expenditure of 100 mil- lions in the emtgation of one million of the Irish people. He thought he had a tight to ask for the alternative policy which Mr. Chamberlain had to offer. It was said the hon. member for West Birmingham had not altered his opinion, but that Lord Hartington had come round. He had no doubt the noble Lord had discovered that the overwhelming force of opinion among the Liberal party in the country was in favour of the general principle of the bill and of giving autonomy to Ireland, only differing somewhat on questions of detail; that any alternative policy of coercion was abso- lutely and totally out of the question, and tbat a policy of coneession to Ireland was already inevitable. II the noble , Lord had come round it would be something like a calamity to the country and the House if they did not discover some method by which the verdict of the Liberal party could be given in favour of the principle of autonomy apart from the details. He was satisfied that we ceuld concede this great measure both in the interest of Ireland and of England. He had come ta the conclusion that the Act of Union so far as it suppressed Irish autonomy had worked untold discontent and mischief both in her legislation and administration. Irish measures had been treated from an English point of view, and it was only when Ireland was on the point of rebellion that grievances had been listened to It was absolutely essential that a great change should be made in the system of administration in Ireland in order that it might be brought into harmony with the views of the Irish people. That glasses weye separate and antago- nistic in Ireland came from the system of English rule, and the way to cure the evil was to grant them what it was proposed to do by the bill—autonomy. On the question of retaining the Irish members or a portion of them at West- minster, be should be pleased if some arrangement should be come to, but he did not think it would ever work if the Irish members were to come to London to reargue Irish questions or by way of appeal from the Irish Parliament, and he did not think such a change in the bill would give satisfaction to the Irish members or to the Irish people. He thought the proposal that Ulster should be excluded from the operation of the bill establishing an Irish Parlia- ment was bad, and that it would be hardly possible to de- sire anything more inexpedient. He could not believe that the bill would lead to separation or disintegration of
The Central News Athens correspondent says Stephanspoulos was elected by 138 votes against 78 votes for the Delyannis candidate. li. Triesupis will now be called upon to borax a Miniiitry.

the Empire. Mr. CH.spurr contended that Irish sedition was only for- midable when people were afraid to meet it, and said if they got rid of the Prime Minister one half the Irish difficulty would begin to disappear, and he believed the day was not far distant when a Government would be formed which would have the courage to use the " resources of civilisa- tion" to break up the "vile conspiracy "of the League.— Mr. LABOUCITERE was delighted that permanent coercion as against Ireland was impossible. Referring to the strong ex- pressions to be found in the speeches of Mr. Parnell and others, he remarked that if the test were applied to the speeches of Lord R. Churchill the noble Lord would have the grace frankly to admit that he regretted about two-thirds of all that he ever said. In the course of criticism of the attitude of Mr. Chamberlain, he said the right hon. gentle- man always reminded him of Moses coming down from Mount Sinai. He was just as aghast at anybody not ac- cepting his inspired plan as Moses would have been had any Israelite suggested an amendment in the Ten Com- mandments. Speaking on the prospects of the hill, he said if it could be shown that either from obstinacy or prejudice they were unable to carry the measure through the House he would prefer the passing of the bill as a resolution simply. —The debate was continued by Mr. T. D. SULLIVAN. who added his pledge of Irish good faith.—Mr. HANBURY con- continued the Opposition argument on the measure ; and Sir Lyon Playfair stated with freshness the case in defence of the Bill.—Mr. A. Elliott ibjected to the Bill because it would not maintain oar nation intact in the face of tbe world, and Mr. Justin M'Carthy moved the adjournment of the debate. LOWE'S CHARITY.—Sir J. SWINEURNE called attention to the scheme of the Charity Commissioners relating to Lowe's Charity in the City of Lichfield; and moved that, in the opinion of the House, every scheme of the Charity Commissioners ought to provide for the majority of the trustees or managers being directly elected by the ratepayers in the locality to which the charity extended.—Dr. FOSTER seconded the motion. After some further discussion, the resolution was agreed to. The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes to three. HOUSE OF COMMONS.--WEDNESDAY.

_ The House met at half-past twelve o'clock. POOR LAW GUARD UN S (IRELAND) BILL.—Mr. E. HARRINGTON moved the second reading of the Poor Law Guardians (Ireland) Bill.—Mr. MORLEY said he believed the House was likely to pass the bill, as it did in the last Parliament. On most of the proposals in the bill there was substantial agreement in all parts of the House. The two points as to which there was a distinct difference of opinion were, first, as to the retention of proxy voting, and next as to the number of ex-officio guardians. There was much objection to proxy voting in any form, and he should not he surprised if, when the Government brought in their Local Government Bill, proxy voting disappeared from England. He did not, therefore, object to the present bill removing that feature from poor-law elections in Ireland.— The bill was read a second time by a majority of nearly a hundred. RAILWAY REGULATION. Mr. CHANNING moved the second reading of the Railway Regulation Bill. In the course of the debate, Mr. MUNDELLA said the loss of life from railway accidents was appalling, but he believed that there was not a more exemplary class of officials in the world than those on English railways. He maintained that Parliament should not relieve railway directors of the re- sponsibility which primarily lay upon them. Many ob- jects of the bill were in steady process of accomplishment. There was, however, a regular and steady diminution of the loss of life year by year. He felt reluctant to take upon the Board of Trade the responsibility that the bill would give, but there was a great deal that was valuable in the bill, if the objectionable parts were removed. He did not think he would be justified in refusing the second reading of the bill, but he suggested that it should be sent to a Select Committee.—The bill was read a second time and referred to a Select Committee. MIOCELLANEOUS.—Sir JULIAN GOLDRIIID rose to move the second reading of the Parliamentary Voters Registra- tion Bill, but had only spoken two or three minutes when the debate stood adjourned at a quarter to six o'clock.— The following bills were introduced and read a first time: Mr. Boord, to enable barristers to recover fees and be liable at law to persons employing them ; Mr. Burt, to amend the law of distress. The House adjourned at five minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS—THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. The Duke of Devonshire took the oath and subscribed to

the roll of the new Parliament. Tim CROFTERS BILL.—The second reading of the Crofters Bill was moved in the House of Lords by the Earl of DAL- 'mum, who stated that although it did not contain every- thing recommended by the Crofters Commission it would contain nearly everything that in the opinion of Her Majesty's Government it ought to contain, and that it met the reasonable wants of the crofters, so far as they could be met by legislation.—The Earl of FIFE contended that the measure introduced unsound principles.—The bill was read a second time. Their Lordshiris adjourned at ten minutes to seven o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THIIRSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. THE ARMS BILL.

Mr. Joun MORLEY moved the second reading of the Arms (Ireland) Bill, which, he said, was to continue the Peace Preservation Act passed in 1881. There was, he continued, a great difference between the general state of things in the country at tke present moment and the state of things in Ireland in 1881, when the Act was passed. In the first four mouths of 1881 the agrarian outrages of a serious kind were 556, while in the first four months of 1886 the number was only 184. It might be asked, what was the cause for the continuance of this Act? The true use of the Arms Act was that it prevented the growth of the prac- tice—which was likely to become formidable in times of ex- citement—of carrying arms at fairs, races, markets, proces- sions, and other gatherings. The Iriah Government found the Peace Preservation Act in existence and in working order, and they thought it only consistent with prudence and common sense to retain it for the purpose he had men- tioned.—Mr. PARNELL held that if this law was to be passed at all it should against all sections of the people. When the House allowed Ireland to legislate for herself the need for passing such a measure as this, to be used against any section of Irishmen, would have disappeared for ever.—Lord R. CHURCHILL, replying to the recent statement of Sir H. James that because of the language be (Lord Randolph) had used in Ulster he was "half a traitor," contended that he had not exoeeded in that speech the line of accepted constitutional anthoder in Ink country. ile believed Wit the come-

quences of such legislation as was proposed by the present Government would be civil war, and he was of opinion that those who took part in resisting those consequences would be rig'lt.—Sir H JAMES remarked that be had not referred to any particular individual in what he said. He could give an assurance that when be was speaking the noble lord was not in his mind, and having given thp.t assurance he had not a word to withdraw of what hishad said.—Mr. BRADLAIIGIS understood that Lord R. Churchill had advised the Orangemen to resort to arms when all constitutional means had failed. No doctrine more dangerous or more intentionally treasonable could possibly be maintained. Mr. GLADSTONE said be understood that Lord R. Churchill advocated the doctrine that after the constitutional means were exhausted the people of Ulster should resort to armed resistance. It might be asked why the Government bad not taken notice of these grave and painful circumstances. The reason was, first, that he well knew the strength of the law. and the strength of the love of the law, and the determination to maintain the law in this ccuntry to be such that no rash assault upon it, coming from whom it might, could in truth do anything to weaken the founda- tion of public and national obedience. Another reason was the fact that the words of the noble Lord bad received no extenuation or apology from any of those who sat near him in that House and who were associated with him in office; and a third reason was this—he felt with regard to the measure before the House touching the government of Ireland that the Gov- ernment were making such demands upon the time and generosity of the House. that it was their prime duty to avoid the introduction of any subject that would be likely to create angry controversy. He would adhere to that method unless overwhelming necessity compelled him to abandon it.—After considerable debate, Mr. J. MORLEY said, in reply, that the Government were considering whether, if this bill were passed, the Lord Lieutenant should proclaim those parts of Ireland in which the Peace Pre- servation Act was not at present in force.—Sir M. Hicks- Beach having spoken in support of the second reading, the bill was read a second time by 303 to 80. The House adjourned at two o'clock.

TFIE FREE LIBRARY MOVEMENT. On Tuesday evening, a second meeting of persons who desire to have the Warrington Lending Library made free was held in the Cocoa Rooms, Horsemar- ket-street, for the purpose of receiving the report of the deputation appointed at the previous meeting to wait on the Library Committee. There was a large attendance, the club room being crowded. Mr. T. Morris was elected to presitle, on the motion of Mr.' John Walker. The Csainares, who had formed one of the deputa- tion, then made a statement as to their interview with the committee. They had, he said, some little con- versation with the committee, a fuller aceount of which would be given by Mr. Walker, but in the end they came away feeling rather unhappy. They did not half like their reception; it stuck to him all night, and the next morning he wrote a letter to Mr. Beamont, the chairman of the committee, a gentle- man whom he (the chairman) admired very much for his extraordinary work and benevolence, especially in connection with the education of the young children of this town. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Beamont could not bear to have a School Board in the town because, if they had, their rates, already heavy enough, would be a good deal heavier, and so if they could get a few gentlemen like Mr. Beamont to pull out their purse and assist them, he (the chairman) said long might they live and have plenty money to give effect to their philanthrophy. (Hear, hear.) Well, in reply to his letter, Mr. Beamont wrote the following letter :

Dear Mr. Morris,—There is no one whom I would sooner oblige than you. I admire and would imitate much that you do and the benevolence which prompts It; but on this library question I am and must continue of a different opinion from you. I admire a library such as ours in which people of every class can and do participate. The humblest reader has a quiet and well-lighted and well-ordered room to meet in from 10 a m. to 9-30 pan.,and for the sacrifice of three half-pence a week he can take out books to read at home; but the home of some working-men and its discomforts and the noises of the children and of household work is not one of the beet places for study. I had the pleasure to know Eau Burritt, the blacksmith, who during his toilsome oc- cupation found time, without a free library, to make him- self master of many languages, and I also knew Mr. Sam Holmes, of Liverpool, who, while he was a bricksetter, by husbanding his time and his half-pence rose to be Mayor of Liverpool and one of its most accomplished speakers and public men. There was no public free library in Liverpool tben, and! am far from believing that any of my neigh- bours in Warrington may not rise, as our library is now, to occupy tbe honourable seat which the Mayor now occupies. For these reasons, I should be disinclined to change its con- stitution, even though we had not a deficit in the ex- chequer. At present, however, the committee feel bound to pay their debts and to deliver up the library in as good a condition as they received it, which they cannot do if they adopt the new eourse urged apoa them by the deputation -which waited upon the committee; but I am so strong a believer in thrift that I cannot and no not doubt that it is in the power of every man, however poor his lot, to rise if he seriously tries.—l remain, dear Mr. Morris, Yours truly, W. BEAMONT." Referring to the sentence " for these reasons I should be disinclined to change its constitution even thongh we had not a deficit in the exchequer," the Chairman said that was a reason for not freeing the library whioh seemed to influence the committee although they gave no tangible expression to it. (Hear, hear.) They The would see that Mr. Beamont went on the is• sum-ption that every man that wanted books could afford to pay 55 a year for them, but when he (the chairman) saw scores of people going for soup to the Drill Shed a few weeks ago, people who would not go unless starvation stared them in the face, he said these people could no more fined 55 a year for books than other people who drove into the town night and morning could afford to pay four times 5s a year. {Hear, hear.) He had several conversations with one er two members of the Library Committee on the sub- ject-, and one of them roeuti9ned to him that they might s.uggeat to the committee that working-men should only pay is 3d, one-fourth of the fee paid by the present subscribers. He thought that a very good suggestion. (Hear, hear.) The committee had pointed out to the deputation that there was a mu- seum, art gallery, kc. to keep up, and he said let them keep them for they were grand institutions, and were, in fact, the next best thing to the library. They wanted to see as well as read, but if there was any difficulty the museum and art gallery should go on their own account and be supported by gentlemen in the town so that the Library might be free. (Ap- plause). Mr. WALKER reported that the deputation they ap- pointed at the previous meeting arranged to get an interview as soon as they could with the Library Committee, but they found there was no meeting to be held for nearly a month, and that it would be inconve- nient for the committee to have a special meeting. However, they met the committee on Friday evening last, but they did not get on quite as well as at any rate they should have liked. They found the com- mittee had considered the matter, and that so far as they could see, they were quite unfavourable to the Idea of making an effort to get rid of the subscription to the lending library. They expressed themselves as in sympathy with the object of the deputation, and said it was a good thing if it could be done, but they did not see how it could be done, as it was a question of ways and means. From a hint or two thrown out, the deputation rather thought—and that impression was supported by the letter from Mr. Beamont just read that there were other considerations than merely monetary considerations. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Whitham, Mr. Morris, and himself endeavoured to as- certain these considerations, if there were any, but , they could not get at them. They then addressed themselves to the matter of ways and means, but they were not permitted to go very -far into the question. So far as the Library Committee were concerned, they gathered that the committee were Izoo or £3OO in debt in consequence of the recent extensive altera- tion and beautifying of the building, that if they abolished the subscriptions that would cause a loss of £l5O a year, and that they did not see how that loss could be recouped. They were at present spending the whole of the proceeds of tbs penny rate, about £530, and they did not see how they were to carry on the museum, library, and art gallery as they had been carried on. As touching ways and means a sugges- tion had been made by one of the members of the Library Committee, but they found, that the gentle- man—Mr. Robert Davies—who had made that sug- gestion did not approve of it after further considera- tion. The suggestion was one which the deputation, , after considering it before they went to the commit- tee, very much approved of as a feasible way of solv- ing the difficulty. It was this, that subscriptions of 5s a year should still continue to be received, and that from the fund provided by these subscrip- tions the new books should be bought. The subscribers of 5s would have the exclusive use of the new books tor 12 months, after which these along with all the other books in the lending depart- ment should be issued free. The library would im- mediately become a free library to the general public, while those who continued to subscribe ss. a year would have, in consideration of that subscription, the exclusive use of all new books for twelve months. The deputation thought that a capital suggestion, as they would not only be gaining practically all they wanted—a free lending library; but they would also be provided with a fund from which new books could be bought. But for some reasons unexplained the committee thought this scheme hardly practicable, and when the deputation endeavoured to show that it would work they found nothing could be done in the matter. It was pointed out to the committee by Mr. Whitham that although Is. 6d. a quarter might appear a small subscription on the face of it, still it might involve not merely sa. a year but 15s. if there was a family of readers with different tastes; that there were people who had not this money; and that it was desirable that children who were growing up and passing from achools should have books placed to their hands without making it an additional burden upon their parents who paid for the library through the rates. (Hear, hear.) He was glad to see Mr. Beam.ont'a letter, because it showed that interest was being taken in the subject, although it explained— unsatisfactorily to him he might say—what they could not quite understand at their interview, name- ly, that there was a radical objection apart from any consideration of ways and means to taking that step of freeing the library. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Beamont, they would see, said he was disinclined to change the constitution of the library even though there were not a deficit. Mr. Beamont thought the present the best system of carrying on the library, and that as Si they provided books and a good room for people to read them in, those that wanted to make progress could make progress. Well, they admitted all that, but they contended that books were infinitely more valuable when read at one's own fireside, and that children were much more likely to grow up into readers if they were enabled to read at home than if sent to a public reading-room. (Hear, hear.) They further said that this had been found to be so by ex- perience in every town of the kingdom of anything like the sine of Warrington, and that they did not see that Warrincton should be behind other towns and maintain a system which he, at all events, thought I was illegal. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the money side of the question a gentleman acquainted with the Birmingham Free Library said quite casu- ally that the book most inquired for at the library was a sixpenny one—Pitmen's Manual of Phono- graphy—and if people would go to borrow and read at a library a sixpenny book it clearly showed that

_ HOUSE OF LORDS,—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after four o'clock. The Ormakirk Railway Bill was read a second time. Tine INFANTS' BILL.—The LORD CMANCELLOR moved the eecond reading of the Infants' Bill, the object of which, be said, was to amend the law in regard to the custody of infants. Lord BRAMWELL and Lord ASIROURNE supported the bill, the latter pointing out that it had been greatly im- proved since it was originally presentesl.—After a few cri- ticisms from Lord Halsbury and Earl Beauchamp, both of whom expressed approval of the objects of the measure, the bill was read a second time. QuEEN ANwn's Bourrrx.—The Duke of BUCKINGHAM and CHANDOS moved the second reading of the Incumbents of Benefices Loans Extension Bill. He explained that the ob- ject of the bill was to enable the Governors of the Queen Anne's Bounty to extend the term over which repayments may be made in respect of beneficee.—The Archbishop of CANTERBURY declared that his experience had convinced him of the necessity of the extension proposed by the measure.—The bill was read a second time. I A GLFT 'TO THB NATION.—EarI SPENCER, in reply to the Earl of Wemyss, stated that the presentation made by Mr. Watts of his works to the nation had not been definitely arranged. There was no room forte pictures in the National Gallery ; but they would be hung in the South Kensington Museum, and if the hanging was satisfactory to Mr. Watts I the offer would be finally made, and would be gratefully accepted on behalf of the nation. MISCILLANROUS.—The Drowned Persons (Discovery and Interment Bill and the Burial Grounds (Scotland) Act, 1885, Amendment Bill were read a third time.—On the mo- tion of the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Select Committee on the Church Patronage Bill was appointed.—The National Debt Bill passed through-Committee.—The Earl of Harrow- by presented petitions from the Operative Cotton Spinners' Association of Oldham in favour of State-directed colonisa- tion.
'Their lordships rose at 5-25. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY.

O'Brien, who drew the attention of the Chief Secretary to an adver- tisement in the " Belfast Newsletter," inviting tenders for 20,000 Snider rifles, and inviting the services of drill in- structors, Mr. J. Moneey said: The Irish Government have no information that would lead them to believe there is any serious meaning to be attached to the advertisement. (Hear, hear, from the Parnellites.) Persons in earnest on such a subject would hardly have recourse to an advertise- ment ; besides, understand, there are no manufacturers of such arms in Belfast. The unlicensed carrying of arms in a proclaimed district, and the assembling of parties for the purposes of drill, are offences well known to the law. The constabulary are well aware of their duty in regard to such offences, and do not at present apprehend any difficulty in carrying it out. (Hear, hear.) THE GOVERNMENT OF INDIA.—Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply to Mr. J. Maclean, said that he would propose the appoint- ment of a committee to inquire into the administration of British India en Monday next. THE COMMERCIAL TREATY WITH SPAIN—Mr. FORWOOD asked the Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs whether under the new Spanish Convention Spain grants to Great Britain the most complete favoured nation treatment in all that relates to trade and navigation, or whether the grant is not for the most complete favoured nation treatment, but is limited to be co-extensive in amount of benefit with that accorded to France and Germany ?—Mr. BRYCE : As the new convention when brought into force gives to the British the sante benefits as are enjoyed by the French and German subjects, and as French and German subjects enjoy in matters of trade and navigation the same treatment as natives, it is clear that British subjects enjoy the .same ad- vantage as Spaniards themselves. THE HOME RI/LB DEBATE. The adjourned debate on the second reading of the Government of Ireland Bill was resumed at five minutes to five o'clock by Sir 'RICHARD CROSS, who argued that the bill would not produce good government in Ireland because the Prime Minister was putting safeguards In his bill which indicated distrust of the future government, and because the aspirations of the Irish people went beyond the bill. Even if their representatives gave assurances that the bill would be accepted, they could not act up to them. He turned from the Irish people to the Prime Minister, and referring to the Land Purchase Bill remarked that it was not the first time he had offered a bribe to a country. Thee, reverting to Ireland, he characterised the people of that country as, after all, a warm-hearted people, and sketched out a possible alterna- tive policy in a generous administration of the law and such conduct as would show them that Parliament would not refuse to consider any just grievance they might plead. All which the Parnellites received derisively and with some ironical exclamations betraying a keen recollec- tion of the proposal to suppress the National League. By the time Mr. STANSTIBLD rose to reply to Sir R. Cross, the House bad begun to fill up. The right hon. gentleman re- pudiated the description of the precautionary measures in the bill as indications of distrust in the Irish people, and expressed his belief in a genuine change of Irish feeling caused by the Prime Minister's message of peace to Ireland'. The feature of his speech was a vigorous onslaught upon the Marquis of Salisbury, whose address on Saturday he characterised as revelliog and excelling in calculated reck- lessness. He anticipated, however, from this oration much benefit to the Prime Minister's cause in the country, and tome opening of the eyes on the part of Liberals whose assistance his lordship was willing .toiltceept, but not in a spirit of trust. Mr. Stansfield answering Sir H. James, said the Imperial Parliament had power to repeal this mea- sure if it passed, and therefore retained the essential part of its sovereignty. And, replying to Mr. Chamberlain, he argued that the bill really opened the door to the federation which that right hon. gentleman desires, and bars the way to the colonial independence or separation which he dreads. —Mr. King, Sir J. P. Corry, Mr. Hobbouse, and Mr. Hughes delivered their sentiments against the bill, while Mr. Rogers and Mr. Yeo spoke warmly in its favour, the latter eliciting assenting cheers from the Prime Minister when he declared that his vote for the second reading would not affect his liberty of voting on the details in Committee.—Mr. Buyea commenced an able speech in answer to the constitutional law arguments of Sir H. James with a much-cheered declara- tion that the Government would show no unwillingness to I consult the constituencies. The Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs adduced fresh historical parallels in support of the Government policy, and in an effeeiive peroration warned the Liberals against being made the catspaws of their ene- mies.—After this two more speeches—one from each side of the House—were contributed in opposition to the bill, Mr. Hall and Viscount Wolmer joining bands, so to speak, against the measure.—Then Mr. Slum Lerevne moved the adjournment of the debate. The House adjourned at five minutes to one o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. THE JUITENILE TEMPLAR ORDER- The quarterly session of the District Council of the South-West Lancashire Juvenile Temples wa9 held , in the Miesien Hall, Chowbent, on Saturday after. 1 noon, when Brother I. Antlers, of Liverpool, D.S.J.T., presided. Most of the district officers were present, I and there was a lei ge attendance of delegates, includ- ing Bros. E. Newman, F. Urea, and G. Clarke, of larlestown. The quarterly reports as to the state of the various temples were of a very satisfactory char- acter. Various questions affecting the order were discussed, and the following resolution was passed :—"That inasmuch ! as the Juvenile Order of Good Templars has for its object the saving of the children from the evils of profanity and degradation, having for its motto truth, love, and purity, 1 this Council sincerely accords to the leaders of the move-' ment for the passing into law ef the Intoxicating Liquors (Sale to Children) Bill its entire sympathy with the object they have in view, viz, to make it an offence to sell intoxi- cating liquors to young children whether for consumption elf or on the premises." It was ordered that a copy of the resolution should be sent to Mr. Conybeare, M.P., who has charge of the measure. The following resolution was also carried unanimously :—" That this Counl hears with sincere regret of the death of Bro. J. P. Morewood, of Wid- nes, who held the office of district counsellor during the year 1884-5, and hereby records its deep sense of the loss which our Order has sustained." Other matters affecting the Order were discussed; the next session, to be held in August next, being fixed for ithouttipert. A substantial tea was afterwards partaken of, after which a large procession was formed. The members and, officers appeared in their regalia, and were headed by the handsome bAnner of the Chowbent City of Refuge Lodge and the Atherton Brass Band. After parading the streets a public meeting was held in the Mission Hall, under the presidency of Bro. R. Anders, D.S.J.T. A reciting contest took place, and Bro. Morris Jones, of Liverpool, gave an excellent address.

NEWTON RACES AND, PUBLIC HOLIDAYS. IMPORTANT ALTEBATIONS. For many years past the annual races at Newton Common have been the occasion for a general holiday I at Earlestown, Newton, and surrounding districts, I but this year an important alteration in that respect I has been decided upon. Up to two or three years ago the races bad usually occupied three days, ' namely. Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday, and it had been customary for all the works and plaoes of ' business to stop for those three days and the rest of the week, while the various Sunday schools and places of worship arranged their annual treats for one of the three race days. The restriction ' of the races to two days, and those days Tuesday and Wednesday, however, have created a revulsion of feeling against a prolonged holiday among the work- people of the district, as well as other inhabitants. The question has been much discussed during the last week oi two, while the officers and teachers of Sunday schools bad under consideration the advisability of holding the festivi- ties in connection with the various schools in Whit week instead of during the two days on which the races are to be held. It has been pointed out that in holding its general holiday during race week, Earlestown did that when all other towns were engaged in business, and consequently there are no cheap trips or other means of haying enjoyable outs to districts outside their own immediate locality. It I was understood that the matter rested with the 1 workmen in the various works, and arrangements were made for taking their opinion upon the advisability of postponing the holidays until Whit-week. The men employed at the Viaduct works were canvassed on Tuesday, and when the votes were counted it was ascer- tained that a very large majority were io favour of continu- ing at work during race week and stopping at Whitsuntide. The following notice was accordingly posted at the works: —" I find that the result of the canvas is that a large ma- jority are in favour of the holidays being in Whit week, instead ef in the race week, as before. The usual annual holiday, therefore, will be observed at Whitsuntide this year. If any man desires leave of absence at race week he can obtain it by asking permission from his foreman. (Signed) J.' W. Ematrrr.—Viaduct Works, 19th May." This decision appears to have given satisfaction among the inhabitants of the town generally. It is stated that the men at the Vulcan Foundry are in favour of the proposed alteration, but would like those who desired it to have one or two half days in race week on condition that they work up the lost time. It is also expected that the other works in the vicinity will follow the same course. It has already been decided by the majority of the Sunday schools to post- pone their annual treats to Whitsuntide. and there is little doubt that this will be done by nearly all, if not every, place of worship in the district.

there were people who could not or would not afford that small sum, and that they were people too who went with the determination and energy to study and make progress. Mr. Morris had suggested the pos- sibility of carrying on the museum and art gallery separately, but tle difficulty_ in the way of that was that all of these institutions were carried on munici- pally through the rates, and they could not well be separated. In conclusion Mr. Walker said that per- sonally he should be glad to see the library subscrip- tion reduceebbut just as a means to an end, and that was the ultimate abolishing of the fee altogether. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The Cuellar/a; remarked that it had been said to him that it was only Radical working-men, who were urging that thing forward, but be was glad to be able to say that there were both sorts at that meeting. The first man he spoke to on coming into the room happened to be a Conser- vative, and he was told that there were others present. (Hear, hear) Mr. H. WHITHAM said he could assure them that he bad not felt at all satisfied with the proceedings of last Friday night. He had no hesitation in saying that the chairman of the committee, Mr. Beamont, had already made up his mind that the library, as well as the museum and art gal- lery, as now carried on, were quite sufficient to meet all the needs and weal of the working-men of this town, and be was not prepared to listen to what the deputation had to say in any sense or form. That was certainly the convic- tion that he (Mr. Whitham) came away with. Mr. Morris was certainly not received very favourably, nor was Mr. Walker, or himself, by the committee. liat. Walker made aa attempt to show by figures, that he must have spent a good deal of time in working out, bow the present institution sould be carried on by reducing various expenses in such s way as would not injure the institution, but he must can- didly tell them that the committee would not listen to the figures. ("Shame.") They were told plainly by Mr. Beamont that they were wasting the time of the committee; that he himself had come into town first to attend to Infir- mary business and then Library business, and it was scarcely rigi, t for the deputation to keep a gentleman like him so long from home. He knew Mr. Beamont had been a power working for the good of the town, but there were certain duties that a gentleman holding his position was obliged to render to the town, or, if not rendering them, he should vacate the position he held, or else be would Injure the town. He thought the proceedings of Mr. Beamont and his friends on Friday night were calculated to injure the town, and, he might say, the deputation did not receive help from one member of the committee. Tbere r was no doubt that Warrington stood in a peculiar position with regard to its library. Other towns were fixing up first class free libraries and making every provision for the growing youth to libraries, themselves. (Hear, hear.) But it was not altogether education that was wanted. There were some of them who had got up to a mature age who had not got any special hobby in botany, geology, or any of the other " ologies" but who wanted to read for pleasure. (Hear, hear.) Suppose he wanted to read a novel, be wield not go down to the Library night after night to read it; but unless be did this he woeld have to pay 5s a year. He said the working-men were entitled to the privilege of reading in their own homes so long as they paid a penny rate. (Hear, hear.) It was, however, not only the work- ing-men who found it difficult to pay a 5s subscription, for it was only last month he saw in the press that the members of no less an aristocratic institution than the Literary and Philosophical Society did not pay their subscription, and it was in arrears. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) If the mem- bers of that society did not pay their subscriptions there ' was some excuse for a working-man declining to pay ss. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Whitbam having spoken in favour ef the chairman's suggestion of a reduced fee, said there was another objection to a Free Library he had heard, namely, that working-men would so handle the books that they would be unfit for young ladies to handle. That was a very serious objection. (Laughter.) But if they got a Free Library perhaps these very delicate young ladies might be- come members of " Mudies' " or "Smith's." (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. Whitham concluded by moving "That the committee be requested to take such further step as may result in either materially reducing the subecription or in declaring the institution absolutely free," Mr. W. ROBERTS said that having undertaken a task that would be of great benefit to the working classes of the town, he thought they might not to be discouraged by the recep- tion their deputation bad got at the Library Committee. He thought they would find ths more they went into that matter the more they would have public opinion at their back. (Hear, hear.) Personally, he thought the best thing they could do would be to have a public meeting of work- ing men to consider the qua-lion, and he believed that if they had that there would be such a manifestation of feel- ing in favour of a free library that their representatives would be lxund to take the matter up. The result of that would be that some one would champion their cause in the Town Council, and there would be a thorough discussion of the question. rersonally, he felt the Library Committee were responsible to the ratepayers, and while there might be gentlemen at present who were not disposed to entertain the question—some of them were not disposed to entertain it for a moment, as they had no sympathy with the move- ment—he contended that tbat should be the very reason to inspire them to go forward with the movement. It appeared that at the meeting held the other day the arguments raised against the scheme were on the ground of pounds, shillings, and pence; but they were told that night by the letter of Mr. Beamont of another thing altogethet. Were they to I take Mr. Beamont's letter, or to take the state- ments made at the meeting held the other day? If it was a matter of pounds, shillings, and pence, tbat ought not to stand in the way of the public interests. (Hear, hear.) He contended that there were other institutions of the kind that were far less remunerative than the library. Why, the Corporation some few years ago took possession of the baths, not because they were a paying concern, but to pro- mote habits of cleanliness they were willing to take over a losing concern to benefi the public. (Hear, hoar.) He took it those present did not object to the 5s subscription so much as the principle of the thing. (Hear, hear.) They said that if a penny rate would enable them to have the use of the library, why should they not have the benefit of it? Mr. Beamont, in his letter, had stated that they had a well-lighted room, and that ought to be sufficient for all purposes; but be should like to ask did any of the sisters or daughters of working-men go and sit in the library to read books? He answered "No." (Hear, hear.) They had to consider their sisters quite as much as anyone else, and he contended that there were scores and hundreds of young women in the town who would gladly avail themselves of the privileges of the free library if they were afforded them. (Hear, hear.) He would suggest means by which the £l5O loss would be met. He believed there were well- adapted rooms in the library which were in use on special occasions by societies such as the Literary and Philoso- phical Society, and be wanted to know whether those socie- ties paid proper sums for the use of those rooms. (.i Voice : " They don't pay their subscriptions," and laughter.) He believed a mere nothing was paid for the use of those rooms. Let a proper charge be made for the use of the room, and let it be hired to working-men for their literary and philoso- phical meetings as well. (A Voice: "We have been re- fused before now.") The CHAIRMAN said the Literary and Philosophical Society paid for the room. Mr. ROBERTS said be believed it was a mere nominal sum, bet he thought a considerable part of the £l5O a year which were now raised by subscriptions might be realised by let- ting the use of the room at a fair price. (Hear, hear ) He noticed that there were receptionsat these rooms sometimes, but there were many good an worthy people in Warrington who were never invited, and they never heard of a represen- tative working-man being invited to a reception of this kind. (Applause.) Mr. NEteD seconded the motion made by Mr. Whitham. Having referred to the financial aspect of the proposed alteration, he said it seemed to him entirely an injus- tice to those who had to help to support the library through a penny rate if they were prevented by the sub- scription barrier from participating in its benefits. They might as well ask the poor to subscribe to help the middle class or the middle class to support the aristocracy. Ha thought that if 'a penny rate was not sufficient to relieve the institution of its subscription their authorities should go in for further Parliamentary powers and an additional rate must be levied. As far as be could understand, the library was the property of the ratepayers, and the Library Committee were ap- pointed by them through their representatives. (Hear, hear.) Whether the town should have a free library was not for the committee to decide; but it was a question for the ratepayers. If a library were provided it would be the means of reducing expenditure in otber ways. (Hear, hear.) He believed there would be fewer people in the workhouse, and that education was the only means to bring about thrifty habits and reduce poverty. (Hear. hear.) If they only went on pressing for the establishment he was certain that ultimately success would attend their efforts. It seemed to him at the present time the poor people were contributing money for the benefit of these whom they had no right to contribute for, and the only way to get at the root of the matter was to make direct representation to the Town Council. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. GANDY said they might accept a reduction of sub- scription as an instalment. He suggested that it might Ise 3d or 4d a mouth. The CHAIRMAN said it was not much more than that at present. He thought it would be better if 41 a quarter. Mr. GANDY: The less the better, but it should be paid in small instalments. Mr. KNOWLES said that ever since he read the first article ' on this subject in the Warrington "Examiner" he had felt inierested in it, and in his talk with many working-men in Warrington they seemed to coincide with his opinion that the Library should be free. Mr. Knowles then referred to the heaviness of the fee when there were several readers in a family, instancing his OWR family in which there were three readers, each of whom were interested in a different class of books. He thought the present arrangement Was prepos- terous, and the best thing they could de was to agitate a little longer until they saw a chance of holding a public meeting, and then, he believed, the question would come to a point. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Lterr suggested that the words in the resolution as to reducing the subscription be left out. He agreed with Mr. Nield that it would be better to go in for greater powers than to have a complicated subscription of, say, 4td or 3td per quarter. Mr. WHITHAM said that further powers would mean more taxation, and this would tell against working-mee, inasmuch as their employers would have to pay the increased taxes. (Hear, hear ) Mr. WALSER contended that they shosild go in for freeing the library altogether, because, in his opinion, the taking of

fees in addition to a rate, and for a special privilege to the.-- subscribers was illegal. In order to meet the financial aeficit that might occur, they could have a volun- tary rate of id in the pound. such as he understood there WAS for similar purposes in Wig,m, Richmond, and Southport, in addition to the compulsory rate of id ia the X. Be thought by that means they could realise at least £2OO. If the committee tried to carry out Mr. Robert Davies' suggestion, with the aid of a voluntary rate, they would probably have £2OO or £3OO a year, which would cover any deficit and leave a margin. (Hear, hear.) . .

After a little further discussion, the proposition was altered to the following :—" That the cemmitt,e to be ap- pointed by this meeting be requested to continue their efforts with a view to beeing the lending department of the Warrington Library." This was carried unanimously, and a committee having been appointed, a vote of thanks th. the chairman brought the proceedings to a close.

TERRIBLE TRAGEDY AT KIRKHAM : THREE CHILDREN MURDERED BY THEIR FATHER. On Saturday night a policeman named Alfred Bligh, stationed at Kirkham, after sending his house- keeper out, locked the door of his house and proceeded with remarkable deliberation to murder his three children by strangling them, after which he battered in their skulls with a hatchet, and then gashed his own throat with a razor. When the housekeeper re- turned she found Bligh lying upon a bed with his children, who were dead. Upon an alarm being given. thetman jumped up and rushed to tie window, through which he sprang, and in the fall sustained a severe wound on his head. There is not the least liklihood of his recovery. He had been a widower for eight months and it is believed that his mind had become unsettled by the death of his wife. In the room where the shocking tragedy was enacted a letter written by Bligh was found. In it he wrote: "I as driven to do this. I could stand it no longer. Bury us all in.. ene grave with my wife." Further inquiry has brought out the followtng facts :—Pelice-constable Alfred Bligh, the perpetra- tor of the crime, who is now hovering between life and death, is a native of Norfolk, and about 30 yeara of age, of medium height, and a man of much deter • mination and pluck, but subject to violent outbreaks of temper. He joined the county constabulary in Oc— tober, 185;3. haring just left a situation as coachman at Oldham, where he had married Elizabeth Turner, his late wife. Unfortunately he was in debt when he left Oldham, and had been summoned to the comity court of that town for a debt of about La. This era pears to some extent to have rendered his married. life unhappy, with the fact that he had ascertained that his wife had had two children previous to her marriage, of which he was not aware until about eighteen moaths after that event. On the death of his wife in childbed, in December, 1884, he induced his sister-in-law, Annie Turner, then living at West- houghton, near Bolton, to come and keep house for him, and this led to an intimacy which resul- ted in the birth of a child. The pollee authorities insisted that she should at ones leave the police quarters inhabited by Blida- and she did so. As he some time ago ceased to cona tribute to the maintenance of the child the woman- took affiliation proceedings against him, and the sum— mons was to have been heard at Bolton on Thursday. This circumstance, his dismissal from the police form- es the certain consequence, and the distressing state of his affairs generally, seem to have had a depressing effect upon the man's mind. The wound in Bligh'st neck, inflicted with a razor after murdering his three- children, has not divided any artery, though many ; large blood vessels are severed, and as he can take foci it is now believed that he will recover. Four letterEt were wrif-teu by Bligh on Saturday tight, while Mrs. Pickford wag prepiaing tile chil- dren for bed, two are addressed to a sister at Aslatoei; under-Lyne, one of them containing two policies of insurance in the Police Insurance Club, for £5O and. £6O respectively. Another was to a girl in service in. Lytham; and the fourth letter is believed to have been sent to a sister at Oldham. The letter to his- sister at Ashton-under-Lyne runs thus :- 17, Freckleton-street, Dear Sister,—You will be surprised when you receive these policlea and letter, but you can come as so•Aa as you rec:iye them, as there wi I only be trouble vrheu you receive these that is enclosed. I have had to resign the police force through Annie Turner. the has summoned ins to father a child, and have had to leave threu,:h her, and I think I am doing what is right. If not, God will forgive me. I have bad nothing else but trouble sinoe I got rnarried. I am in the Police Insurance Club, and I have made you my nominee, and there will be plenty to bury us .11 and keep father in the club. I am a little behind, but you you vrt.l have plenty to keep it no, end bury us in the same grave as Lizze [his late wife). I owe Mrs. rickford £3; she can eh ker have toe furniture or you cast pay her the money ; and put a gravestone over us. With Loeb to all, hoping to meet you in a better world tome day, ALFRED BLT6II. He also wrote to his wife's daughter, Alice Turner, as follows Freckleton-street.—You can write to your Aunt Sarah that you received this. You might hear some good news after you receive this.—Alanam- Baron."

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: THE INQUEST.

The inquest on the bodies of the three children— Lily, aged 6 years: Gertrude, aged 4 3 ears ; and Nellie, aged 18 months—was held on Monday, at the Kirkham Police Station, by Dr. Gilbertson. The first witnees called was

Mrs. Pickford, but she added nothing to what has been already stated, except that she could not make herself contented at the circus, feeling certain that something was going to happen," and she" thought possibly Thigh might have hung himself." She thought this because he had had a bit of trouble. She had seen him speaking to Superintendent Stafford, and asked," How have you gone on ?" and he replied, "It is as you thought it would be—it's domino.' He them, said he had been discharged from the police, and "ha had three little children and no work.' She said she would stick to him. He seemed hardly to know what he was doing. When she and her son got into the house at to 30 on Saturday night, her son said, refer- ring to Bligh, "Mother, he's not on duty here; he's in. bed,he's snoring." Witness went to the bottom of the stairs, and heard groaning. She called for a candle, and I her son said, " Mother, I cannot; you frighten me." She got a candle herself, and found Bligh lying on. his right side on the bed, bleeding from a wound in I his throat. She said to him," What have you done thisut didfor notr' then et h but eh he edi did notb t speak.they w e Sheredead, saw the children, shechil dsm, b after found they were all strangled. Mrs. Camp, wife of Sergeant Camp. deposed to hearing Bligh go into the house on Saturday night, and to Mrs. Pickford telling her Bligh had cut hiff throat. Police Constable Knott deposed to finding Bligh and the children as above stated, and Mr. Stßiford gave some particulars as to his connection with the- Mrs . Ann Mellor, of Ashton-under-Lyne, Bligh'' sister, gave evidence as to the receipt of a letter from him on Sunday morning. Dr. Thomas Shaw described the strangulation and fractures of the skulls of the children. The jury returned a verdict of "Wilful musder against Alfred Bligh."

On Tuesday the funeral of the three murdere& children took place at the Parish Church, Kirkham. A large number of floral wreaths and crosses were sent by residents of the neighbourhood, including three from the Infant School which had been attended by the eldest of the children. The funeral was wit- nessed by about 2000, persons, who had come to Kixk- ham from miles round that town. It will probably be at least a fortnight before Con- stable Bligh will be placed on his trial. Since his re— turn to consciousness he has been exceedingly quiet, bat affects to be utterly unconscious of what took place on Saturday night. He is progressing slowly. The police have the letter the prisouer sent to his sister-in-law. In it he says he Las determined to de- stroy himself and children, and that he thus would never, as he bad told her, pay anything. He farther says the act is owing to his being summoned.

accuse him of that. "You would not," he says, "confide thorough representative in- stitutions to the Hottentots for instance ; " ir and as the listener is left to infer, why should you confide them to those who are no better —to Irishmen ? If his lordship does not mean this, what does he mean? And why does he refer to the Hottentots in this con- nection ? He has no confidence in the Irish as a people, and whatever might have been the case last November it is obvious that at Present he neither dissembles his love nor hesitates to kick them down staits. "The habits the Irish have acquired," he tells us, "are very bad—they have become habituated to the use of knives and slugs, which is wholly inconsistent with the placing of un- limited confidence in them." He speaks of them in the mass as robbers and murderers; they are Hottentots with another name, and are to be held down with a hand of Jon. Lord SALISBURY goes on to remark that he is not one of those who would "say anything in disparagement of the Roman Catholic relig- ion," or of its" wonderful system of organised discipline; " but this much he does say "It is impossible in contemplating the future of Ireland, in contemplating the future of your loyalist friends who are in the main Protestants—it is impossible to ignore the fact that your confidence is seriously dimin- ished, because this tremendous, this griev- ously misused weapon is in the hands of their opponents." This, to be sure, is not disoar- agement—it is simply "pretty Fanny's way." It comes, in brief, to this, that so long as the Roman Catholic clergy stand aloof from the National League, or oppose it, they are to be patted on the back; but the moment they show, as they have shown, that they are dis- posed to take the side of the people in dt- manding Home Rule they are not to be trusted; their tremendous weanon is griev- ously misused. Lord SALISBURY has shown his hand, and it is, perhaps, well that he has done so; it is a hand that is all "clubs," and no "hearts ;" and if we are not much mistaken it will prove to be unattractive to Lord HARTINGTON and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, and hateful to the Irish people.
LOCAL NEWS.
Titz STRIKE at the Tharsia Copper Wmks, Widnes, was concluded on Tuesday evening, when the men accepted the masters terms of a reduction of 4,3 d per week.

, . , BAPTIST CHAPEL, IV ne subject the 'Nev. R. Yeatrnan's address on Sunday morning in the Nelson-street Baptist Chapel was "Christian confidence," and in the evening "Two Royal visits." MR. JAMES FOLEY, formerly lay reader at the Widnes Parish Church, on Sunday conducted services at the "Orange Hall." 'there were very few persons present. Mr. Foley intends to conduct services each Sunday. RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS' ACCOUNTS.—Mr. Dolby has commenced the audit of the accounts of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, and has expressed his entire satisfaction with the manner in which Mr. Marshall had kept the books.

RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE —During the past month 1,653 volumes have been issued, being an increase of 218 on the corresponding month last year. Mr. J. 'P. Brun- ner had presented the Library with seven Parliamentary returns.

WIDNES WESLEYAN CIRCUIT—Owing to Mr. Cattle, of Lancaster, being unable to attend the next Wesleyan Con- ference, Mr. Joseph Robinson, of Widnes, hai been ap- pointed one of the ten lay representatives from the Widnes district.

MOSS BANK WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.—The B.nn- day School anniversary was celebrated on Sunday, when Mr. Robert Norman, of Runcorn, preached two sermons to good congregations. The ccholars sing special hymns. The collections realised £4

THE tSUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.—The inquest upon Patrick Bahan, ten years of age, son of Patrick Bahan, chemical labourer, Caroline-street, adjourned to permit of a post inortena examination being made, has been further adjourned in consequence of the illness of the coroner, Mr. S. Brighouse. KILLING • , BROTHER.—At Stafford Assizes a farmer's son named Daniels, was indicted for having murdered his brother at Stone. A quarrel had arisen between them, and the prisoner, in a' rage, seiznl a double-barrelled gun and shot his brother. The jury found hint guilty of manslaughter, and he was sentenced to twenty years' penal servitude.

MESSRS. JAMES MUSFRATT & SONS, WIDNES.—MeSSTS. Edmund K. Muspratt, James L. M uepratt, and Sydney K. Muspratt, chemical manufacturere' Widnes. who carried on business under the style of James Muspratt and S„ns, have dissolved partnership, and in future the business will be carried on, under the same title, by Mr. Edmund K. M uspratt. CONOREGATION'AL SUNDAY SCHOOL, Ruerooare.—The anniversary services were held on Sunday in Bethesda Chapel. The pulpit was occupied morning and evening by the Rev. J. T. Woodhouse, of Southport, who preached to large congregations. Specitl hymns were Bung by•the choir, aided by the scholars. Collections were made id aid of the school funds. NEw SALVATION ARMY BARRACKS AT RUNCOB.N.—Tbe new structure on the site of the old hall in High-street, to be used as a Salvation Army Barracks, is rapidly approach- ing completion, and is expected to be opened by General tooth in Whit-week. The contract for the building is being carried out by Mr. F J. Coxhead, of Leytonstone. Essex, for the sum of £1,300. Accommodation will be provided for 1,200 persons. A WIDNES MILKSELLER IN TROUBLE —At Widnes Petty Sessions en Thursday, Geerge Johnson, a mil keener, was charged with leaving his horse and trap in Market- street on the 10:h inst. a longer time than was necessary. P.C. 1013 proved that he was watching the horse and cart for ten minutes, and then found the defendant at the bar of the Market Hotel.—The defendant said he had gone in for a parcel, which had been left at the hotel. He was fined 5s and costs, 7s. 6d. DEATH OF BIRDS OF PASSAGE —Daring the past ten days it has ben sad to see the swallows and martins lying dead and dying about the village of Hale. Tne severity of the weather has been more than they could stand. They de- pend chit fly for their food on the insects they catch while on the wing, but these, owing to the cold weather and the continntlly falling rain, have been driven away. In some gardens in the outskirts of Runcorn birds were found dead through the cold and scarcity of food. DEATH FROM AN OVERDOSE OF LAUDANUM AT WIDNES. —On Thursday morning, at Widnes, a labourer named Robert Roberts, residing at 9, Thomas-street, died through taking an overdose of laudanum on the previous night. The man had been confined to bed for a period of three months with a serious illness, and was unable to sleep. On Wednesday night he sent a girl for some laudanum. The chemist gave instructions that from 10 to 15 drops should be taken, but the deceased took 40 drops, with a fatal re- sult. SECOND STARR-BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY, WIDNES.— The third appropriation took place on Wednesday night in the National Schools. Number 43 was drawn in the ballot, entitling the owners—Catherine F. and Arthur C. Lewis— to £4OO free of interest for l2r years. During the evening a concert was given by members and friends, and an ad- dress on the principles and objects of the Starr-Bosvkett Building Societies was delivered by Mr. S. Owens. Mr. R. Fogg presided. The societies in the town now number upwards of 700 members. THE PROPOSED COUNTY COURT FOR WIDNES.—The fol- lowing letter has been received by Mr. W. T. Husband with reference to the above :—" Southport, May 16, 1886.—My dear Sir,—l have received your letter of May 13, and the copy of the resolution which your Provisional Committee have been good enough to pass with reference to myself. Please express my thanks to them for it, and assure them that I will do my utmost to attain the object we have in view. I have heard nothing more since I last wrote to you on the subject. To-morrow I return to London.—Yours very faithfully, T. C. EDWARDS MOSS. William Thomas Hus- band, Eeq." TERRIBLE ACCIDENT TO A BOY NEAR WIDNES.—Wm. Clewes, 15 years of age, who resides at Frederick-street, Simms Cross, met with a terrible accident on Tuesday morning. He was crossing the Cheshire Lines Railway on his way to Cronton, when an express dashed up, and before he could get out of the way the ergine struck him on the head, and threw him into the hedge side. The unfortunate youth was picked up in an insensible condition, and was removed to Widnes Accident Hospital, where his severe injuries were attended to by Dr. McDonald and Dr. Mc. Cambridge, under whose care he is progressing more favourably than was anticipated. A WIDNES DOCTOR AND His CERTIFICATE.—During the hearing of a School Board case at Widnes Petty Ses- sions on Thursday, much amusement was caused. The mother of Mary Connor appeared to repel an accusation that she had wilfully neglected to send her daughter to school, and. handed in the following epistle :—" This is to certify that Mary Connor is not able to follow his employ- ment:" Upon Mr. Gossage reading this certificate aloud there was much laughter. Mr. Gossage observed that the signature was printed instead of written, and stated that in future be should refuse to take any notice of certificates to ' which was affixed a printed signature. WIDNES SCHOOL Bon AT WORK.—On behalf of Widnes School Board, Mr. G. H. Denby on Thursday prosecuted the following persons for neglecting to send their children regu- larly to school :—Mich. Roach, Martin Rourke, Thos. Flan- nigan, Peter Riley, Robert Jones, Denis Farrell, Michael Connor' Martin Connor, Michael Kuockton. Patrick Myles, Robert Hoey (two cases), John Houghton, William Platt, John Johnson, William Webster, Henry Annels,, John Coombes, Richard (Hassey, John Brannen, Peter Cosgrove, James Steward, Henry McGee. The usual fine of 5s was imposed in each case. Alexander Standen, eon of Charles Standen, was committed to an industrial schools. LAWN 111 tiN B.—Runcorn. v. MIRACULOUS ESCAPE AT RUITCORN.— On Wednesday morning Joseph Ditch&ld, aged two years and six months, son of a labourer living at 24, Princess-street, had a narrow escape from a violent death. A lurry belonging to Mr. John Moores, in charge of a carter named Wright, was pas- sing the post office. The boy, who was sitting on the kerb stone, got op, and was running across the road apparently with the object of getting hold of the lorry behind, when his foot caught in a dust heap, and he fell down. The hind wheel of the waggon grazed his head and face, inflicting a severe scar, and removing the hair from one part of his scalp. Dr. McDougall, who happened to be in a neighbour. _ _ _ _ _
ing office, attended. to the child and had him conveyed home.

RUNCORN RECREATION FOOTBALL CLUB —During the past season this team has played 18 matches, won 10, drawn 4, and lost 4; gained 20 tries (from which 7 goals were kicked), 1 drop goal, and 53 minor points, against 5 tries and 34 minor points. The second team played 15 matches, of which they won 11 and lost 4. The officers for the next season have been appointed. Mr. John Acton is captain of the Ist team and Mr. W. Woodward sub-captain. Mr. H. Grounds is captain and Mr. G. H. Jones sub-captain of the second team. Mr. H. Pendlebury is re-elected secretary, with Mr. E. Pearson as assistant; and Mr. T. W. Forster is treasurer. The committee is composed of Messrs. James Green, T. Whinvates, D. Littlemore, S. Lewis, 'l'. Charles- ton, T. Carr. W. Wishlade, W. Johnson, and T. Turnbull. STABBED B V A FATHER AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, David Ankers. labourer, of 3, Gerrard- street, Widnes, was charged with unlawfally wounding his son, Samuel Ankers. About eleven o'clock the son went home and found his parents engaged in a quarrel. Hearing his father call his mother "foul names" he interfered, whereupon the prisoner drew his pocket knife and stabbed his son on the right shoulder. Feeling blood running down his back, the son went to Dr. McDoruld'e surgery, where he had the wound dressed. Dr. McDonald deposed that the wound was an inch in length, and an inch and a half deep, penetrating to the shoulder blade. The wound was not dangerous, and the injured man would be able to follow his employment in a few days if he were careful. When ap- prehended by P.C. Evans, the prisoner said he had no knife with him, but before the magistrates be stated that he was cutting tobacco with something of that kind, when his son struck him. The son admitted striking his father after he received the wound. The prisoner was committed to the assizes for trial.

ACTION AGAINST MR. W. J. SHORE. OF • RUNCORN.

At Manchester Assizes, on Wednesday, an action was brctieht by the Altrincham Benefit Building Society against Mr. W. J. Shore, of Runcorn.—Mr. Ambrose, Q.b., M.P., Mr. Yates. and Mr. Brierley were counsel for the plaintiffs; Mr. French, Q.C.. and Mr. Arkle for the defendant.—The action was brought to recover subscriptions in respect to several shares alleged te have been taken by the defendant, William James Shore, in the Altrincham Permanent Benefit Building Society. The defendant was registered a member of the society in 1873, taking eight shares, on which lOs each per month was payable; and In the following year he tooli five additional shares. In respect of the former he received an advance of LISO, and of the latter £3OO. By way of security he executed a mortgage upon some property which, Mr. Ambrose said, turned out to be worthless, lie had not paid any subscription to the society since ISB3.—Mr. French stated that the defendant was a minor when the first transaction took place; that although the shares were taken ae,cl the money advanced on two separate occasions, they were in reality cue transaction, as the terms set cut in the mortgage deed were that the property was to be security for the money then advanced and any subsequent advances that might be made. Shore was in the employ of his uncle, a man named Steele, amid for some purpose of his own Steele put the ne., hew forward as the borrower and an owner of preperty. At the time of the first advance thedefendant was only 20 years of age, being born in'aTanuary 1853, while the liahiliry was incurred on the 17th November, 1873.—Mr. Ambrose pointed out that under the provisions of the sratute (10 George IV.).infants were enabled to contract with building !societies with the censent of the parents, guardian, or master. In this case the uncle was the defendant's marter, and the defendant was made a mem- her of the society with his authority.—The Judge said he should hold that the defendant Was a membet of the society, and was liable under the deed.—Judgment was given for the plaintiffs.

WEST LANCASHIRE • FOOTBALL UNION. -At a meeting of the executive committee of the above union, held at Liverpool on Saturday evening, it was unanimously decided to give the following charitable institutions £lO each out of the net pro- ceeds of the final tie played at Fairfield on Satur- day, the 10th ult, between ASpull and Warrington: —Liverpool Infirmary, Stanley Hospital, Southern Hospital, Wigan Infirmary, and Warring on Infir- mary. 'i BOWLING- I.IA.NDICIP AT OROFT.-A handicap , bowling sweepstakes was commenced on Saturday I afternoon, on the green of the General Elliot Hotel, I Croft, and there was a good attendance of specta- tors. Thirty-five names were entered, and four I persons taking two chances brought the number to 1 thirty-nine. The members having been handi- capped, and the amount of prizes arranged, £5 be- ing given by the proprietor, play commenced at half-past four, and continued till dusk, Nyhen the , contest was adjourned till next Saturday. Each game was 21 up. The 31d General Elliot has been • i almost entirely pulled down, and a commodious and well-arranged hotel erected. The bar parlours ' I are very comfortably seated, and do credit to Messrs. )1 S. E. and R. Johnson, of Warrington.

div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
Another death from an overdose of laud- anum. This week the victim is a Widnes man. Is it not time that laudanum was proscribed as a poison, and safeguarded as such?

The imp of imps has been at the office of the " Liverpool Echo," and this is the result as seen in Thursday's paper under the head of " Latest News Items '':—" Canon Bards- ley, late rector of St. Ann's, Manchester, died early this morning. No hopes of his recovery are entertained."

The Home Rule Question is giving rise to a literature of its own. The N ttional Press Agency has done good service by issu- ing Mr. Gladstone's manifesto, and speeches, at one penny each; and the Irish National League, not to be left behind, have just pub- lished three tracts—one on "Ulster," another on "The Elections of 1885," and the third on "Coercion."

Maria Sharratt, the daughter of a miner, was, with general acclamation, crowned Queen of the May at Golborne on Saturday. It was a sort of day when, as Goldsmith has it, "Winter lingering chills the lap of May;" but the Golborne folk come of a hardy stock. It was sufficient for them that the day was line; as for the rest, they could keep themselves warm by merry-makinz.

"Newton Races" have always been a powerful factor in determining the holidays of this district ; but they are not all-power- ful. There was something like a revolt at Warrington last year; and now Newton itself is making a set against them. The men em- ployed at the Viaduct Works have decided, by a large majority, to disregard " race week," and take their holidays at Whitsun- tide. This is sensible ; they want to go abroad when the "cheap trips" are avail- able.

The players of th..., "three-card trick" still find victims. Two men were sent to gaol on Monday by the Newton magistrates for practicing on the innocents of Newton Fair. While we think rogues should be sent to prison, we have little sympathy for those who fall into their hands in this particular way. Honest citizens who think they can win money by playing with three cards, when, if the play be fair, the chances must be two to one against them, deserve to suffer in some degree for their folly.

The Baptists and Independents of the Weaver Valley are showing a good example of brethren dwelling together in harmony by the way they are. combining to erect chapel and school to serve for a joint congregation. Dr. McLaren (Baptist) and Mr. William Crosfield, J.P. (Independent), laid the founda- tion stones on Tuesday; and both made speeches which reveal that they are Reformers in inatters religious as well as in matters political.

Fancy Mr. Bradlaugh having to lecture Lord Randolph Churchill for talking treason- able trash inside the House of Commons as well as out of it I And yet that is what happened in the House on Thursday evening. The Prime Minister gravely rebuked his lordship for defending appeals to physical force. What if the natives of India had to act up to the teachings of this ex Indian Secretary? The fact is Lord Randolph—not o put too fine a point on it—has been , making a fool of himself."

Lord Salisbury finds that, he has "put his foot in it" by talking of coercion and emi- gration as a remedy for Ireland's ills. He has tried since Saturday to explain himself away; but it won't do. After Byron, it may be said— Explaining his position to the nation, I wish he would explain his explanation.

Liberals of all sorts—there are several kinds just now—ought to feel very much obliged to his lordship. The light he flashes is certainly erratic; but it has enabled some who were groping their way to see whither they were going. If the Home Rule Bill passes the second reading, we may thank Lord Salisbury for having made that possible.

It doesn't do to prophesy, of course, but I there will be a dissolution—sometime; and it is as well to be ready for the sudden death of the present Parliament. The Ministerialists need not fear; they will find their constitu- ents.with them. Some of those who have halted in the march are likely to have a bad quarter of an hour. They may think that they can rely, at a pinch, upon Tory votes but those who read between the lines of Lord Salisbury's speech will see that this is de- pending on a broken reed.
