div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, MAY 22, 1886.

t,THE movement in the direction of making e Lending Department of the Warrington ihratY free to the public is gaining in• strength, although those who support it are 111°t yet able to report much progress. The ) ePutation on behalf of the public that in- terviewed the Library Committee on Friday evening met witn a reception which was any- thing but encouragi:ig. They were confronted ;with the difficulty that would be caused by the 'oss of the subscriptions, if the Library were made free. It was a question, some of the Committee thought, of ways • and means, though the Chairman intimated that there Were other things to consider, and the letter Which he afterwards wrote on the subject (which will be found in another column) shows that for the present, at any rate, he is 913Posed'to the principle of lending books to th.e public free of charge. This is a peculiar view to take in face of an Act of Parliament Passed to establish Public Libraries, and blish them not by subscriptions, either pub- lic or private, but by means of a rate of °he penny in the pound. This rate is i,evied in Warrington as in other towns, the uifference being that, whilst the inhabitants Of other towns can have books lent to them iree of charge, the people of Warrington are called upon to pay, in addition to the rate, a subscription of is. 6d. per quarter, or ss. Der year. This is an obnoxious tax upon , flowledge, which has been imposed for 30 Years too long, and it is therefore high time ...to take means to get rid of it altogether. The Library Committee, if they cannot of themselves see their way to taking this course, are certainly entitled to ask how it can be done. Assuming that the question of ways and means is the chief consideration, we will endeavour to show that there are two or three Ways of overcoming the financial difficulty. There is an income, aparl from subscriptions, Of £560 per year, namely, £533 from the Penny rate, and £l7 from fines, ezc. The question is, how to make this sum cover the Year's expenses. Taking the official figures for 1885 as a basis for calculation, we venture to say it might be done by apportioning the e,xPenditure for 1886 as follows, comparing It at the same time with the actual expendi- ture for 1885 : Estimated expen- Actual expen- diture for 1886. diture for 1885.
Salaries Sinking Fund B6 ... ... ....... 86 Museum 5 Art Gallery Library
Eatablishment expenses.. 148

Total £536 Total £687 It Will be seen that the total estimated ex- penditure leaves a balance in hand of £24., 410 of which might be devoted, if required, to extra assistance in the evening, to enable the Library staff to cope with the increased demand for books which would undoubtedly and happily follow on the abolition of the fee. The rest (Li+) could be added, if the Commit- tee thought fit, to the £6o set apart for Library expenditure; it would meet extra "wear and - tear." By way of explanation. we may say that We have not touched either the sinking fund, because that sum must be met, or salaries, be- cause they are not high, and the officials Would have more work if the Library were t free. The reduction of Lio in the Museum -uepartment is "neither here nor there." Hay- ing a good collection to begin with, the public Would, in all likelihood, be content to wait aWhile for further specimens. With regard to the Art Gallery, it may seem a big drop in expenditure to go from £4.2 to Liz; but we nlay point out that the expenditure for xBB5 Was nearly three times as much as that for 1884. As a matter of fact, the estimate kZ z) is only £4 less than the sum spent Ott the Art Gallery two years ago. "Es- tablishment expenses " are no doubt difficult to keep down, for under this head We have insurance, cleaning, rates, gas, Water, coke, repairs, &c.; but it is not much ,to suggest that it would be possible by a little self-denial to save Lio out of £l5B. It ,Will be seen that the principal saving would have to be in the Library—that is to say, the Committee would have to spend L oo less on liew books, &c.; and with regard to this we have llot the slightest hesitation in saying that it is a sacrifice which the ratepayers as a body ould willingly make in order to secure the Inestimable boon of free access to the thou- ands of volumes already provided for them 111 the Lending Department of the Library.

Objection may be taken to this budget. as objection is taken to every budget, but it cannot be said of it that it does not cover the question of ways and means; that it does not make ends meet; or that, if strictly adhered to, it would not put the Library Committee in a position to do away with the subscrip- tions, and make the Library free. Touching another point, Mr. ROBERT DAVIES has abandoned a suggestion he made, but which is, however, worth con- sidering, namely, that it might be possible to allow the subscribers to spend the £lso, which they contribute, through a book-buying Committee of their own appointing, the lunderstanding being that they would have Ithe exclusive use of these books for twelve imonths. after which they would be added to the Library. The ordinary Lending Depart- ment of the Library would meantime be free to the subscribers as well as to the public. By this means the Lending Library, con- ducted on such a basis of expenditure as we have marked out, could be kept open to all, with the advantage of having year by year a supply of new books over and above what might be purchased by the Library Commit- tee itself. There would, it should be stated, probably be a falling off of subscriptions under a proposal of this kind; but, on the other hand, is it not possible that, if a public appeal were made, there would be a corres- ponding increase in the number of gentle- men, like Mr. DAVIES, Mr. BEAMONT, (SLC,, who now contribute a guinea each? There is .an end, of course, to any proposal of this kind, if the subscribers are not prepared to fall in with it; but, before declaring against it, they had better ask themselves how they would stand if the Library Committee, having regard to the law, were to refuse their subscriptions and close the Lending Library to them as to the rest of the ratepayers. Five shillings a year would not enable them to borrow books from either MUDIE'S or SMITH.s Library. At present they are getting more than they pay for as subscribers, and it would not be un- reasonable to appeal to them to assist in carrying out the plan suggested—until, at lany rate, the Library Committee were out of debt, and could see their way, without diffi- culty, to dispensing with their aid. Another way of meeting the loss which would arise, if the subscription fee were abolished, might be found in resorting to an additional Voluntary Rate in aid of I the Library, as is done at Wigan, I Southport, and Richmond. An ordinary ;halfpenny rate, in Warrington, would bring ;in £266 ; but if it were a Voluntary IRate there would be some who would refuse to pay it, and it would not, of course, yield so much. But if it realised one half only, namely, £133, that would be within a • few pounds of the total sum obtained from subscriptions to the Library; and it is ob- vious that, with an additional income from the rates, and some such reduction of ex- pencliture as we have indicated, the Com- mittee would be in an easy position as to ways and means The main question is—are the Library Committee willing to move? If the Chair- man, Mr. BEAMONT, is to be accepted as the exponent of their views, it would seem that the difficulty is not .one of finance, but of policy. He would be disinclined, even if there were no deficit, to make the Library free ; and he points to what Ermiu BURRITT and Nita S HOLMES accomplished " without a Free Library." But blacksmiths are not all Burritts, nor are all bricksetters Holmes's; and the chances are that the thorny path of , these men would have been made easier by free access to the best books in the kingdom. DANTE, SHAKESPERE, and MILTON—not to mention a host of others—accomplished great things without knowing anything of gas, or steam, or electricity ; but is that any 'reason why we should not make use of these things when they are brought to our very doors? There was a time when water had to be fetched from the well, and great things were done in those days. But it was inconvenient none the less; and not even Mr. BEAMONT will deny that it is much handier for the house-wife to have the water "laid on" in the kitchen. And so with books ; they were good for the people when they were chained to reading desks ; they are good for them when they can be seen at the Reading-rooms of our Libraries; but they are a hundred-fold more useful when they can be taken home and employed and enjoyed by the fireside. Mr. BEAMONT seeks to prove too much; if "the humblest reader" is sufficiently pro- vided for when he is furnished with "a quiet and well ordered and well lighted room," how comes it that books are lent out at all ? Why should subscribers want to take home the books they borrow? What is sauce for the goose should be sauce for the gander. The humblest readers can enjoy a book at home as well as the haughtiest; and in some cases find the conditions for study all that they can desire. At any rate, the question of reading at home, or at the Read- ing-room is one which they ought to be allowed to decide for themselves. The hum- blest householders have contributed for years to establish the Warrington Library; and they have a right to demand, as they do demand, that, if books are lent out at all, qiey shall be lent out free of charge.

LORD SALISBURY seems to have shaken off the restraint which was imposed upon him whilst for a brief space he was Prime Minister; for he spoke at St. James's Hall on Saturday with his old recklessness and with his old bitterness. He believes himself to be for the time master of the situation, and he is disposed to "strike and spare not." If he can only keep the wavering Whizs and Radicals to his side until another General Electibn is over, he is confident that the Tories will then be not only in office but in power ; and in that case Irishmen may ex- pect to drink the bitter cup of coercion to the dregs. They are, so far as he is concerned, to have not one or two, but twenty years of dragooning; and meantime, if any money is to be spent, it is to be spent in shippinz them off to the other side of the world. He cannot remove Ireland, but it is possible to remove Irishmen, and if a million or so are got out of the way, it will be all the easier to crush those that remain. This is the reward which Irishmen are to have for voting Tory at the last Election. They may have thought the Tories were going to do something for them when it was announced that the Crimes Act would be allowed to lapse ; but that was sheer hallucination. Indeed, Lord SALISBURY says it is " an abominable insinuation" to suggest that he ever gave any encourage- ment to the Parnellites ; from which we are to conclude either that his statement is "a Salisbury," or that when he as Prime Minister dispensed with the Crimes Act, immediately after gaining office by the aid of the Irish vote, he had it in his mind to wheel suddenly round and prepare for the suppression of the National League. He does not encourage the Irish now none will

THE FARMEa AND TILE POLICEMAN—Richard Whitlow, farmer, High Leigh, was charged with haying been drunk I and disorderly on the let May.—Mr. Jenkins, of Warring- I ton. defended.—Sergeant Bossons said that on the night of I the Ist May, about 11 o'clock, be was on duty at Broom Edge, not far from the Jolly Thrasher Inn. That public- hoc's was being closed, and the defendant, along with 20 or 30 Irish labourers, were turned out. The defendant then began to shout "Where is my friend the sergeant ; let him report me, lam a-- sight drunker now than I wae the other time." Witness then went up to defendant and 'I told him to go home, but he still made a noise, and con- tinued to do so whilst going along the road. In reply to idr Jenkins, Sergeant Boseons said he had reported the de- fendant on a previous occasion, and Whitlow was then ordered to pay the costs. THE HOME RULE QUESTIO. Mr. Nelson, a Birmingham working man, recently wrote to Mr. Chambbrlain, stating that his attitude on the Irish question was fatal to his prospect of succeeding Mr. Glad- stone in the leadership of the Liberal party. To this the right hon. gentleman's secretary has replied :—"Mr: Cham- berlain can only refer you,to his speech to the Liberal As- sociation for his views on the matter. As regards the leader- ship of the Liberal party, Mr. Chamberlain has only to say that he would sooner give tip all part in politics than con- sent to measures which he firmly believes would be disas- trous to the best interests of the country." The "Birmingham Daily Post" on Saturday declines to believe that Mr. Chamberlain has gone over to Lord Hartington's side as an opponent of the Home Rule prin-

ciple. A London correspondent writes :—Lord Hartiegton has hitherto hesitated. He hesitates no longer. He is quite ready to form a Government, if he is called upon to do so. With sech a majority as he has obtained in prospect, be is not oppressed by the fear of consequences. The Irish Loyal and Patriotic League called a meeting on Monday night at Bermondsey, in support of the unity of the empire, but the Southwark Radical Association issued a handbill announcing a meeting an hour earlier in the same place, with the consequence that the room was packed with Irishmen and Radicals long before the hour of meeting. When Mr. Dumphreys, who contested West Birmingham against Mr. Chamberlain, appeared there were loud cheers for Gladstone and Parnell. Groans were given when Mr. Dumphreys took the chair' and immediately a local Radical proposed Mr. Soulter should take the chair. Mr. Dumphrevs declined to give way, and a lively alterca- tion ensiled, Mr. Soulter maintaining his right to the chair because the voice of the meeting had elected him. Mr. Scimitar snatched up the chair and appropriated it to him- self. Mr. Dumphreys then took his seat on a back form. but an instant later a number of excited roughs stormed the platform and dragged Mr. Dumphreys and the Ulster isle- gates therefrom. A free fight followed between some local Radicals and the Loyalists, during which one of the lave, was knocked down and kicked. Those supporting the Loyal- ists were then ejected from the room, and Mr. Soulter, oc- cupying the chair, expressed a hope that now the "cause of the disturbance " had left they would have on orderly and peaceful meeting. Ultimately a resolution favouring Home Rule was carried with enthusiasm. Mr. Herbert Gladstone, replying to a Welsh correspond- ent, writes from the War Office, under date May 14th, that he is not aware that the newly-elected Parliament is moral- ly bound to submit the question of Home Rule to the country; but he is of opinion that it would be to the dis- tinct advantage of the Government proposals that the , electors should be asked to decide between conciliation and coercion. Mr. Parnell has received the following telegram from St. Paul. Minnesota, United States :—" Greeting to Parnell and Gladstone. Representative Irish Americans of the An- cient Order of Hibernians from thirty-five States and Terri- tories, assembled in convention, hail with pleasure the champions of liberty' and wish you God speed.—llimay F. SHERIDAN, National League." The Ulster advertisement for rifles which came under Parliamentary notice is treated as a joke in Ireland. A re- ply to it has appeared in the advertisement columns of the Typeraly Nationalist, calling for an enormous consignment of eggs with which to repel the advance of 20,000 Orange- men with rifles, under the command of Mews. Johnston, Kane. and Anderson. LORD HARTINGTON AT BRADFORD.—Lord Hartington addressed a meeting held at Bradford on Tuesday evening, called by the Liberal Committee for the Maintenance of the Legislative Union between Great Britain and 'related. Commencing with a reference to the death of Mr. Forster, he said he had every reason to believe that on the Irish question that gentleman would have been on the same aide as that which he himself had taken. He maintained that the Government proposals had failed to command the ap- proval of the vast majority of the Liberal party, and, re- plying to the argument that by voting for the secoud read- ! ing of the Home Rule Bill Liberals would only be pledging themselves to an abstract resolution, he said they bad always hitherto refused to pledge themselves to an abstract resolution until they had before them the plan and the provisions and the details by which the abstract resolution was to be carried into effect. The Government had had every opportunity for producing and formulating and completing its plan, and by that plan and by no ahmtaact resolution it must stand or fall. There were few even of the most thick-and-thin supporters of the Govern- ment who bad ventured to commit themselves to approval of the plan as it now stood. It had been hinted that if the House of Commons could be induced to pass the second reading and affirm this abstract resolution in favour of autonomy for Ireland the bill might be withdrawn and re- introduced in altered form hereafter; but against any such proposal he protested. If the Government was s ttisfied, as by this time he believed it was, that the plan was not one which would commend itself to the country, there was but one course open—the Government ought to withdraw the bill and leave the representatives of the people free to deal with the future bill as they were dealing with the present bill. Referring to Mr. Chamberlain's demand, the noble Marquis said it was plain that the Government could not without sacrificing the whole measure grant him the con- cession he asked for. LORD SALISBURY AND Trig HOME BULB MEASURES.— A conference of delegates of Conservative Associations was held in London on Saturday, under the presidency of Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, M.P. Several members of the late Salis- bury Cabinet were present, and a resolution was pasce4 con- demning the proposed establishment of a separate Parlia- ment in Dublin. At a great public meeting held in the evening a resolution was passed declaring the confidence of the Conservative party in Lord Salisbury as the upholder of the "well-tried and beneficent institutions of these realms," and pronouncing against Mr. Gladstone's pro- posals. The Marquis of Salisbury delivered an address in which he spoke of the certainty of final victory for the Con- servative forces. He said that the policy he should uphold was the traditional policy of the Tory party. Mr. Gladstone had attempted by "political legerdemain" to reconcile all sections of the Liberal party. He had told the English Liberals that the securities in his bill against the spoliation of the Irish landlords were ample, and he said to the Par- nellites, " You will have the Irish landlords in your power." The noble Marquis declared himself strongly in favour of local government, but he knew that such a scheme would not suit the Irish members. Mr. Gladstone's proposals" must" lead to separation. Expressing the fear that the wonderful organisation of the Roman Catholic Church would be used for the attainment of temporal ends, be repudiated with "contempt and indignation" the argu- ment that the Irish people were as well suited for the exer- cise of political freedom as the English are. Dealing with the question of coercion, he asserted that only lawbreakers were coerced, and he promised the Irish that if they would abandon the practice of murdering, maiming, mutilating, and boycotting there would be no demand for coercion. He suggested that much good might have been done by emi- grating a million Irishmen to distant colonies, where they would be sure to prosper. He predicted that the constitu- encies would shortly be appealed to, and declared that the Conservatives would show themselves to be the most powerful party. In a second speech Lord Salisbury said the policy of Premier was " insane." On Wednesday a meeting of the Grand Habitation of the Primrose League was held in London. Lord Salisbury, who presided as Grand Master, moved the adoption of the report. Enormous assistance was rendered at. the last general election by the Primrose League, and the help was all the more precious and efficient, because it did not act as a strict patty organi- sation or within rigid party lines. In a second speech Lord Salisbury referred to certain misrepresentations which he stated bad been made in the House of Commons concerning his speech of Saturday night, among them being that he had prescribed 20 years of coercion for Ireland. This was a most grotesque misrepresentation of what he said. He recommended a policy of government, pursued resolutely, wisely, and consistently. He also denied having recom- mended the expenditure of a large amount for emigration from Ireland. A requisition was presented, on Wednesday afternoon, to the officers of the Burnley Liberal Association, asking them to tonvene a meeting to consi ier the relationship of Mr. Rylands to the constituency. The meetieg is convened at , the request of the supporters of Mr. Gladstone's policy, , who intend to bring forward a supporter of that policy in gacestaoftetd by a hesittipngarmliaemmebnetrairny tchoneeevsepnotndoefnat odfistsholeution is Bir- mingham Post that Mr. Gladstone is disposed to accept a reasonable compromise which would place at his service the votes of Mr. Chamberlain and his followers. Negotiations to this end are "in full progress, and are being sustained by parties of great influence." The same correspondent, who asserts that Mr. Bright intends to speak in the debate, indi- cates that the compromise may lead to the substitution for the hill of a resolution in favour of Home Rule. Mr. Frederic Harrison, chairman Jf the London Positivist Committee, states that an overwhelming majority ~e Eng- lish Positivists desire still, as for twenty years they have desired, to see a really National Government established in Ireland. The statements current with respect to Mr. Bright's con- templated participation in the debate on the Government of Ireland Bill are unauthorised. Mr. Bright's present in- tention is to abstain from taking part in the debate. Mr. Frederick Milbank, M.P., has intimated his intention to retire from public life at the next general election. He states that he is led to this step in consequence of ill health, but it was a great satisfaction that probably his last vote would be in favour of Horne Rule. The Daily News says :—The Radical dissidents have pro- posed the following as the basis of Government ftiaotiolrehn non their part :—The withdrawal of the Govern d Bill the desirableness' of ecsounbscedtiitnugtioanuotfoanormesyoltnotion affirming Ireland, subject to three con- ditions laid down by Mr. Gladstone in his autumn mani-

feste. A meeting of dissentient Liberal membera of Parliament was held on Thursday evening at the Honse of Comm?ns, tinder the chairmaaship of Mr. Chamberlain, to consider the political situation. Complaint was made of the atticks which have been made on Liberal members who are oppos- ing the Irish proposals, but the opinion of the meeting ap- peared to be that a reconciliation was still possible. In a letter to his constituents Mr. Chamberlain says be cannot surrender hope that even now some means may be found to re-unite the Liberal party. If the Home Rile Bill were withdrawo he should be sanguine that, with more time for discussion and consideration, something like a general agreement would be arrived at.

MAY DAY AT GO! BORNE. The village of Golborne was very busy on Saturday afternoon when the May Dar festivities for 1586 took place. Several special trains were run from various towns in the vicinity, and there was a large influx of visitors. A high wind prevailed during the whole of the day, but for- tunately the weather was fine. The children assembled on I the field at 2 o'clock, where a procession was formed in the enclosure, preparatory to proceeding through the village.

At about three o'clock a start was made from the field, the route taken being by way of Grundy-street, Legh-street, and Church-street. to the Smithies, and then back to the field by way of Bridge - street, entering the ground by Caunce's Court. The procession was witnessed by a large number of people who crowded the streets. First in order came the Ashton Fire Brigade and the Golborne Braes Band, and there followed: flower girls, standard bearer, butchees. Red Riding Hoedo, joiners, gleaners, bakers, weavers, standard bearer, sailor boys, gip. sits, footballers, gleaners, colliers, hospital nurses, black- smith and strikers, queen rosebud, fairy queen, Americans, standard bearer, little soldiers, milk maids, Robin Hoods,
Y

lady archers, standard bearers, bakers. Darby and Joan, old men and women. King Coffee, niggers, stonemasons, stan- dard bearer, plasterers, slaters, shoemakers, cloggers, stable boys, standard bearer, his satanic majesty and his wives, Edge Green brase band, ex-queen, marines and queen's body guards, may-pole dancers, sword bearer, sceptre bearer, crown bearer, the May Queen, and carriage with maid of honour. 'The p-incipal part in the procession wae, of course, taken by children, many of whom wore very pretty costumes. The bearers of the crown and sceptre were resplendently attired. The children who represented various industries were clad in the working clothes used by the class which they represented, the miners carrying picks and the bakers wearing white caps and amens. King Coffee and the niggers were the subject of some merriment, the sable monarch himself having a very comical look. The May Queen was, of course, the most prominent figure in the procession. She was seated in a carriage, supplied by Mr. Connor, of Sankey-street, War- rington, which was drawn by four greys. Sle was attended by her pages and beefeaters. Maria Sharratt, the daughter of a Golborne miner, was selected as the Queen of May, the choice being decided by vote. She was attired in a cream coloured cashmere dress, with a train of purple velvet trimmed with gold lace and lined with satin to match the dress- Her youthful majesty carried a large bouquet of flowers. The procession altogether num- bered about s..ven hundred persons, evidencing the popularity that this annual festival is gaining. After promenading the streets the procession marched round the enclosure in the field, where a throne had been erected. It was decorated with lace, and surmounted with flags. The

steps of the dais were covered with scarlet cloth: centred with navy blue. The maids of honour took places on either side of the Throne. The May pole was erected in the middle of the enclosure, a platform of wood having been

.1 GENERAL NEWS.
A widow named Mary Meredith has died at Llangrove, near Monmouth, at the age.of.lo3 years.

- Two brothers named Pritchard were killed by a fall of reek at the Llanberis quarries on Tuesday. In consequence of the death of Mrs. Bristown, the Vice- Chancellor will not sit at Liverpool until further notice.

_ The English team won the cricket match against the Australians at Lord Sheffield's Park, on Saturday, by eight wickets. Mr. John Cheatham, owner of extensive cotton mills at Stalybridge, died on Tuesday morning at Southport, in his 85th year. _ The annual district meeting of the United Methodist _ _
Free Churches in the Rochdale —district was held on Wed.
nesday, at Heywood. The report snowed satisfactory pro- gress..
Early on Wednesday morning her Majesty's frigata Val- orous came into collision with a trawler off the Lizard. The
war ship was but sl_ightly injured, but considerable damage
. . was done to the fishing vessel. Two men, William Gilding and George Hucknall, were on Wednesday, at Nottingham, fined £lO each for having

wrongfully filled up a number of voting papers in connec- tion with tbe recent election of poor-law guardians. Mr. Gladstone, in acknowledging the receipt of resolutions adopted at a recent meeting of anti-Home Rule Liberals at Belfast, says he regards it as a matter of deep regret to find himself separated from a body whom he respects so highly as the Liberals of Ulster.

In the Court of Appeal. en Wednesday, before the Master el the Rolls and Lords Justices Bowen and Fiy, the case of " Marriott s Chamberlain" came on for hearing. The master of the Rolls confirmed the decision of the Court below, and the other judges concurring, the appeal was
.. .. dismissed with costs. _ '-- A Dublin tradesman named Caimes was found in ,a dviniz state near his place of business on Wedresday night, his

body bearing from 2:5 to 30 wounds, inflict,d apparently with a knife. He expired on Thursday. Cairnes, who is spoken of as an "Irish-American," is supposed to have in- curred tbe hostility of s )me secret society. In the Manchester Assize Court, on Wednesday, an ac- tion was brought by Mr. George Lowe, farmer, Worsley, against the Barten-upon-Irwell Guardians, for damage done to his farm produce by smoke and soot arising frora fires of moss and peat on the sewage farm of the defend- ants. The jury awarded the plaintiff £lBO damages. RNMARKABLR SEIZURE OF A SMUGGLING 81117.—A small cutter was taken to Hull, on Monday, having been seized by the Customs on the Lincolnshire coast off the Humber, having on board a cargo of 18 bales of tobacco. 'Through an accident to the rudder, the vessel had been driven ashore, and the coastguard, on going to render assistance, found the tobacco on board. MR. RUSKIN ON FUNBRAL RBFORM.—MT. Ruskin writes to the secretary of the Church of England Funeral Associa- tion Coniston, May 18th.—Sir,--I entirely approve of the aims of the Faneral Reform Association; but, if I could stop people from wasting their money while they were alive, they might bury themselves how they liked for aught I oare.—Faithfully yours, Jowl RUSKIN." AGRARIAN MURDER.—On Sariday night, Patrick Quig- ley, residing at Knock James, within four miles of Tulla, was shot dead while sitting at his fireside. The shot WAS _ _ _

fired through the window, and blew off the top of the man's skull. The crime is agrarian deeeased having taken the grazing of a boycotted farm on the property of Major Ma- boy, who left the country three years ago. BURIAL SCANDAL AT A WORKHOUSE.— By order of the Home Secretary, a coffin was exhumed at Leicester Cen3e- tery, on Monday, in the presence of the Town Clerk and other officials under singular circumstances. A short time ago a body was discovered at the workhouse four days after its supposed interment, and strange rumours were circula- t-d as to what the coffin actually contained. On being opened the coffin was found to be empty. Ax ANCIENT LANCASHIRB FAMILY. The death is an- nounced, at Sansaw Hall, near Shrewsbury, in the 60th year of his age, of the Rev. F. G Tippinge. Mr. Tippinge, who was the fifth eon of the late Mr. Thomas Tippinge, of Davenport Hall, Cheshire, was a descendant of one of the most celebrated Manchester families of the last century, and of an ancient Lancashire family, residents of Tipping Hall. THE ALLEGED MURDER OF MR. PRELLER.—lelegrams from St. Louis state that Hugh Brooks, alias Maxwell, now on his triel for the marder of Mr. Arthur Preller at an hotel in that city, has coufessed to having caused the death of the latter, but asserts that it was due to an accidental overdose of chloroform which was given in order to perform an operation. When he found Mr. Preller was dying be made every effort to revive him, and being horrified at his failure subsequently took to drinking heavily. THIRTY MEN BURIAD.—The last arriving mail steamer at Liverpool from New York brings particulars of the terrible catastrophe at Minniapolie' where a wall fell, killing eight men and injuring nearly adozen others. Excavations were being carried on near a building at the corner of Second- street and First-avenue, on the sth inst. The wall was five stories high, and fell with a great crash, burying about 30 men who were near. Most of them managed to crawl out uninjured, but eight of the unfortunate people were killed outright. Nearly a dozen others were injured, six of them seriously. Arrameer TO BURN Dower A WORKHOUSE.—An extra- ordinary outrage hy three tramps has been investigated by the Longtown magistrate. The men were inmates of the vagrant ward at Halburn Workhouse. Towards midnight a porter noticed the ward lighted up and sparks flying about. The prisoners had collected the sleeping rugs from the male and female wards, broken up a bedstead, and made a bonfire. The master stated that the workhouse narrowly escaped be- ing burned down. The prisoners assaulted the masters and matron when remonstrated with. They were committed to prison for one month each. LORD HARTINGTON AT KRIGHLEY.—The corner stone of a new wing of the Keighley Mecbanice' Institute and Tech- nical College was laid on Wednesday. Lord Hartington and Mr. Isaac Holtien, M.P., took part in the proceedings. Lord Hartingten presided at a meeting held in the evening. He referred to the depression of trade, and said that while be did not wish to intrude any question that might be re- garded as political, the intelligent working classes would see that their future prosperity in competition with foreign manufacturers depended nate so much upon free trade or fair trade as on the progress of technical education. He complimented Keighley in advancing in this direction by maintaining such an institute as they possessed. STATISTICS —While there are 30,600 ministers every Sun- day proclaiming salvation for the lost and guilty, there are at the same time more than 40,000 Sabbath-breaking malt- stars at work upon an article which shall create disorder and misery everywhere around. And while there are 20,000 houses Open on Sunday for the worship of the Most High, there are at the same time 100,000 houses open devo- ted to the worship of Bacchus ; and, while there are 50,000 devoted persons engaged in Sunday school instruction, and endeavouring to instil into the minds of children the prin- ciples of truth and righteousness, there are 200,000 persons at least engaged in one way or another in connection with the a Ile of intoxicating liquors, and thus as far as their in- fluence is concerned doing all they can to destroy the good work of the self-denying labourers referred to.— Weekly Record. btu Cummits Druen.—lt was announced on Wednesday by an Irish newspaper that Sir C. Dilke had "suffered a vevere check" in the Divorce Court in reference to further proceedings in the Crawford case. An order, it was said, had been made "directing him to supply particulars of the additional evidence which he is said to possess." The ap- plication to the Registrar has been that the Queen's Proc- tor should be allowed to proceed without"giving these par- tieulars, and this was decided against Sir C. Dilke, who appealed through the Queen's Proctor to the Court, which then confirmed the order." It would scarcely be possible to introduce a greater number of misstatements as to fact and practice in a short paragraph. As a matter of fact Sir C. Dilke is no longer a party to the case. The petition against him was dismissed with costs, and he is not even made aware of what takes place in reference to it. It is for the Queen's Proctor to establish his right to intervene, and there is much difference of opinion as to whether he will succeed in obtaining the reopening of the case. COLLIBRY DISASTBR AT BOLD.—FOUR MEN INSURED. —A serious accident happened in the Bold Colliery. near St. rielens Junction, on Wednesday, whereby three men were seriously injured. Another was injured, but not so severely, and five others had narrow escapes. The colliery in question belongs to Messrs. Mercer an 4 Company, and is situated between St. Helens Junction and Collin's Green. On Wednesday morn- ing a gang of nine men Samuel Beckett (foreman), John Brown, Thomas Fitzgerald, Daniel Prestage, John Kelly, John Karl, Robert Brannan, Thomas Birmingham, and George Matthews ware lowered. A large hole was ex- cavated in the centre at the bottom, leaving a circular side which it was intended to blast. Five holes, three feet four inches deep and three inches in diameter, were drilled at regular intervals, into each of which about three pounds of powder was rammed. Three shot holes had been rammed, Brown was engaged at a fourth, another man at the last one, and others were gathering the tools together prier to ascending, when suddenly and without the slightest warning the shot which Brown was completing "went off" with most serious consequences. Brown's right hand was blown off, and his right eye was shock- ingly injured; Fitzgerald had his thigh broken; Prestage's eyes were injured, which rendered him blind, and his fore- head was badly cut; tend Kelly had his head cut; while others were blown down and sustained severe shocks. As soon as possible the whole of the men were raised to the surface, and the three first-named were conveyed to the Cottage Hoenital at Peasley Cross, followed im- mediately by Dr. Casey. Fortunately Dr Knowles happened to be on a preessional visit to the hospital, and be also rendered invaluable aid in attending to the injured. Brown is in a dangerous condition, his right hand and , right eye having been removed. His wife and family of six children reside in Little Lever, near Bolton, and were to Come and join him at St. Helens next week. Prestage, who is twenty-seven years of age, is at present quite blind, and it is doubtful 'whether he will recover his sight. Fitz- gerald, twenty-one years of age, lodges at Collin's-green, but lies in the hospital with a broken thigh and other less serious injuries. Kelly, wins° head was cut, was able to walk home.

EARLESTOWN. THE Vu.Duar WORKS EXCURSION. The men em- ploved by the London and North-Western Railway Co. at the Viaduct Works, Earlest,swn, were on Wednesday can- vassed as to the destinations for their annual excursions. There was a large majority in favour of London and Black- pool, and the excursions, as for several years passed, will run to those places.

NawTex -FAIL—The bi-annual May cattle fair was held at Newton on Menday. There was a very large dis- play of fine cattle, and a good number of buyers. Sales, however, were not very brisk, although the prices realised will compare favourably with those of Previous years. The fair was attended by the customary sweet and gingerbread stalls, erected near the Town Hall, while there was also a penny show. BRBACH OP TIIII PRA.ca.—At the Warrington Occa- sional Court House, on Wednesday, before Mr. E. Greenall, Daniel Garnett, of Earlestown, was charged under a war- rant with being disorderly and committing a breach of the peace at Earlestown, on the 12th April. The prisoner had been summoned to appear at Newton Petty Sessions, but he failed to appear, and a warrant for his apprehension was granted. Me was bound over to keep the peace for six months.

LOCAL CAIEB AT LivERPOOL A861211113.—At the Liver- pool Assizes on Thursday, John Johnson (37), labourer, for having, at Golborne, on the 16th April, burglariously broken and entered the house of Martha Harrison, and stolen a quantity of wearing apparel, was sent to gaol for three months, Mary Ellen Gleave (25), servant, for having, at Ashton-in-Makerfield,_stolen. from her mistress a quantitr of
jewellery, was sent to gaol for twelve months, with hard labour.

INDEPHXDRIU MISTHODI9T SOtEOOI9, LOWTOI4.—The anniversary services, in connection with the Lowton Inde- pendent Methodist Sunday and Day Schools, were held on Sunday, when two sermons were preached by Mr. T. Worthington, of Wigan. Mr. R. Henshall, of Warrington, delivered an address in the morning to the teachers, scholars, and friends. The customary procession, which follows the morning service, was interfered with by the rain. There was the usual array at musical accompani- ments to the singing. The collections amounted to £l5O Is ed.

EABLBSTOWN CO-OPERATITS SocrETY.—The 102nd quarterly meeting of this society was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall. Earlestown, ou Monday evening. Mr. J. Latham presided, and there was a large attendance of members. The reprt wad balance sheet showed that the sales for the quarter amounted to £3,350 7s 3/-d, the profit made beinz £415, whish allowed of a dividend of 2s 7d in the pound to members, and is 3d to nos-members, carrying a balance of £2 17s 5d to the contingent fund. Messrs. J. Judson (re- elected) and R. Higgins were elected to serve on the Com- mittee of Management.

GOOD Tame wax.—The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held on Mon- day evening, when Brother George Clarke, D.C., presided. The digest of business for the quarterly session of the Dis- trict Lodge, to be held at Earlestown, was considered, and the lodge representatives were instructed thereon. Sick, absentee, visiting, and finance committees were appointed, and an interesting address was given by Brother T. 0. Roberts. A report of the Juvenile remple District Session, at Chowbent, was submitted. Several readings, were afterwards given, the session being a pleasant one.

THE THREE-CARD TRICE AT NEWTON.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Monday, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, Thomas Williams, of Manchester, and James Smith, of Liverpiool, were charged with playing the three-card trick at Newton during the fair held that day. Police-constables Spencer and Lee gave evidenee to the effect that they found the pri- soners in compamy with two others playing the three-card trick in the road near the railway station. A young man, residing at Golborne also gave evidence that be had played the game with the prisoners, and he had lost lOs 6d.—The prisoners were each committed for 14 days without the option of a fine. PROPOSED WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION POE EARLESTOWN.—A few weeks ago a public conference was held at Earlestown under the auspices of the Etrlestown and District Band of Hope and Temperance Union, and a suggestion was made that a Women's Temperance Associa- tion for Earlestown should be formed. Since then the ques- tion has been well rec ived by local temperance workers, and a preliminary meeting to consider the advisability of establishing for Earlestown a branch of the British Women's Temperance League was held in the Good Templars lodge room, Bridge-street, on Friday evening. There was a fair attendance and Mr. John Taylor presided. The Rev. F. N. Shimmin was among those present. The matter was con- sidered at some length, and it was ultimately decided to call the ladies of Earlestown together, so as to obtain their opinion upon the matter. PAINFUL SUDDEN DEATH AT NEWTON. A sudden death, under circumstances of a peculiarly sad character oc• ccurred at Newton on Monday. For a short time past Miss Margaret Fairclough, 25 years of age, and residing in Park- road, had suffered from an affection to one of her eyes and an abscess formed, which it is supposed was the immediate cause of death. The deceased lady attended St. Peter's Church, Newton, on Suuday evening last, but suddenly ex- pired on the following day. The painful circumstances occasioned many expressions of sympathy. This was evi- denced at the interment of the remains in St. Peter's Churchyard en Thursday afternoon. The coffin bore several splendid wreaths, including two from her friends and for- mer fellow workers, one from Mrs J. H. Birley, and another , from Miss L. E. Holmes. The Rev. H. Monk (vicar) con- ducted the funeral ceremony. The arrangements for the funeral were efficiently carried out by Mr. Jones, of Earles- town.

This VIADUCT INTITUTE SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES.— The annual examinations of the students tauabt by Mr. Thomas Abbott, of Bacup, in connection with the Science and Art Classes at the Viaduct Institate, have been taking place during the present month and will conclude on the 31st inst. On the 3rd six students were examined in model and freehand drawing, and on tne 4th six students were ex- amined in art geometry and perspective. On Saturday week 33 were examined in machine construction, whilst on Monday ten sat for mathematics. On Saturday last twenty- four were examined in solid and plane geometry. On the 2Peth there will be an examination in steam, and on the 31st in applied mechanics. The arrangements for the examina- tion are being carried out by the following committee : Mr. James Fairclough, of Warrington (chairman), Rev. T. R. Matthews, Messrs. F. Harwood, C. Ashton, W. Craw- ford, J. Massey, and W. Grimshaw, with the energetic sec- retary (Mr. B. Harrison.) FORMATION OF I DRAUGHTEI CLUB.—With the view of exciting an increased interest in the pleasure and bene- fit derived from draught playing a meeting was held in the ; Welcome Coffee Palace, Market-place, Earlestown, on Fri- day evening. There was a large attendance, and Mr. John Makin, of Haydock, presided. The discussion was of an enthusiastic character, and the advisability of forming a local draught club was unanimously supported. It was ul- timately decided that a club for Earlestown and district should he formed, and the following officers were appointed: —President, Mr. John Makin ; secretary, Mr. S. Wight- man ; treasurer. Mr. William Walker ; committee, Messrs. George Clarke, John Clarke, Walter Linsond, Thomas Gout- den, William Allinson, and Joseph Dearden. The hearti- ness which the formation of the club has caused is shown by the fact that 34 members had joined up to Wednesday night. It was also decided to hold a meeting each wsek at which practice games would be played, and learners instruc- ted in the " myeteriee "of the art. TB Witsrarzew CONFER/INCR.—The annual confer- ence in connection with the Wesleyan Methodist Connexion of the Liverpool District was resumed at the Si. Helens Town Hall, on Friday last. It was shows that there is con- nex.ional property in the district to the value of £690,966, an increase on the year of £1.493. The meeting passed a resolution expressing its sympathy with the Rev. F. Payne for his zealous labours at Colwyn Bay, and commeedieg the Colwyn Bay scheme to the support of the Connexion. After being examined in theology by the Rev. J. Chalmers. M.A., the following young ministers were recommended to the conference for ordination, namely, Revs. F. Platt, J. Reynolds, T. Jackson, and E. H. Davies. Eight young men, after examination by the chairman, were recommen- ded as candidates for the ministry. The Rev. F. Ballard, M.A., moved the following resolution :—" This dietrict com- mittee respectfully submits to the Conference that it is highly desirable tbat the question of the strict limit of three years, as the time of residence in a circuit, should be fur- ther considered, with a view to the modifications of that limit in cases where it is specially desirable."—This was carried with only three dissentients.—A motion was carried by the Rev. G. T. Selby, to the effect that memorialists on mission stations might appeal direct to the conference The conference terminated on Friday afternoon. LOCAL HUSSARS AT SOUTHPORT.— The local troop of tbe Lancashire Hussars. on Monday, returned from Southport, where they had undergone their annual week's training, and drill. The competition for horses for the troop and regimental prizes took place, on Thursday, at Southport. As a whole the animals were pronounced to be much superior to any that have taken part in any pre- vious contest, and in several cases the judges experienced considerable difficulty in arriving at a decision, owing to the horses being of almost equal merit. The following is a return of the awards: A Troop (Ashton- in-Mekerfield) : 1, Corporal Turner, rider and owner; 2, Private Shaw, rider, Garswood Hall Coal and Iron Company, owners ; 3, Private Ogden, rider, J. Lyons, owner. B Troop (St. Helens and Wigan and neighbourhood: 1, Private Alker, rider and owner; 2, Private Dillon, rider, Mr. Bradburn, owner; 3, Corporal Sumner, rider, Mr. Simms, owner. C Troop (Newton and Liverpool) : 1, Private Pimblett, rider, Evans and Co , owners; 2, Corporal Abbott, rider and owner; 3, Corporal Gilbert, rider and owner. D Troop (Ormskirk and Lathom) : 1, Private Rotherham, rider, Edward Foster, owner; 2, Private Glover, rider, Frederick Marsh, Owner; 3, Private Edwards, rider, Edward Wainwright, owner. The winners of the first prizes in the above and previous troop contests then competed for the regimental prize, with the result that it was awarded to Private Ellans, rider, Gil- bert Marsh, owner. The annual inspection took place on Saturday, at noon, on the sands, in the vicinity of the Palace Railway Station. The weather, unfortunately, was boisterous and cold. The reviewing officer was Col. Phillips, commanding the 14th Regimental District. On Sunday morning the Hussars paraded on foot at the Victorial Hotel, and, headed by the band, who played sacred music, marched along the Promenade and past St. Marie's Roman Catholic Church, where a detachment, about fifty in number separated from the column and entered the sacred building, the remainder proceeding to Holy Trinity, and attended Divine service there.

The dancers, girls of as the Liverpool Exhibition 18 sometimes rather thirteen or fourteen years of age, thirty-two in number, misleadingly called, the visitors from Warrington were very prettily dressed. The work of plaiting and unplaiting the ribbons was no easy one in the teeth of the Although placed in various parts of the vast build- gale that was blowing, and the performance, which was not mg, and in that close neighbourhood which invites attended by any accident or delay, was a very creditable contrast with specimens of the best workmanship one. The coronation of the May Queen followed, the crown not only of the British Islands but of foreign coun- hearer, with bended knee, making frequent obeisance, and tries as well, the samples of Warrington skill and the playing of the national anthem proclaimed the cere- industry cannot but add to the industrial reputa- mony duly carried out. Next came the presentation to her tion of the town. majesty of the sceptre by the ex•queen, the marines gave a On entering the building by the spacious front royal salute, and the band played Rule Brittania. Other entrance and passing through a splendid collection ceremonial followed, and was concluded by the playing of of ships' models and other objects mainly of nauti- the national anthem. Afterwards the band played for danc- cal interest, the visitor's attention is attracted ing on the field until dusk. In a field near where the pro- to the roomy galleries to the right by an ceedings took place a cumber of shooting galleries and travelling shows had been erected, and they received a fair interesting display. In this department One share of patronage. The various places of refreshment in of the most admired exhibits is that of the village also did a good business, but everything passed Messrs. Crosfield and Sons, soap manufact- off qaietly and without disorder.—The committee of man- ' urers of this town. This exhibit, we believe, agement was as follows :—Chairman, Dr. Dobb ; Messrs. E. has already been seen and admired by a la/Tie num- Last, G. Pitt, W. Walmsley, J. Pimblett, J. Collier, T. ber of townspeople who were, by the kindbpermis- Mort, J. Wakefield, J. this:forth, J. Sankey, J. Caunce, I. sion of Messrs. Crosfield, indulged with a view of it Taylor, N. Hurst, J. Bata, C. W ithnel I ; A. Caunce, trea- before it was despatched from the works to Liver- surer; and T. Berwick, hon. sec. and M.C. !pool. It consists of a large temple-like erection constructed entirely of soap and enclosed in a I handsome glass case. The architectural design of the structure is a mixture of the Moorish and Byzantine styles, there being a main central build- ing with smaller erections at each corner each sur- mounted with a dome and minaret. The numerous pillars, arches, carvings, &c., give occasion for the use of a great variety of mottled and other soaps; and the soap has been so skilfully manufactured and so judiciously used that at first sight one is almost inclined to think that the main part of the building is constructed of the finest marble. Plants in pot are placed at various points of the edi- fice and considerably heighten the effect. The desi- gner of this exhibit, which is probably the first of its kind compounded of such material, and un- doubtedly takes its places as one of the most original and noteworthy in the whole exhibition, is Mr. Gray, designer for Messrs. Garnett and Sons, Sankey-street. Messrs. Crosfield have also a kiosk in the exhibiti an grounds near to the Indian village, but in the early part of the week this, like several other of the out-door erections, was not complete. It promises, ho wever, to be a very elegant struc- ture, and will doubtless be a familiar sight to most of the visitors later on. Here Messrs. Crosfield will have on view and sale samples of their soaps. In the main building of the exhibiticn, close to Messrs. Crosfield's exhibit, Messrs. Lever Brothers, soap manufacturers, of Warrington, have their well appointed stall. At this stall Messrs. Lever bring into prominence the sunlight self-washer soap, a special manufacture of theirs. It is claimed for this soap that it is a successful attempt on the part of the firm to deal with the problem of producing a soap of very high cleansing power, but which will not injuri- ously affect fine fabrics, bright and delicate colours,. or tender skins. It may also be used in any water, hot or cold, hard or soft, and while lathering freely does not wear away quickly. It is indeed a product of manufacturing skill well worthy of a place in an exhibition which was intended to bring together things which are the best and most notable of their kind. The soap is very agreeable both in colour and scent, and is neatly wrapped and packed in elegant cardboard boxes. Another interesting ex- hibit of Messrs. Lever is a machine for stamping and forming the tablets. One of the departments of the Exhibition which is of general interest is gallery C, in which a large number of well-known house furnishers display their designs. There are here to be seen modes of furnishing, some of which are on so grand and elaborate a scale that they would be out of place in any but palatial residences, and which in- deed can only be indulged in by people with very deep purses, while on the othe hand there is to be seen a model workman's cottage, so tastefully and appropriately furnished that many a humble house- wife might derive a useful lesson from it. In this department Warrington is well represented by Messrs. H. Garnett and Sons, Sankey-street, who hit a happy medium in their exhibits of bedroom furniture, wall decorations, floor coverings, ,tc. These consist in the first place of an old-fashioned oak fire-place, having seats on each side screened from the draught and sur- mounted with frieze and cornice. Near to this there are a solid mahogany wardrobe to fit the corner of a room, and a solid oak wardrobe, of a new design, with panel ends framed door, and elaborate panels enclosing sliding trays, the drawers and doors being mounted with solid brass handles of novel construction. To make the set complete there is a commodious washstand, with oval lava- tory top, surrounded by fine Belgian marble; the same marble enclosed in oak framing forming the back; toilette tables to match, with pedestal under- neath, and with carved doors; toilette glass made oblong and swinging from the top, supported by jewel drawers and shelf on each side; bedside ped- estal in keeping with the other things; and three ohairs with stuffed seats. There is also a handsome oak writing table with a cupboard at the end for books, and hanging from the roof are two valuable Venetian lamps. On the whole it is not too much to say that the space placed at Messrs. Garnett's disposal, which, we understand, was less than had been applied for, has been used to the very best ad- vantage. The framework of the structure has been designed and erected by Messrs. Garnett and Sons, and the painting and decorating of the interior by Messrs. 11. and S. Chandley. Particulars of other local exhibits will be given next. week.

SIR THOMAS ERSKINE MAY, late Clerk to the House Of Commons, whoa few days ago was raised to the peerage by the title of Baron Farnborough, on resigning office, died at his residence at the House of Commons, on Monday night. SPORTS AT Sr. HHLBNS.—OR reference to our adver- tising columns it will be seen that next Saturday the an- nual sports under the auspices of the St. Helens Cricket Club will be held on the ground at Denton's Green-lane. An excellent programme has been arranged. A petition presented by Sir William ThassAll, Bart., for the winding up of the London and Leeds Banking Com- pany was on Thursday dismissed by Mr. Justice Kay. His Lordship, having been informed that the bank was solvent, said the petitioner and his solicitor had been guilty of a gross fraud. On Thursday night a cashier named Shaw, employed by Lloyd's Banking Company at Birmingham, who had been suspended on account of irregularities in his books, com- mitted suicide just as a police officer was entering his resi- dence at Aston with a warrant for his apprehension on charges of embezzlement.

A MYSTERIOUS AFFAIR.—Mary /114Nulty, aged 75, of 8, Maddrell•street, Liverpool, was taken to the Northern Hos- pital on the ambnlance. on Saturday, and died about twenty minutes to one from extensive injuries in the region of the abdomen. It is stated that the oil woman and her son, a middle-aged man, occupied a room at the address named, and the sou on going home about eleven o'clock on Satur- day night, found his mother in bed, and was taking her something to eat, when he noticed that the bedclothes were bloody. He at once called in a doctor, and also the Catho- lic priest of the district. The former found that the old woman had extensive wounds in the abdomen. When asked about them she accounted for them by saying that she bad fallen on a spade In the cellar when fetching coal. On the other hand, the doctor is positive that the injuries bad not been caused by the utensil named. In support of that theory is the circumstances that a knife is said to have been found in the bed, the natural Inference being that the case is one of suicide.

ANOTHER COLUMBINE ENCODE—News has just been received at Jersey respecting the safety of a young woman, named Journeaux, who drifted out to sea on April 15th, in an emen boat, while her companion, a young Frenchman, had got out to recover a drifting oar. No tidings were re- ceived of her until on Tuesday morning, when her parents received the following telegram from the Colonial Secre- tary :—" St. John's, Newfoundland —Daughter Leui.sa picked up near England, and lasded at St. George's Bay. Quite well."

Mather: "Yes, my child." Small boy: "flow do they get their night-dresses on over their wings?" %JUT OF MS MISERY AT LAST.--,6 Let me see. You knew yson, didn't you?" "Oh yes, I knew him well." Well, poor fellow, he's out of his misery at last." "What! "I be dead ?" "No, but his wife is." When I goes a-shopping," said an old lady, "1 allers aeke for what I wants, and, if they have it, and it's cheap and it's suitable, and I feel inclined to take it, and it can't be got at any place for less, I almost Idlers take it, without chaffering all day, as most people do." Sunday school teacher: Now, children, we must bear in mind that between our last week's lesson and this quite a Period of time is represented as having elapsed. lltlling this time a very important event has taken place. Yes, Annie (noticing a little girl at the end of the clan smiling knowingly) you may tell us what it is.—Annie, delightedly: We've all got our spring hats I HE MISSED IT.—Tact is a great thing. A few evenings ago a lady who makes desperate endeavours to hold the fleeting charms of youth, asked a young gentleman to sing her a song, adding archly, " something suited to me," and instead of giving " You haunt my dreams" or something equally complimentary, he struck into "The last rose of summer," because, forsooth, it suited his voice. And now invitations from that house arc known to him no more. The following unique story is told of Tiger Tail, the Seminole chief. A sewing machine agent drifted into his dominion one day and set up a machine in Tiger Tail's tent. The old chief with great deliberation watched him put it through its paces. He then arose, brushed the agent to one Ride, and, seating himself, adjusted his feet in the treadle. Re started the wheel, and found that he could make it go. Re sewed up one piece of cloth and down another, and then gravely and critically examined his work. At last he ap- Peared to be satisfied that it was all right. He then tarned quietly to his wives, who had watched the proceedings with Intereattand kicked them, one after the other, out of his tent. Gar THE Jon.—The other morning a boy about fourteen Years of age knocked at the door of a house on Brash-street, and asked the woman if she didn't want the snow cleaning Off the walk. "How much ?" she cautiously inquired. "Thirty cents." "I won't pay it. If you want to do the work for ten cents, you can go ahead." He leaned on the handle of his snow-shovel and looked thoughtful. and she finally queried : "Well what do you say ?" " It's just as that woman around the corner told me," he replied. "I shovelled off her now and she gave me fifty cents. I told her I was coming to you, and she said—" "I don't know her. What business is it to her." "Yes, but—" "What did she say ?" "She said I'd get left. She said that any woman who wore a plush sacque and passed it off for a three-hundred-dollar sealskin would be mean enough to go out nights and shovel her own snow." "Boy !" Whispered the woman as she turned white clear around her nook. "I want you to clean off the snow. When you are through give you a silver dollar, and I want you to go around and tell that woman that any one who buys and wears dollar stirs jewellery and fourteen-shilling shoes hasn't got sense enough to fall off a bob-tailed car !"—Detroit Free .Prese:

div.p: Colonel Peterby met Jim Webster a few days ago. Jim was recently married. "How do you like matrimony, Jim ?" asked Colonel Peterby. He shook his head dubiously. "What's the matter?" "-Yer see, boss, before we were married, when I knocked at de dore, she use ter say, Am dat yeu, honeysuckle?' New, when I comes home, she bawls out, Clean off dam hoofs before you comes in dat dore, you black moke!'" His Firm EFFORT.—An American paper tells a good story of Horace Greeley at .the expense of the late Stanley Huntley, who was once a reporter on the New York Tribune. Huntley was sent to report a meeting of a Farmers' Club, of which at that time Mr. Greeley was pre- sident. The members got into a dispute over a new kind of potato, and the reporter—it was his first journalistic effort —gave a very funny account of it, which he took to the ' office, and, not finding the city-editor in at the time, threw into the dummy-box for the compositors, and it was sent upstairs in the usual way. The next day the article ap- peared on the first page of the Tribune, and young Huntley, thought he bad "struck it rich" in his new situation, and looked forward to being made managing editor. When he arrived at the office and entered the city-room, he noticed a smile spread over the other reporters' faces; but, attri- buting it to jealousy, he seated himself calmly at his desk. In a few minutes the city-editor called him, and said that Mr. Greeley wanted to see him. Casting a look of triumph around the room, the young reporter walked into Mr. Greeley's offiee The door was closed. He rapped gently. "Come in !" responued a shrill falsetto voice. Mr. Huntley did so. Mr. Greeley wheeled round in his chair with, "Well, sir, what can Ido for you?" "You sent for me, sir." "For you? What is your name I?" "Stanley Hunt- ley." "Oh! So you are the blockhead who wrote up that Farmers' Club ?" The hopes of the future humorist expe- rienced a sudden decline. "Why did you do it ?" "They acted disgracefully, sir." "Yes, I know; but what did you do with your copy ?" "I didn't copy it, sir; I wrote it all myself." "Yes, yes; but what did you do with your manuscript ?" "I shoved it into a hole in the wall and whistled." "Young man, how long have you been on the press ?" "Twenty-four hours, sir." " Well, sir," said the editor, a merry twinkle coming into his eyes, "you didn't know, of course, the rule of the office. But you oughtn't to have written that report. Of course they are a pack of fools—they always have been; but you shouldn't have said so—at least, not in the Tribune. Young man, I'm the pre- sident of that club !"

1 NOTES BY THE WAY. On Saturday morning, at Sheffield, Lord Sheffield's Eleven gained a decided victory by eight wickets over the Australian team. At the close of Friday's play no doubt could be felt as to the result, Lord Sheffield's Eleven only wanting 18 runs to win with eight wickets to fall. All threugh the match the Englishmen showed to greater ad- vantage that their opponents. The Colonists have thus get through their first engagement of the season. Ou one oc- casion only, viz., 1878—their first appearance in England— have the Australians suffered defeat in their first encounter. Looking at the game all round, it may be said that the visitors threw away much of their chance of success by their mistakes, Garrett being perhaps the worst in this respect. i Their batting performances were,with one or two exceptions, disappointing, the two new mem being sadly wanting in confidence, while Giffen. Jarvis, and Jones failed to add the figures expected of them. Bounor was the one to shine most conspicuously by his tall hitting. Is the first innings Scott's 23 were compiled with patience and skill. When in the field they proved themselves well able to keep the runs down, and if they can only manage this as well in the future, it is thought that it will be the means of winning them many of tke county games. The Colts' match at Enfield last week end Proved more successful than that of the previous week. The weather was again bad. This placed the " youngsters " at a disad- vantage as far as showing up with the ball was concerned. Notwithstanding there was one man present who thoroughly earned another trial. This was Heyes, of Accrington, who took seven wickets for 37 runs, six being clean bowled, and against the wind. ibis a right-arm bowler, about medium pace, with rather high delivery, and has a curious swing- ing action of the arm when in the act of delivering. Teggin, the new man played in the Eleven, also came off well, and deserves the confidence reposed in him. His performance as an all-round man was good. With the ball he got ten wickets for 45 runs, and in the field effected two marvellous catches. With the bat he also did the best of his side. The match between M.C.C. and• Ground and Derbyshire was terminated on Saturday, the county winning by an inn- ings and 25 runs. The annual match between the Marvlebone Club and Lancashire was begun and finished in one day at Lord's on Saturday. The M.C.C. team tette a weak one, and on a bard wicket would probably have had no chance with Lancashire. As it was however, a good match ensued, and Larcashire won in the end by six wickets. Watson took six wickets for eight rune, and Rylott obtained seven wickets for 22

runs. At Kennington Oval, on Tuesday, Sutrey beat Hampshire by an innings with 50 runs to spare. Overnight Hants, having completed an innings for 69, had dismissed four Surrey batsmen for 107. On Tuesday Surrey raised tlieir total to 183 before they were all dismissed, and then, curiously enough, they got rid ef Hampshire a second time for 69, and thus won as stated. The cricket match at Nottingham on Wedcesday ended in a draw' as was inevitable after two days had been spoiled by rain. EAch side completed an innings, the Australians scoring 109 and Notts 104, and the visitors had lost two wickets for 12 runs in the second innings when stumps were drawn. The Australianipricketers made their first public appear- ance in London, bn Thursday, when they were opposed to the Surrey Eleven at the Oval. Rain somewhat interfered with play, but Surtey completed a first innings of 171, and the Australians, who had half an hour's batting, lost two wickets for 12 runs. Late in the afternoon the Prince of Wales and Prince Edward visited the ground, and the Aus- tralian Eleven, together with some leading Surrey players, were introduced to their Royal Highnesses. The dismal weather greatly interfered with the matches I.C.C. v. Sus- sex at Lord's, and Cambridge University T. An England Eleven at Cambridge.

div.head: WARRINGTON BENEVOLENT
div.p: THE WARRINGTON BENEVOLENT
SOCIETY.

On Tuesday afternoon, a meeting was held in the Town Hall to consider, and if thought desirable, to pass the reso- lutions of the committee in favour of the establishing of a Benevolent Society in Warrington. The Mayor presided, and there were also present the Revs. S. Wilkinson, J. Mc- Turk, J. Drummond, E. C. E. Carleton; Messrs. C. Broad- bent, R. Davies, J. Smethurst, J. L. Whittle (hon. sec.), and several ladies.—The MAYOR said it would no doubt be fresh in their recollection that the point they left off at their last meeting. Mr. Davies then framed a series of resolutions which he (the Mayor) thought met, almost without excep- tion, he unanimous approval of the ladies and gentlemen then assembled. Those resolutions.were discussed seriatim, but it was deemed desirable not to be in a hurry to confirm them, but to take time to consider the effect of what Mr. Davies had proposed. With a view to that they adjourned for a fortnight, and now that fortnight having expired Mr. Davies would no doubt intimate to them whether it was his intention to put the resolutions formally before the meet- ing, that they might either confirm or reject them. He (the Mayor) thought they could not be much wrong in forming a permanent benevolent association, whether or not there was any immediate necessity for calling the ser- vices of the association iato requisition. If any emergency were to occur there would be a permanently organised asso- ciation to which to refer in cases of extreme poverty which could not be dealt with through the medium of the Board of Guardians. Mr. Devuo said he could not himself see that there was need for very much change in his previous proposals, but he suggested that instead of the cemmittee consisting of twelve ladies and twelve gentlemen, as previously appointed, they have twenty-four gentlemen. That society was to be au investigation society as much as a benevolent society, and he thought that at least two or three gentlemen ought to attend each sub-committee meeting. He found on inquiry that three gentlemen were expected to attend the sub-com- mittee's meetings at Bowdon.—Mr. Davies then read over a code of rules which be had prepared, and after some dis- cussion the Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON proposed the adoption of the rules. It might seem, he said, a good deal to take over the whole body of rules that bad been brought before them, but if there was any difficulty in the future they would have the opportunity of making amendments. He thought, however, that very few amendments would be needed, as there was nobody had given so much time to the consideration of that matter as Mr. Davies. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. BROADMINT seconded the proposition. Every one, he said, must feel very mach obliged to Mr. Davies for the trouble and pains and kindly thought be had given to that subject, and he certainly seamed to have hit off the desires of those who had taken an interest in that work. He (Mr. Broadbent) was glad that that society was about to be formed, and he thought it would be a very good thing in Warrington, and whether it did much or little for the pre- sent it would be a nucleus, and would be ready in case of any further distress. (Hear, hear.) Unfortunately there was always a good deal ef distress in a manufacturing town, and there was a kind of distress which did not come before even such an excellent organisation as the Mayor and Mrs. Harrison had lately presided over. One of the best resalts of the society they were about to form would, he hoped, be the appointment of visiting committees so that ladies in particular would have the opportunity of inquiring in people's own homes and thus get to know what the conditions were of those who would not come forward publicly to make application for relief. There were always a number of day labourers on the verge of pau- perism as it were, but be was afraid that owing to the long continued depression in the manufacturing trade they might find destitution creeping up into the ranks of the artisan class, and amongst a class who would be very unwilling to make any public application for relief. In these cases the necessity for visitation would be particularly required, and he thought they would find the ladies the most valuable and useful members of the society.—The Rev. S. Wuxi/i- -sm; suported the resolution, although he suggested the omission of a rule that had been mentioned to the effect that non-subscribers should have relief tickets to dispose of. He thought if they allowed people who would not subscribe 5s a year to have tickets it would open a door to a good deal of abuse. (Hear, hear.)—lt was agreed to omit the role referred to, and the resolution proposed by Mr. Carle- ton was passed in the following form :—" That a society be formed under the name of the Warrington Benevolent and Charitable Investigation Society upon the basis of the rules submitted by Mr. Davies, and that such rules be adopted."—The MAYOR then mentioned that there was a balance in hand from the distress fund of £95 85 id, out of which there were several small accounts to be paid. There was also a balance of unpaid subscriptions of £lO3, which he thought would be paid immediately on a hint to the gen- tlemen who had promised them. If these subscriptions were paid in they would have a balance in hand of at least £l5O, so that they would not by any means be in an impecu- nious position to begin with. The Mayor having mentioned that he would communicate with the gentlemen who had promised subscriptions, the meeting proceeded to consider the business of obtaining offices, &c., for the newly-formed ocietv.

FIVE ATTEMPTED SUICIDES FROM DRINI. -- In the Liverpool City Police Court, on Saturday, Plicebe Herbert, 37 years of age, was charged with attempting to commit suicide on Friday night by attempting to take poison (cop- peras.) In answer to the charge, she said she and her hus- band had been drinking.—Thomas Jackson, '39 years, was charged with attempting to commit suicide by taking poi- scn. In answer to the charge he said, "My wife drinks."— James S. Crane, 25 years of age, was charged with attempt- ing to commit suicide by taking poison. In answer to the charge the prisoner said, "It was drink."—James Graham, 18 years of age, was charged with haying attempted to commit suicide by cutting his throat. His mother, who attended in court, said "It was all through the drink he did this rash act. It will be a warning to him ; he will not do it again."—Amelia Howard, 26 years of age, was charged with attempting to colimit suicide by jumping into a canal. The gaol doctor's note stated that the prisoner was conva- lescent from the effects of drink.—The first case was re- manded for a week. The friends of the other prisoners were allowed to take them home.
