div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

The political situation, though nominally the Same—for the Holise of Commons is still engaged on the second reading of the Government of Ireland Bill—is considerably altered from last week. On Friday the stoutest friends of the Liberal party had given up all hope of the passage of the bill. An ad- Terse majority of from fifty to sixty was freely spoken of, and the chief topic of conversation re- lated to what would follow on the defeat of the Government. As far as the bill was concerned there was little apprehension. This measure, or some other not one whit less complete, must sooner or later pass the House of Commons, whether it be piloted by Liberals or Conservatives. What was feared was the accession of the Conservatives to power through the split in the Liberal camp. Mr. Disraeli came into power in 1874 through a similar division of counsel, and for more than ten years the taxpayer has been reminded of what that cost. The apprehension that a repetition of this calamity was in store cast a feeling of depression over the more Crowded benches of the House of Commons. It was Lord Salisbury's speech of Saturday night that gave the first impetus to change. The Conser- vative chief and his colleagues have hitherto held their tongue with admirable success, leaving their work to be done by Lord Hartington, Mr. Chamber- lain, and Mr. Goschen. It would have been so easy to have maintained this productive silence. Lord Salisbury broke it with a vengeance, and with trumpet-toned voice and emphatic gesture promul- gated the Conservative policy of twenty years of coercion. This remarkable outburst was received with gratitude by many Liberals, who had tainted themselves by attendance upon the meeting at Devonshire House, at Prince's Gardens, or at both. The fact is, many of those whose names figure in the train of Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain would be exceedingly glad if they were permitted to retire. Here was an opportunity suddenly pro- vided from an unexpected quarter. Twenty years' coercion was publicly proclaimed as the alterna- tive of Mr. Gladstone's policy, and that, clearly, would not do. Several members openly announced their return to the Ministerial fold, whilst the bulk are at this moment engaged in endeavours to build a bridge over which they may march back with safety and dignity. It is an exceedingly awkward thing for hon. members, some of whom sit in Parliament for the first time to find them- selves in opposition to the declared will of their constituents. Of the hundred or less Liberal mem- bers, upon whom Lord Salisbury counts to bring him back to power, there is, as far as I know, only one who occupies his position with the approval of his constituents. That is a great f .ct quite unique in political history, and its influence is being felt in daily increasing weight. As to the leaders of revolt, Lord Harsington is clearly implacable and irreconcileable. His speech at Bradford on Tuesday makes an end of all hope of his doing other than opposing the Government of Ireland Sill. The speech does more than define Lord Hartington's position in the present juncture. It strands him in politics for years to come, just as Mr. Goschen was stranded by his averlion to the extension of the suffrage. As for Mr. Chamberlain, I have had the advantage of a long conversation with him, in which, with his usual frankness. he has defined and defended his position. He, too, is un- approachable on the matter of vating for the second reading. But he is sincerely anxious to see the fissure in the Liberal ranks filled up, though I am bound to say it- must be on his own terms. These are the dropping of the bill and the passing of a resolution affirming the principle of Home Rule in Ireland, the terms to be taken from sentences used , by Mr. Gladstone in his manifesto. This is a sug- gestion which Mr. Gladstone at present declines to adopt, and hope is still centred in the movement, and in the rank and file of the mutisieers, to areturn to allegiance. The Reform Club is to-day engaged in a struggle, the result of which may have important effects upon its constitution and career. According to the exist- ing rules, every resolution concerning the club is submitted to a general and extraordinary meeting of members, and is accepted or rejected by such members, subject to the right of any twenty mem- bers to demand a ballot of the club upon the ques- tion at issue. But no notice of such ballot is sent to the country members, and as a consequence the great majority of those members have no knowledge of the ballot taking place. At the last annual meet- ing Sir Joseph Pease submitted a motion substitut- ing for the personal ballot a vote of the club taken by papers to be sent to every member in the United Kingdom. This proposition was negatived at the annual meeting, and is being balloted upon to-day. It looks innocent enough, but as a matter of fact it is a revolt of the Liberal and Radical section of the club against the domination of the Whig portion. There is a large body of old fogies who, having no- thing else to do, almost live at the Reform Club, scrupulously attend every meeting and vote down every proposal that is tlinted with Radicalism. The Liberal section, like Mr. Gladstone in respect of his Irish policy, want to appeal to the country. Hence to-day's struggle, the issue of which is not announ- ced at the time of writing. The death of Sir Erskine May came with a sudden shock upon the House of Commons, engaged at the moment with the adjourned debate on the Government of Ireland Bill. It is characteristic of the late clerk of the House of Commons that the various stages of his departure have been sudden revelations to the assembly in which he passed so much of his life. About two months ar6m the papers came out with the announcement that the state of Sir Erskine May's health was such that he contemplated early retirement from office. A few weeks later the Speaker communicated to the House the resignation of Sir Erskine May, who at the previous sitting had walked quietly out of his chair, not mentioning to anyboey except to his immediate colleagues that that would be his last appearance. He was essentially a modest retiring man, • never pushing his own in- terests. Had it been otherwise, he might now have been sitting in the House of Lords but at the table, not on one of the benches. He said very little about the gross job which withheld from him the just reward of his long career of public service. But I know he felt it very deeply. I have a private letter from him, written at the time, in which, whilst anxiously insistinfs that he had taken no steps to secure the post which a Conservative Min- ister appropriated for family purposes, he partially discloses his yearning for it, and affirms his convic- tion that had a Liberal Government been in office when the post fell vacant; it would naturally have been assigned to him. It would be too much to say that a slight paid to him was the cause of his death; but it undoubtedly had a depressing effect from which he never recovered. The public have opportunity fromitime to time to not ice tie childish side of Lord Randolph Churchill's character. It is, naturally, more familiar , to his friends. It is his habit when his purpose is crossed to retire to a corner, after the manner of the naughty child, and with pinafore applied to dry I eyes declare he" won't play." Very recently a ru- mour was current that he had had adesperate quar- rel with Air. W. H. Smith. The fact that he subse- quently ostentatiously cultivated conversation with Mr. Smith in the House of Commons was not suffi- . cient to dispose of the report. Like th e little ch ild in the corner, Lord Randolph would come out to play the moment it suited his humour. Just before he went to India, he had such a quarrel with Mr. Gorst, who, to the great amusement of the House, was for several weeks publicly ignored. The latest victim of his sweet temper is Sir Henry James. In a speech the other night the Ex- Attorney-General, it will be remembered, made some pungent statements which seemed to refer to Lord Randolph's reckless procedure with regard to Ulster. • Meeting him in the cloak-room immediately after- I wards, Sir Henry James made a remark to Lord Randolph, upon which his high and mightiness turned and said, "I beg you will never address me any more. Ido not mean to speak to you again," and so strolled forth. This is the kind of thing that shakes the hopes of those who look to Lord Randolph to secure for himself a permanently high place in political life.

- A fortnight ago I wrote of the pitiful disaster that had befallen Mr. Montagu Williams, and of the impending operation. It turned out that the com- plaint was a cancer. The operation, a very delicate and terrible one, was successfully performed, though it has left Mr. Williams in a ,prostrate state and by no means free from danger. The Colonies have had one singular effect. They have filled the West-end with foreign costumes. We shall certainly have a re-action from all the Japanese influence that has hitherto prevailed. We should probably have had it in any case; for the fashion has too long stayed in. But India now is to have its turn. It certainly does not admit the mine varieties, and the colours are stronger and less harmonious, but some change will be a relief. Red and yellow for brunettes has suddenly become fas- hionable, and the cause is the Colonies.

div.p: Xetteo to the (Editor.

THE GRAND OLD MAN. Sir —Your readers may have noticed from Press reports that England is now entertaining one of America's greateet poets. Oliver Wendell Holmes is a scholar any nation might be proud of, and it is with the greatest pleasure I send you a short copy of a speech he delivered a few years ago. Such an opinion, by such a man. about England's greatest statesman. Mr. Gladstone, should fill every Eng- liihman's heart with confidence that we shall, with his guidance, pass through the present oriels in such a fashion that no portion of the Empire shall have cause for com- plaint. Mr. Holmes said "1 loon across the Atlantic, and see Mr. Gladstone only four months younger than myself, standing erect with Patrick's grievances on one shoulder, and Pharaoh's pyramids on the other, an Atlas whose in- tervals of repose are paroxysms of learned labour." Sir, these words should be printed in letters of geld, they are clear and sustaining. All honour to the man who uttered them !—Yours, ' AN ADMIRER OF THE "AUTOCRAT."

THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION. Sir,—lt is a matter of considerable satisfaction to me to notice the increasing interest which is being taken in this important subject. I have little doubt that when the rate- payers of the borough have became thoroughly acqnainted with the whole of the varied phases of the case such pres- sure will be brought to bear Upoll the powers that be as will lfrad to a satisfactory and permanent settlement of the diffi- culty. There is one feature of the case which has not as yet been publicly noticed and it is this—there are a large number of persons who are neither residents nor ratepayers in the Irorouvh, nearly all of whom belong to the "hopper circle," and cvuld well affozd to pay their guinea a year to Mudie's or Smith's Library, who, taking advantage of the compara- tively low rate of subscription pay their 53 per annum:, and so avail themselves to the fall of the advantages which are only intended for the inhabitants of Warrington. Let it be borne in mind that the difference between the 5s per annum which these outsiders pay and what it costs to keep the Library agoing is made up by the heavily burdened rate- payers of the tawn. Surely this state of things is unfair, if not illegal.
Hoping that the committee which has taken up the whole question will inquiro further into this grievdnce,—l am, yours, A READER.

-- Sir,—lt may be gathered from what one reads and hears that the people who do not believe ia making the library entirely free are very fond of arithmetic. They say that the subscription fee is only eighteenpencs a quarter, which is rather less than three halfpence a week, and that three halfpence a week is rather lees than a farthing a day, and then they come forward with what they seem to think the crushing argument, " Who that cares to borrow books wouldn't put aside a farthing a day for the privilege ?" tiers you have one of those plausible assumptions which do excellent service when you cannot bring forward any tangible facts to expose their fallacy. It seems so self- evident that anybody, however poor, who cares for books will be willing to put three halfpence a week aside in order to get them; but then it seems equally self-evident, apart from experience or knowledge to the contrary, that, as cool- ing water at first gets denser and denser, so long as the cool- ing process continues the water will increase in weight; or that it is absurd to suppose any thing could remain on an earth that is whirling round in sp ce. But when indis- putable facts are brought forward to show that water does not become heavier beyond a certain point, and that the earth on which we live really is whirling through space, these so-called "self-evident" assumptions are given up. 8o it ought to be with the argument that all who care to read books will lay by a copper or two a week to enable them to do so.. The experience of almost every considera-. ble town in England conclusively proves that the freeing of a library immensely increases the number of readers. This is the fact that demolishes what seems to be the favourite argument of the opponents of a free library in Warrington. It shows clearly that there are people who care for books who are prevented from enjoying them by subscription barriers. And the reason for this would ba made quite plain to some of these well-provided-for preachers of self-denial could they but have a practical ex- perience of how the poor live. They would then learn that the payment of a library subscription means in many Oases the stiuting of some necessary, and, in the case of some of the most provident poor, the lessening of the small fund which is being painfully gathered together to meet the necessities of old age or misfortune.

div.head: READER.
div.p: READER.
Sir,—l should like to say a few words respecting the free- ing..of our public library.

Why can it not be made free? We have a splendid col- lection of books on its shelves, and possess abundant facili- ties for extensive reading by our large population. The sum of £530 is paid out of the rates to support the institution, but those only receive the full benefits of its privileges who pay a subscription of ss. per year. The subscription is certainly not excessive, but is really a bar to many people in the town who would be all Ike better if they availed themselves of its advantages. It is said that any man may read any bcok he likes if he will go to the reading room and ask for it—of course reading it there. But, sir, as has been pointed out by others, the reading-room is not the best place in which to read. To be thoroughly enjoyed a book should be read at home. It requires no slight effort of will to turn out in mid-winter—in inclement weather— after a hard day's work to go to the reading-room to read— particularly if the man, or young person, is poorly and in- sufficiently clad.

I should like to say a word respecting Mr. Beamont's letter to Mr. Morris. In it he says that any man who is sincerely desirous of rising may very well do so with the facilities already existing: True—no one attempts to dis- pute it—but is it not equally true that a man might do so without our having a public library at all, as these men did to whom Mr. Beamont refers? And where is the logic of taking £530 out of the rates to support our present institu- tion, and stopping short at the £l5O required to make it ab- solutely free on the ground that people who desire to rise mv do so at very little expense to themselves? To me it seems like straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel to gulp down without the least distortion of visage that £530, and yet to stand aghast at the poor £l5O. Sir, we must have the library free—absolutely free—and nothing less will satisfy us. The question of ways and means can and will be solved.

A love of reading elevates a man's character, and it will be a grand thing when the masses of our towns and cities become readers. Life will lose half its hardness and dreari- ness—will become invested with sweetness and brightness— and men will realise that instead of being mere machines condemned to labour they are beings with souls—"only a little lower than the angels." What a revenge on centuries of neglect and oppression when amongst our working-rcen we may count sages, philosophers, ancboets; when itsball no longer be said of them that-- .

Knowledge to their eyes her ample page, Rich with the spoils of time din °e'er unroll, Chill penury repressed their noble rage, And froze the genial current of the soul. Let us help to bring about the good time coming—remove every barrier in the way of advancement—and free our Library. JOHN GANDY. Church-street, Warrington.

Y.M.C.A. FOTt ST. HELENS. Sir,—About eighteen months ago a public meeting was held in the Ragged School, Waterloo-street, St. Helens, to consider the question of forming a branch of the Y.51.C.A. in St. Helens. Resolutions in favour of its formation were unanimously passed. and applications for membership tendered, the only thing required being the X s. d. which would be necessary for its construction and support. Not- withstanding the earnest endeavours of the workers who volunteered their services, this was net forthcoming, and Swing to the lack of encouragement given them by our in- fluential friends the venture was abolished, and now seems to be entirely forgotten. The advantages of this institution in other towns to the Christian young man are too widely known to need my mentioning in detail, but as a place of resort for our young men and a safeguard and shield against the temptations cf the present age it stands without a rival. Our town has an abundance of young men of earnest Christian character needing some place where to spend their leisure time and to enable them to meet with friends in harmony with their views. Such an institution as this would unite members of every denomination in the bond of brotherly love, and bring about means conducive to the good of their present and eternal welfare. If oar town is to be won for the Saviour, and if in the place of drink and vice we wish to see soberness and purity exist, I believe it is only by the earnest united efforts of our young men that this Object will be achieved. Cannot our ministers and wealthy Christian friends do something in the matter ? Ancelogiaing for trespassing upon your valuable spac,,—l remain, yours faithfully, ONE DEEPLY INTERESTED.

THE HOME RULE DEBATE. The adjourned debate on the second reading 3f the Gov- ernment of Ireland Bill was resumed by Mr. Jusme A. MCCARTHY, who said the prospects of the debate bad during the last few days improved b3th by what had occurred in- side and outside the House. He criticised the speech of the Marquis of Salisbury, and characterised it as bombast. Be ' said it did not give any other scheme for government of Ireland but coercion. Lord Hattington'e speech, beyond saying be would not do this or that, hid out no plan. The bill of the Government, therefore, was the only real pro- posal that they bad before them. He did not, however, ap- prove of all the proposals contained in the bill. They ac- cepted it, as it gave them local self-government and a Par- liament on College Green. Alluding to the proposal for excluding the Irish members from that House, be said he did not know before that some of the English mernbere were so attached to them that they would wreck the bill alto- gether rather than lose the enjoyment and advantage of their presence. Ireland could not afford to wait fer the working out of a scheme of Imperial federation, and they thought that the best thing that could be done would be to form an Irish Parliament, which would be really to form a portion of a federation at any time that a scheme for that purpose should be brought forward. He felt certain the Premier would not haul down his flag to brag, and he trusted he would not listen to any proposal for the mutilation of his measure. He also hoped that he would not hang up the Bill for another session. He urged him to go on in his course, adhere to his scheme, and let those opposed to ttorae Rule do their worst. (Cheers.) An appeal to the country on this measure was urged. He had no fear of the result. If that appeal was made, all be had to say was—God defend the right.—Mr. FINL&Y op- posed the Bill, as it destroyed the Imperial Parliament. He believed it would only be used by Irish members as a step- ping stone to other measures. He strongly denied that it would give autonomy to Ireland. He was ready to give a large measure of local self-government to Ireland that would be compatable with the union, but the present Bill was incompatable. It had nothing like finality about it, and if it became law it must be followed by the Land Purchase Bill. To reject the bill was the path of honour, and he hoped for the Liberal party it would be found the path of safety also.— Mr. SERGEANT SIIWN supported the second reading- of the J. F. O'BRIEN said, although he had in 1867 beera sentenced to be hanged, drawn, and quartered for having joined in an armed resistance to the British Government, he still lived to give his strongest support to the bill. The carrying out of this message ef peace was the surest way of securing peace in Ireland and good will both at home and abroad.
[LEFT SITTING.]

div.head: SOCIAL REVOLT (No. 2).
div.p: THE SOCIAL REVOLT (No. 2).

Sir,—We want manufacturers to come forward and state plainly what the abuses are that are hampering trade; what evils there are that can be remedied; what men, who if sent to Parliament will tear asunder the bends that are squeez- ing out the life of British trade. We want to be agreed as to what these bonds are, and to keow that it is these, and not the earnings of the workmen that want to be dealt with. In every branch of trade, whether of iron, cotton, or coal, the output is increasing to an alarming extent, and all this while the labourers's earnings are surely, and not so slowly. decreasing. While the state of things to which I have referred is be- coming daily more apparent, good easy souls are busying themselves to find out a way of relieving the distress. A few rich ladies and gentlemen mostly unconnected with trade, and as a rule of Tory leaning, meet together, and think that by forming a Permanent Relief Society they are doing something to avert and banish from our midst what is fast becoming chronic distress. Mistress Partington with her mop was never engaged in a more hopeless task. It is like looking at the topmost branch of a tree for the worm that is eating away at the root. The Rector, in a letter sent to the Mayor, utterly oblivious of the fact that he and his party are the chief obstacles in the way of land reform, makes such suggestions as to him appear good. "There should be a great benefit club established, to which all should subscribe, all ahould insure, according to their means, when in work, as for sickness and relief." Gentlemen becoming honorary members by subscribing LI is should then "kindly appoint" from the working-men members the working committee After holding meetings in "schoolrooms," dining together. old and young, rich and poor, should all go together to places of worship. Could childishness go further than this The Rector must be up in a balloon, and not know what is really going on in this mundane world of ours. The whole of the Rector's letter, as a contribution to the various sug- gestions given for relieving .distress, is simply a staving off of the day when the masses, who are now depending upon weekly wages, will rise in their own might, determined no longer to have as their adviser either a Tory Hector, or to receive as charity that which they know to be their own.

The battle of trade will have to be fought out by work- men and their employers combining against cast and privi- lege. Trade must not be driven away because a squirearchy wants to fatten on royalty rents. People must not be im- poverished bezauee a hierarchy requires tithes for its sub- sistence. As Mr. Thomas Morris said before the Liverpool Polytechnic Society :—" The time that has been spent in grumbling over depression must now be spent in improving our methods and our products, and if we do this our lost laurels will be regained and fresh one won; and so long as England has a lump of ironstone, a piece of limestone, and a cob of coal, she will command the respect of all the buyers and users of iron in the world." We shall now begin to perceive that the doctrine preached by Henry George is quite true. "It is the continuous in- crease of rent, the price that labour is compelled to pay for the use of the land, which strips the many of the wealth they justly earn, to pile it up in the bands of the few who do nothing to earn it. Why should they who suffer from this injustice hesitate for one moment to sweep it away ? Who are the landlords that they should be permitted to reap where they have not sown ?' In a further communication I will notice the recently- issued report of the Royal Commission on Trade Depres- sion.—Yours,
H. WHITHAM.
"WEDNESDAY'S OBSERVER."

"We beg to announce to our readers that Wednesday's ' Observer' will be discontinued in future. For some time past, with the Wednesday's, the Newton (published on Fri- day mornings), and the Warrington issue on Saturday, we have had three late nights a week, and very often all night. With more time on our hands we think we shall be able to turn out a much better Saturday's paper, conminlng all the week's news, and as we cortemplate opening out in other distrlct,, it will be impossible, at present, to keep on the Wednesday's issue with any degree of satisfaction. Should an election crop up at any time, we shall always be prepared to resume the Wednesday's issue."— Warringt on Observer. Poor thing! it sickened in the night and died, But no one cared for it, so no one cried. Its origin was somewhere in the gutter; Its best of speech was something of a stutter. To tell the truth it really never meant, So when it did it was by accident. A party tool in every shady action, Yet to its party ne'er gave satisfaction. Poor thing indeed! 'tis gone, as all things should (Of the earth earthy) to its native mud. It ought to have an epitaph, but then, To name its worth would puzzle gods and men; Still this much we may say of it with fervour, "Alike in life and death; here lies the 'Observer." —ED. Ex.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

JUBILEE SINGERS.—A concert of sacred slave melodies was given in the Congregational School-room, Lymm, on Tuesday evening, by the Canadian Jubilee Singers. There was a good attendance, and the concert was much enjoyed.

ADJOURNED VESTRY MEwriNG.—The adjourned Easter vestry meeting was held in the vestry on Tuesday evening, the Rev. G. W. Guest in the chair. There were present— the Rev. E. G. Lomax and Messrs. T. P. Norris, A. W. Cal- lender, T. A. Jones, H. S. Saville, T. Ardern, C. Clegg, Dr. Beabazon, Dr. Fox, fte. The alterations in the plans of Mr. C. Clegg for the erection of a porch over the north door of the church were laid before the meeting and passed, this being the only business. LYMM WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—On Monday night a meet- ing of the congregation worshipping at the above chapel was held in the schoolroom to consider "the present condi- tion of the work and what can be done to create a greater interest in the same." Tea was provided at 6-30 by the generosityof Mr. and Mrs. Dodds, to which about 120 per- sons sat down. After tea the meeting was addressed by the Rev. James McTurk, of Warrington, chairman ; Mr. Brown, the Rev. James Scarborough. returned missionary from China; and Messrs. Dodds, Newburn, F. 0. Moston, James Gilberts and Mairs.

LYMM LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—The following letters from Mr. Gladstone and Mr. John Morley, have been received by Mr. J. A. Swanwick, chairman of the Lymm Liberal Associa- tion :—" 10, Downing-street, May 7th, 1886. —Sir,—! am directed by Mr. Gladstone to thank you for the communica- tion with which you have favoured him, on behalf of the Lymm District Liberal Association.—l am, sir, your obe- dient servant, G. W. SPENCER LYTTELTON.—J. A. Swan- wick, Esq."—" Irish Office, Great Queen-street.—Sir,—l am directed by Mr. Morley to acknowledge the receipt of your letter dated the sth inst., and to saw that he has re- ceived with mach satisfaction the resolution of the Lymm Liberal Association in support of the Irish policy of the Government.—l am, your obedient servant, T. BROWNING. J. A. Swanwick, Esq." THE PRIMROSE LEAOI7I.—OR Thursday evening a tea party to celebrate the opening of the Lymm habitation of the above league was held in a tent erected en the grounds of Mr. T. P. Norris, Eagle Brow House. There was a good attendance. After tea a meeting was held presided over by Mr. T. P. Norris. Sir W. C. Brooks, M.P., was present, and in the course of an address referred to the Irish question. He said that they could not afford to let Ireland be as it was when once it had a Parliament of its own, to become the nest, the nucleus, the resting place, and the eathering position of any nation, be it France or America, who choose to have hostile designs on England. (Cheers.) If they could afford it they dare not, because they dare not face the the injustice of doing so, because they would be behaving treacherously, and wrongly, and timorously to that other portion of Ireland which was loyal. There were two Irelands. There was the loyal Ireland and the disloyal Ireland, and should they for the sake of pleasing the die. loyal portion of Ireland sacrifice those law-abiding, those good and true men who stood up for them, and who felt that they had placed themselves under their protection ? (A voice: "Never.") It was scandalous to suggest such a thing, and he was sure that the good sense and the good feeling of Englishmen and ot Scotchmen would never allow it to be done. (Cheers.) He saw a scene in the House of Commons the other night that delighted him. It was a silent but a most sig- nificant one, and they would be glad to hear of it. One of their Conservative members, turning to the phalanx of Irishmen, said," What want you? What injurious posi- tion is there from which we are not anxious to relieve you? What grievance have you that is not yet nnredressed ?" There was silence, silence like the silence in that tent. The Irish had no grievance. On the contrary, we have stepped beyond those positions which ought to be observed as be- tween man and man, and the tenants of Ireland had privi- leges and enjoyments that did not belong to the tenants of England and of Scotland, and the Irish had no grievance of which they could complain except that Ireland was not their own as they desired it to be.—Addresses were also given by Mr. Booth Barry and oth or gentlemen, and various resolutions passed.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

THE COLLINGWOOD ACCIDENT.— MT. WOODALL, replying to Captain Price, said it was not intended to add Colonel Hope to the committee to inquire into the bursting of the gun on board the Collingwood. He would, however, be in- vited to give his opinion on the subject. The evidence of independent persons would be gladly accepted by the com- mittee making the inquiry. The ordnance committee was responsible for the design of the gun. SCHOOLS IN GERNIANY.—Sir L. PLATFAIR, replying to Sir H. Holland, said the report of Mr. Matthew Arnold on schools in Germany had been received. He had laid a.copy of it on the table that day. He would get the report printed without delay. SOLDIERS AND POLITICS.—Mr. CAMPBELL.BANNERMAN said the Queen's regulations prohibited soldiers attending political meetings. He would make inquiry into the attend- ance of the bandsman at the Primrose neeeting at the Opera House on Saturday.

THE IMPENDING Divistotc—Sir M. Blum asked when it was likely that the debate on the second reading of the Government of Ireland Bill would terminate, and whether the vote on account was to be taken on Monday.—Lord HARTINGTON Said those who opposed the bill did not desire to prolong the debate.—Mr. GLADSTONE Said he could rot then modify the statement he had already made. He would, however, make further inquiry. It was intended to take a vote on account on Monday. The Government of Ireland Bill would be the second order on that day.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

A fire broke out on Friday morning in the joiners' yards of Met.srs. Hunter and Brimms. The damage, which is covered by insurance, is estimated at about £2,000. When the stumps were drawn at the Oval on Friday evening, the Australians, in the second innings, had made 171 for nine wickete ; Giffen and Evans not out. On Friday morning the condition of Constable Bligh showed gradual improvement. The wound is healing, and his recovery is certain. The prisoner is now fully conscious land aware of his position. THE Corriere; TRADE.—The Oldham cotton trade for 'some time past has been in a very depressed condition, and this is painfully manifest by losses declared by limited com- panies. Out of 87 spinning companies, 00 show adverse balances and 27 profits. The losses in the aggregate amount to over £116,000. and profits to £26,000. MURDER IN IRELAND.—At Ballween, county Cork, on Friday, John Neill was committed for trial for the murder of Daniel Neill, by shooting him at Knocks, on the high road between Clonakilty and Dunmanevay, on April 2nd. There is some mystery as to prisoner's personal identity, but witnesses who knew him both in Ireland and America mere positively that he is the murdered man's son, who left that district some years ago. ATTEMPTED MURDER OF AN ALDERMAN.—At twelve o'clock on Friday a shocking affair took place at Poole. Alderman Hamilton was just leaving the town hall, where he had been attending a committee meeting of the Town Council, when a man named John King stepped up to him and, after eome conversation, fired several shots from a small revolver at Mr. Hamilton, whose injuries are serious. King gave himself, tip, and will be charged with attempt to murder. INTERMEDIATE EDUCATION.—On Friday afternoon Earl Spencer and Sir Lyon Playfair received a deputation of Welsh members of Parliament for the purpose of discussing the lines upon which the proposed Welsh Intermediate Edu- cation Bill should be drawn. After a long discussion, in which nearly every member of the deputation took part, Earl Spencer said it remained a question for very grave con- sideration whether the Government would be able to deal with this important sabject within the next few months. Unless circumstances changed very much, there would be very considerable difficulty in introducing any bill of this importance in the present House of Commons. They mast trust the Government to decide this point. THE QIIEW: AND THE COLONIAL EXHIBITION.--Ilet Majesty, with Princess Beatrice, left Windsor by special train on Friday morning for Paddington, mad drove thence to the exhibition. A closed carriage, escorted by her equerries-in-waiting, crossed Hyde Park to the exhibition, where a large crowd assembled at the doors received her Majesty very cordially. The Prince of Wales, as president of the executive committee, received the Queen at the entrance, and escorted her through the colonial sec- tion, which her Majesty had not previously visited. The inspection was quite private, only the commissioners of the various colonies being present. It lasted an hour and a half.

div.head: HOME RULE QUESTION.
div.p: THE HOME RULE QUESTION.

Sir Arthur Bass, the Liberal member for the Burton division. Staffordshire, writes that be is not aware why his name has been placed on the list of doubtful supporters of Mr. Gladstone's Irish Government Bill. He knows that many of the names in the list are those of gentlemen who are supporters of the bill. Per himself he does not think the present bill affords in all its details satisfactory basis for a permanent settlement of the Irish question; but he is prepared to vote for the second reading as an affirmation of the principle that a very large measure of local Govern- ment be conceded to Ireland. It was asserted on Friday that the treasurers of the com- mittee by which the Orange manifesto was issued declared that money was pouring in to them so fast that they did not know what to do with it. They assert that at the pre- sent rate they will have £lOO,OOO for the services of the Orange crusade in less than a month. The London correspondent of the "Dublin Express " states !Positively that the second week in June is fixed upon for the dissolution of Parliament. The date is given him, he says, by an official whose information generally is abso- lutely reliable. Some of the supporters of the Government still express hopes of a majority upon the second reading of the Home Rule Bill. Ttpis expectation is based on the assumption that a number of the Liberal dissentients included in recent calmilations are disposPd to reconsider their position and vote with the Government.
THE SENTENCE OF ALDERMAN JACHNE. NSW YORK, FRIDAY AFTERNOON—The Court has re- fused the appcal to star execution of the sentence on Aid. Jacbue.
THE EXPULSION OF FRENCH PRINCES.
PARIS, FRlDAY.—According to a journal usually well in- formed it is now certain that the Comte de Paris will re- ceive a notice forbidding him to re-enter France.
REPORTED MURDEA OF A MISSIONARY AND BIS WIFE.

A telegram has reached Denton stating that the Rev. John and Mrs. Houghton bad been murdered by the Masai tribe at Golbaubi in the Galla country of Africa. The par- ties are natives of Denton, and were married there in Sep- tember' 1884. They left to join the Rey. Thomas Wakefield on theEist Coast of Africa in October, 1884. The Masais are a tribe living by plunder. It is stated that Mrs. Houghton 1713 a native of Stockpot. GREECE AND TURKEY. SEVERE FIGHTING. TURKISH TROOYS FUT 10 FLIGHT. ATHENS, FAIDLY, 11-40 s..x.—A despatch from the fron- tier, dated ten o'clock this morning, states that firing be- tween the Greek and Turkish outposts continues in the same positions. The Turks are resolutely endeavouring to occupy the positiom of Analipsis, but have been vigorously repulsed at l'hiothendra after severe fighting, the Greeks remaining firm. Greek infantry are pursuing the Turks near St. Athana- sins. The Turkish earthworks opposite Analipsis have been destroyed by the fire of the Greek artillery. The Turks, who were strongly entrenched at Sathosibia, are fall- ing back upon 1-14ssan Melina. At half-past ten o'clock the Greeks reocospred itairaktari.

A Central News telegram, dated Athens, Friday morning, says :--An official telegram from the frontier confirms the statement that the Turks opened an attack upon three forti- fied Greek positions OR the Olympian frontier. The affair was a bloodless one, the Turks, it is stated having opened fire from some distance and then retiring to their original positions.

div.head: NEW GREEK MINISTRY.
div.p: THE NEW GREEK MINISTRY.

A Central News telegram, dated Athens, Friday morning, says :—M. Tricoupis has succeeded in forming his minis- try. The list which will be submitted to the King this morning is as follows !—M. Tricoupis, Minister for Finance and War (provisionally); M. Lombardos, Minister of the Interior; M. Vtoulpiois, Minister of Justice ; M. Mane. tar, Minister of logruction ; M. Theotokis, Minister of Marine. The King will doubtless approve of this Cabinet. Already a calmer feeling begins to prevail, and it is con- fidently believed that Greek troubles are approaching an end.

OUR GERMAN RIVALS.

The London " Echo " of Tuesday calls attention in the following terms to the keen competition of Germany as a commercial rival of France and England :—At the time of the Crimean War there were two things which excited the ridicule of Europe—German pretence to be a military Power and German ambition to become a commercial Power. Since that date the other nations of Europe have certainly had to laugh on the other side of the mouth. The fact that the Germans were too prudent to join England, France, Italy, and Turkey in humbling the Russian Czar is now recognised, though somewhat late, as no proof that the Germans were cowards in battle, mere mili- tary martinets, good for nothing hut the mag- nificent drill which excited and delighted Thomas Carlyle. The Republique Francaise, with a praise- worthy independence of French sentimentalism, is now publishing a series of figures which show that the 'meditative German" was just as foreseeing in his commercial as in his military self-education. German industry, through the cheapness of raw material and the cheapness of wages, is hitting France far more severely in the pacific arena of com- merce than she has been hit by the same competitor upon the field of war. If one wants to get what are known throughout the world as "Articles de Paris" at the cheapest possible price, it is necessary to buy them in Berlin, Frankfort, Cologne, Strasburg, or some German town! We need hardly say that the bloodless campaign of the modern German is threatening England only in a slightly less degree than it is startling France. During the last ten years-1875-1885—the ex- ports of Germany have increased at the rate of eight million francs, and the imports have in- creased during the same period at the rate of four million francs. Germany and the United States. if their commerce develop at the present ratio, bid fair to be the two richest nations in the world in the first decade of the twentieth century. M. Mar- teau, the French economist, has published his rea- sons for believing that neither France nor England will long be able to hold their own against Ger- many unless an almost revolutionary change is made in the French and English prices of coal, iron, and labour. The average cost of coal in Germany is now little more than 7s a ton, and iron is about .E 2 a ton. The average pay of the German metal worker in the greater factories is 3 marks 20 pfen- ning a day, or 3s 3d in English money; while, in the smaller factories the day's wages is 2 marks 70 pfenning, about 2s Bd. The day lasts for ten hours. In Saxony the pay is much lower; the best paid workman only gets an average of 2s 4d for the day's work, while in Silesia skilled men are glad to work for a daily wage of 15d to 2s.

THE PUBLIC HALL.—Mr. Johnson, secretary to the Public Hall Company, applied to the magistrates at the Borough Court on Monday for the renewal of the dramatic license for the Public Hall in Rylands- street for the next twelve months. The application was granted. SUDDEN DEATH.—John Mallett, widower, 56 years of age, of 149, Church-street, died suddenly on Monday. He had been in failing health for six weeks past, and on Saturday got a "recommend" for the Infirmary. He was seen by Mr Smith, assistant at the Infirmary, who prescribed for him. Deceased, however, died on the following Monday. IMPUDENT ASSAULT.—A young man named James Coyne was fined .E 1 and costs, or a month's im- prisonment in default of payment, by the Borough justices yesterday morning for assaulting John Albert Hughes on Sunday evening. Complainant, who lives at Stockton Heath, Was going home and met defendant and two others on Wilderspool-road. Defendant pushed against him, and on Hughes remonstrating "butted "him. Hughes followed companions with the intention of defendant and his. speaking to a policeman, and when near the Bridge defendant struck him in the face. RETIREMENT OF COLONEL 111ANSERGH.—Colonel Mansergh, who has served in the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment for the last 33 years, this year retires from the command. Col. Mansergh succeeded Colonel Blackburne in the command of the regiment in 1874, and has always been a very popular officer. He leaves his regiment with a good record, for, it is stated, he had in that long period, only been three weeks absent, and had not missed a training. Colonel Mansergh, in addition to his con- nection with the regiment he is leaving, has also served in the 2nd Dragoon Guards, and in the 62nd Regiment. He was also one of the officers of the 2nd. Royal Lancashire Militia, now known as the King's Liverpool Militia, to which he was in 1852 gazetted captain. In the following year he was pro- moted to be major of the 4th Royal Lancashire Militia, now the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment. SIR GILBERT GREENALL AND WALTON CHURCH. —The Rev. L.J. T. Darwall, Vicar of Walton, Much to the surprise of some of the parishioners, did not nominate and thus re-appoint Sir Gilbert Greenall as his warden, at the Easter vestry meeting. The following particulars bearing on the matter are taken from the Walton Parish Magazine for May "The Easter vestry was held on Tuesday, April 26th. The minutes of the last meeting having been read, and the church accounts passed, the Vicar nominated Mr. Turner to be his warden in succession to Sir G. Greenall, and Mr. W. Weir was elected people's warden in succession to his father. While fully respecting local customs and usages one cannot but think it advisable for the present that two en- tirely new wardens should be chosen yearly, in order that the office may fall to each and all of the more substantial parishioners in quick rotation for the first time. And the fatepayers are invited to con- sider whether the establishment of any custom as to a two years' tenure of wardenship might not well be deferred until all these have taken a yearly turn. It would seem the best plan in a new parish such as ours is. The Vicar wishes to throw out this hint for ' consideration, and to explain that this was his sole motive in nominating an entirely new warden rather than promoting the people's warden, whose services to the church he would be the last person to under- value."—lt is gratifying to see that the Vicar recog- nises that the lord of the manor is not the only per- son in the parish entitled to consideration; and it is to be hoped that Sir Gilbert will be satisfied with the explanation. It is to Mr. Darwall's credit that he refused to allow the church bell to be rung, at the Warrington election, to celebrate the Conserve ive victory.

ITI)TIOE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that at a meeting of the Local Authority of the Borough of Warrington. held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday, the 19th day of May, 1886, the said Local Authority, for the purpose of preventing the intro- duction of Swine Fever, made the regulations following, that is to say :- 1. These regulations shall commence and take effect from and immediately after the 27th day of May instant, and shall continue in force until the 24th day of Jure next, unless sooner revoked or altered by the Local Authority of the Borough of Warrington. 2. No swine shall be moved into the Borough of Warring_ ton from the district of any other Local Authority un less a Movement Llcerse be tleat obtained, which shall only be granted on a declaration being made by the owner or his agent to the following effect : (1) That such swine has not been elsewhere than on the farm or lands from which the movement is to be made durlug 28 days immediately preceding the date of the application for the license. (2) That swine fever hAs not existed on such farm or lands, or on any adjo;ning farm or lands. (3) That such swine has not been exposed in any market, fair, exhibition, or public sale within the said 28 days. The foregoing regulations shall not restrict the movement of swine by railway through the Borough of Warrington. Dated this Twenty-second day of May, 1896. WM. KY. BROOK, Town Clerk. N B.—Licenses may be oblained from the Inspector of the Local Authority of this borough. who will also supply forms of declaration above mentioned.
